23000: Specific Dynamic Action (SDA), or the bioenergetic cost of digestion and assimilation, has been studied in fish, amphibians, and reptiles to quantify ecological energy balance, and to understand ecological and evolutionary determinants of digestive function. In comparative studies, researchers often extrapolate their SDA results to common body mass using mass-specific SDA (kJ kg-1) or to common food mass using the SDA coefficient (SDA kJ expressed as % ingested kJ). In both cases, raw data are converted to a ratio which per force assumes that the underlying relationship between component variables is isometric (linear, slope = 1, intercept = 0). Departures from isometry (i.e., allometry) between ratio components are known to result in estimation errors, statistical errors, and spurious correlations. By re-analyzing data from two early and influential publications, and by considering my own work on SDA, I demonstrate that these relationships are actually allometric. By comparing mass-specific estimates (kJ kg-1) to estimates based on regression scaling relationships, I demonstrate that large errors are likely (up to ± 35%) when mass-specific ratios are used. Likewise, I demonstrate that the relationship between SDA and ingested energy is allometric and SDA coefficient is not independent of body size. Therefore, the SDA coefficient should not be used to standardize SDA observations for groups of organisms that differ in body size or meal size. As suggested by numerous previous authors in other contexts, I recommend the abandonment of mass-specific increment and SDA coefficient in favor of more robust statistical techniques (ANCOVA, and allometric scaling relationships) that analyze the raw SDA data.

23001: The relationship between fish, local habitat, catchment characteristics spatial position in riffles of the Maquiné river basin (RS, Brazil) was studied. Results were discussed considering present and historical states of conservation of the basin, which was determined from Landsat TM5 images. Fish data were obtained from qualitative and quantitative sampling. The later involved standardized kick-sampling in 24 riffles. Samples were taken seasonally from August 1999 to June 2000. A total of 72 fish species occur at the Maquiné river basin. Only 3 species occur at the headwaters, 1 at the slope of the Serra Geral and 68 from valley bottoms to the river mouth. Among the later, 20 occur exclusively in valley bottom stream sections and not in Coastal Plain habitats. From these, 8 benthic riffle species were investigated for relations with habitat and catchment characteristics. The spatial pattern of assemblage variation allowed the description of four assemblage types. Assemblages were seasonally persistent and proportional abundance was stable. Although local habitat characteristics have significantly contributed to explain variation in the data, the observed patterns reflected the control of catchment characteristics over local habitat and fish assemblages. Although spatial position was important both at the individual stream and basin scales, assemblage characteristics were also related to catchment area. The state of conservation at the catchment scale did not present evident relationships with fish assemblage characteristics and some hypothesis explaining this finding are discussed.

23002: Obtaining reliable counts of amphibians in disturbed habitats is necessary for understanding the effects of disturbance on amphibian populations. Unfortunately, the detectability of amphibians may change when habitats are degraded, making it difficult to compare population counts across habitats. Plethodontid salamanders have been proposed as indicators of forest health in the United States, though their use depends on similar detectability in different forest types. We used realistic field enclosures to compare the detectability of red-backed salamanders, Plethodon cinereus, among roadside habitats where salamander counts are low and interior forest habitats where salamander counts are high. In both daytime cover object surveys and nightime surface counts, marked salamanders were detected at very similar rates in the two habitat types. These results suggest that surface counts of plethodontid salamanders appear to provide a reliable index of population size, at least across the habitat types studied.

23003: Adult Bufo ictericus are the largest anuran occurring at the Pro-Mata reserve in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil. In order to study the diet composition and the diet shift in this toad, we collected 56 adults (SVL 100-166 mm) and 22 juveniles (SVL 23-100 mm). The specimens were collected between October 2002 and February 2003 at ponds, forests and transitional zones from woodland to grassland. All toads were immediately taken to the laboratory and stomach-flushed. The food items were stored in 70% alcohol, identified and measured under a stereomicroscope. We determined the items to class or order. Coleopterans were identified to family level and Hymenopterans divided into Formicidae and non-Formicidae. 19 stomachs of adult toads and 21 of the juveniles contained food items. For adult toads the most important prey by number was Coleoptera (43.33%), Formicidae (37.78%) and Diplopoda (4.44%). The most frequent prey types consumed by juveniles were Formicidae (80.76%), Coleoptera (9.55%) and Collembola (4.21%). On average 9.37 items were found in the stomachs of the adults and 33.90 in those of the juveniles. Concerning the volume of the different prey types in adults, Diplopoda (73.83%) were followed by Coleoptera (19.67%), Formicidae (1.61%) and Orthoptera (1.01%). In spite of Formicidae being the most important prey type by number for juveniles, their total volume made up only 6.07%. The largest volumes were made up by Lepidoptera larvae (33.78%), Coleoptera larvae (27.98%), Coleoptera (20.42%) and Formicidae (6.07%). These data point out that juveniles capture a large amount of Formicidae, whereas adults capture Formicidae but also feed on larger prey such as Diplopoda and large Coleoptera, which represent a better energetic gain. Our data and additional field observations suggest that juvenile toads actively search for food while adult toads are both active foragers and typical sit-and-wait predators.

23004: We report the relationship between red cod (Pseudophycis bachus) recruitment and environmental variables. Commercial catch data of red cod were used as indices of relative recruitment strength for New Zealand red cod fish stocks (east coast South Island, RCO 3; west coast South Island, RCO 7). Catch was assessed against 34 environmental variables that included the Southern Oscillation index, sea surface temperature, weather types, wind speed and direction, and river flows. Lagged correlations were calculated between annual commercial catch and averaged environmental data. Variables most strongly correlated with commercial catch were included in regression analyses. The strongest correlations between commercial catch and explanatory variables for both RCO 3 and RCO 7 were consistently with sea surface temperature over a wide range of time lags followed by frequencies of southwest and northeast flow patterns. The correlations generally operated in the sense that colder is better: negative correlations (≈ - 0.75) with sea surface temperature, positive with the occurrence of cool southwest weather types, negative with the occurrence of warm northeast weather types. The maximum magnitude of the correlation occurs at 14-month lag for both fisheries, corresponding to the late spring/summer of the year prior to the catch year. The commercial fishery is made up largely of two and three-year- old fish, implying that juvenile fish (age ≈ one year) are most sensitive to environmental conditions, but egg and larval life stages may also be affected. Fluctuations in red cod landings are dependent on sea surface temperature, controlled largely by climatic variability, including El Niño and La Niña events. The regression model was subsequently used to predict commercial catches for the fishing industry with remarkable accuracy, indicating that our model is reflecting the relationship between the environment and some aspect of red cod spawning success or survival.

23005: The general biogeographic pattern displayed by the freshwater fish fauna of the South American coast is apparently dominated by dispersal, which represents a serious problem for the reconstruction of its historical biogeography using phylogenetic hypotheses. Coastal biogeographic reconstructions are particularly difficult in southern Brazil, where many freshwater habitats became available only during the Holocene. Here, I use mitochondrial DNA sequences and microsatellite markers to analyse evolutionary relationships in 322 individuals representing ten lineages of Odontesthes silversides (Atheriniformes: Atherinopsidae) from the coastal plain of southern Brazil. Results support the proposal of a monophyletic silverside radiation that has rapidly diversified into a minimum of one strictly marine taxon, three allopatric and two sympatric freshwater species, and two incipient estuarine species. Four freshwater species displayed high levels of genetic variation and some of the most rapid speciation rates reported in fishes (about 5,000 years), which was interpreted as the result of drift in small and isolated populations, combined with the inherited potential of estuarine silversides to invade new adaptive zones. Interestingly, even considering that the radiation is primitively freshwater, it was the detection of a marine-estuarine stage that enabled the proposal of a biogeographic hypothesis for the group. I propose a scenario of divergence chronologically shaped during the last sea-level changes, when a large aquatic body was broken up in many coastal environments by four major depositional sand barriers. The phylogeographic reconstruction presented here represents a new episode for the study of the biogeography of coastal Neotropical biotas. It makes use of a population-level approach employing molecular markers with high mutation rates to reveal localized freshwater endemism, estuarine incipient speciation, and the influence of recent vicariant events in shaping biological diversification and distribution. The results also open an avenue for future comparative biogeographical studies of regional faunas from temperate South America.

23006: Isolated oceanic archipelagos have played a major role in the development of evolutionary theory by offering a unique setting for studying spatial and temporal patterns of biological diversification. However, the evolutionary events that might cause associations between genetic and geographic variation in archipelago radiations are largely unknown. This is especially true in the Galápagos Islands, where molecular studies have revealed conflicting biogeographic patterns due to the dispersal abilities of taxa studied or to multiple colonizations from the mainland. Here we describe the history of diversification of giant Galápagos tortoises using mitochondrial DNA sequences from 802 individuals representing all known extant populations. By combining large sample sizes and powerful phylogeographic approaches (e.g., nested clade analysis and mismatch analysis) we detect patterns of colonization and lineage sorting highly consistent with the chronological formation of the archipelago. Populations from older islands are composed exclusively of endemic haplotypes that define divergent monophyletic clades. Younger populations, although currently differentiated, exhibit patterns of colonization, demographic variation and genetic interchange shaped by very recent volcanism. Our study also identifies the temporal progression of specific evolutionary events related to volcano emergence and island formation. Colonization probably occurs shortly after a volcano emerges via range expansion from older volcanoes. Volcanism can also create temporal shifts from historical to recurrent events, such as promoting gene flow by creating land bridges between isolated volcanoes. The intimate association of spatial and temporal patterns of genetic variation with geophysical aspects of the environment can be mostly attributed to the limited dispersal and unidirectional migration of giant tortoises following a predominant oceanographic current. The endangered giant Galápagos tortoises represent a compelling and rapid allopatric radiation and further exemplify evolutionary processes in one of the world’s greatest natural laboratories of evolution.

23007: The Amazon basin contains the world’s highest diversity of freshwater fishes. Yet, very little is known about the evolutionary processes shaping biological diversification in the Amazon. Historical and current variations in factors promoting selection gradients, changes in landscape evolution, climate, vegetation and river structure have possibly played different roles in the creation and maintenance of population divergence at regional levels. Thus, an appropriate approach to understand processes underlying species formation in the Amazon is to integrate regional molecular comparative studies with geomorphological, climatic and paleoecological data. We are using modern molecular approaches to describe and compare historical and current patterns of population genetic structure of codistributed igarapé fish species from the Rio Negro basin, central Amazon. Here we present results based on 755 bp of the mtDNA ATPase sequenced for 1,200 individuals of the economically-important ornamental species Carnegiella martae, Paracheirodon axelrodi, Nannostomus unifasciatus and Hemigrammus bleheri. Fish were sampled from 15 igarapés across 700 km of middle and upper Rio Negro (total of 60 codistributed populations). All taxa showed moderate to high levels of genetic variability. Intra- specific comparisons revealed that most populations have reduced phylogeographic structure and experienced a recent scenario of biogeographic divergence. Preliminary analyses using coalescence-based methods suggest that three species possibly share a similar historical pattern, with phylogroups from upper areas of the Rio Negro being older and genetically divergent. Further sampling in upper areas of the river and in nearby basins and data collection using molecular markers with higher mutation rates will enable us to test a number of competing hypotheses about the diversification of Rio Negro flooded forest fishes. We expect that this study will provide useful information for protecting the integrity and diversity of ornamental fishery resources and create a database that can grow by additions of comparable surveys on other groups and habitats.

23008: High mercury (Hg) concentrations have been encountered in Negro river basin populations lost of anthropic Hg sources. Many studies have been conducted in gold mining areas, however, the natural dynamics of Hg in Amazon are poorly known. The objective of this work was to investigate the influence of pH and DOC of the water and of anoxic methylation sites (flooded areas and hydromorphic soils) on the Hg bioaccumulation on Hoplias malabaricus and Cichla spp. of the Negro river basin. Samples were made in 33 localities along this basin. The average of Hg concentration was 0.350 ppm (SD = 0.250) in H. malabaricus and 0.337 ppm (SD = 0.244) in Cichla spp. We made collects lost of antropogenic Hg sources, but 29% of H. malabaricus and 18% of Cichla spp. presented Hg concentrations above 0.5 ppm, indicating high basal Hg levels in Negro river basin. The Hg concentration in Cichla spp. and H. malabaricus increased significantly with the standard length (r2 = 0.655, p = 0.000 and r2 = 0.371, p = 0.000 respectively). Using a multiple regression analysis we observed that flooded areas was positively correlated with Hg concentration in H. malabaricus (p = 0.006) and in Cichla spp. (p = 0.000). This was shown to be the most important environmental factor influencing the bioaccumulation. Hg levels were positive influenced by DOC (p = 0.029) and pH (p = 0.007) in H. malabaricus. DOC and pH had not a significant influence in Hg concentration of Cichla spp (p = 0.452 and p = 0.381), but the tendency was the same. Hydromorphic soils didn't influence the Hg concentration. Fish size, flooded areas, pH and DOC explained most of the variation in Hg concentration (about 85%), but additional studies will be needed to better understand the natural dynamic of Hg.

23009: There is little doubt that global amphibian populations are declining precipitously. The reasons for this decline, however, are less clear. Over the past decade, numerous observational studies have identified a recently described fungus at sites of mass frog mortality. Several of these events occurred in relatively pristine locations. Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis is a member of the phylum Chytridiomycota and has been shown to be transmissible and fatal to amphibians. B. dendrobatidis prefers cooler environments, and frog mass mortality events have been correlated to seasonal cooling. This suggests that the fungus may have significant implications for overwintering aquatic frogs. Additionally, some studies suggest that toe clipping, which is widely used for mark and recapture studies, may also influence the survival of amphibians. The effect of toe clipping on survival of infected individuals was unclear. We obtained 16 spotted frogs (Rana luteiventris), all of which were infected with B. dendrobatidis. We first tested the effect that toe- clipping may have on the survival of infected frogs by clipping the toes of 8 of the 16 frogs. After eight weeks of observation, we found no significant effect of toe clipping on survival. Of the frogs that survived, we brought half of the toe-clipped and half of the non-toe clipped individuals into hibernation (water at 2°C) over the course of two weeks. Hibernating frogs had significantly higher mortality than frogs held at room temperature.

23010: To determine density-dependent effects in juvenile endangered June sucker, Chasmistes liorus, we used enclosures located in Provo Bay in Utah Lake, Utah, USA, to experimentally evaluate growth and survival. Juvenile June sucker were added to enclosures at four densities (corresponding to 24, 44, 84, and 164 fish/m2) during July 2002. Each treatment was replicated 5 times. Water level dropped rapidly during the summer, so fish were removed at 3 (2 replicates) and 5 weeks (3 replicates) after the start of the experiment. We measured growth rate and survival during the experiment. Fish survival and growth varied with density. Poorest growth and survival occurred in the lowest density treatment (24 fish/m2). Highest growth and survival occurred in the second lowest density treatment (44 fish/m2), and higher densities exhibited slight decreases in growth and survival. These data suggest an Allee effect in density-dependent growth and survival of juvenile June sucker. The Allee effect indicates that at some low density, population growth rates may be negative, leading to rapid decline of the population to extinction. Patterns of density-dependent growth of juvenile June sucker should guide efforts to augment the population of June suckers in Utah Lake.

23011: Tidal streams provide grounds for sheltering, feeding, and reproduction for several fish species, some of them found there as adults and other only as juveniles. In this study we aim to identify the main primary defensive tactics used by a fish assemblage dwelling over the sandy bottom of a tidal stream in southeastern Brazil. Observations while snorkeling were done at low tide throughout the day. We focused on fish species which dwell over open areas, thus supposedly more exposed to visually oriented and diurnally hunting predators. The gobies Awaous tajasica, Ctenogobius boleosoma, Evorthodus lyricus, and Gobionellus shufeldti, the flounder Citharichthys spilopterus, and the soles Trinectes microphthalmus and T. paulistanus rely on camouflage, showing a remarkable ability to blend with their sandy background. The mojarra Eucinostomus melanopterus and the snook Centropomus mexicanus are counter-shaded with darker yellowish or grayish on back, silvery on flanks and white on belly. The mullet Mugil curema is counter-shaded and swims within the protection of schools. While close to decaying plants fragments, juveniles of the leatherjacket Oligoplites palometa, the grunt Pomadasys ramosus, and the goby Bathygobius soporator adopt a dark color pattern, and their swimming resembles the movement of waterlogged plant debris drifting in the water current. While moving over open areas or when threatened, P. ramosus closely resembles to and behaves like O. palometa, which presents venom glands on its spines and under such circumstances displays a yellowish and dark brown warning pattern. Thus, the tactics used by most of the sand-dwelling fishes are camouflage and counter-shading, as would be expected in areas lacking shelters. Warning coloration and Batesian mimicry are displayed by one species each, which also use camouflage while close to dark debris. The defensive tactics here reported likely are related to diurnal visually oriented predators such as fishes, herons and kingfishers.

23012: In most vertebrates, cartilage plays just two functional roles – a low friction bearing surface (as in your knees) and contour filler (your nose and ears). However, a successful group of vertebrates, the class Chondrichthyes (sharks, ratfish and rays), has an entirely cartilaginous skeleton implying a far broader range of function for this connective tissue than in other animals. Whereas tetrapod cartilage is quite homogeneous in its response to load and in biochemical composition (within a functional group: bearing surface or contour filler), we have found the cartilage of sharks to be highly variable in material properties. Here we report on the biochemical variation that underlies the large differences that we have found in material properties. Cartilage is a fiber- reinforced composite material, with a network of cross-linked collagen fibers suspended in an aqueous gel of proteoglycans. In four species of shark and one hard-prey crushing stingray we have found four-fold differences in proteoglycan (PG) content and two-fold differences in collagen content. The PG content is very tightly correlated with the resilience of the cartilage from these species. Collagen content also appears to have a significant effect on stiffness and strength. The extreme variation in collagen content raises the possibility of non-collagenous fibrous material in the cartilage.

23013: To complement our ongoing comparative morphological study of fossil and living gars, we made a comparative study of 12s and 16s loci in the mitochondrial genomes of all seven living species (Lepisosteus oculatus, L. osseus, L. platorhynchus, L. platostomus, L. tropicus, Atractosteus tristoechus and A. spatula). We also isolated and sequenced these genes in several outgroup taxa (e.g., Polypterus senegalus, Polyodon spathula, Acipenser brevirostrum, Amia calva, Hiodon alosoides, Osteoglossum bicirrhosum, Pantodon bucholzi, Elops saurus and Megalops atlanticus). We extracted DNA from tissue samples preserved in 95% ethanol using standard phenol-chloroform methods. We amplified our sequences using new primer designs based on our alignments and analyses of published sequence data for 12s and 16s in several lower actinopterygians including L. oculatus and A. spatula (GenBank). PCR reaction products were purified and then sequenced using the amplification primers and an ABI Prism 377 Automated DNA Sequencer (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). Fragments were assembled using Sequencher (GeneCodes, Ann Arbor, MI) and sequences were aligned using ClustalX. We reviewed and fine-tuned the alignments by eye using SeaView. We analyzed the final alignments using PAUP (Sinauer Associates, Sunderland, MA). In all trees recovered, Atractosteus is monophyletic and Amia is the sister group of teleosts. 23014: The genus Microlophus is currently distributed along Pacific coastal desert environments, and throughout the Galapagos Archipelago. Both geographic groups approximately correspond to two assemblages, the peruvianus and the occipitalis groups. The peruvianus group is distributed across a linear range of 5000 km along the coastline of southern Ecuador, Peru, and northern Chile, as well as in some desert inland environments. Three species are predominantly intertidal feeders: M. quadrivittatus, M. atacamensis, and M. peruvianus; whereas M. theresiae, M. heterolepis, M. thoracicus, M. theresioides, M. tigris, M. maminensis, and M. yanezi, are ecological generalists and range from coastal up to 150 km inland. We conducted a preliminary phylogenetic analysis based on several mtDNA gene regions. Preliminary results revealed strong differentiation between all species but M. peruvianus and M. tigris in Peru, but also failed in sorting out phylogenetic relationships within the Chilean clade which includes M. quadrivittatus, M. yanezi, M. atacamensis M. maminensis and M. theresioides. This shallow divergence was investigated by network and nested clade methods, and showed a recent colonization from North to South.

23015: This study tests the hypothesis that the rate of proton (H+) leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane is higher in the slow, oxidative (red) locomotor muscle (RM) than in the fast, glycolytic (white) locomotor muscle (WM) in Scomber japonicus (chub mackerel). The mitochondrial electron transport system pumps protons (H+) out of the mitochondrial matrix, but a significant proportion of the H+ leaks back into the matrix, forming a futile cycle that bypasses ATP production and generates heat. This H+ leak depletes the trans-membrane H+ gradient required for ATP synthesis, as well as the resting membrane potential. Maintaining the H+ gradient and the mitochondrial membrane potential against H+ leak requires the consumption of oxygen, the terminal electron acceptor. We compared the rates of H+ leak in mitochondria isolated by differential centrifugation from RM and WM of the chub mackerel. The H+ leak rate is proportional to the rate of oxygen consumption necessary to maintain a given potential across the mitochondrial membrane when all other routes of H+ movement into the mitochondria are inhibited. Mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate was continuously recorded by a polarographic oxygen electrode, while the membrane potential was determined by measuring how the lipophilic probe, triphenylmethylphosphonium (TPMP+), distributes itself across the mitochondrial membrane. The rate of mitochondrial proton leak was greater in RM than in WM of the chub mackerel. At a membrane potential of approximately 140 mV, RM mitochondria consumed an average of 9.8 ± 3.9 nmol O/min/mg of mitochondrial protein, whereas WM mitochondria consumed only 3.7 ± 1.7 nmol O/min/mg; these values differ significantly (t-test, p = 0.04). The higher rate of mitochondrial H+ leak in the RM compared with the WM correlates with the higher respiration rate expected in the aerobic RM. (Funded by NSF#IBN-9973916 and NIH #2R25GM56625)

23016: The genus Moenkhausia is one of the most speciose within Characidae, with approximately 60 nominal species widespread throughout Neotropical region. Encompasses a great variety of forms occupying many different habitats. The features utilized to diagnose this genus are the same ones proposed by Eigenmann since the beginning of the past century, and are distributed in several other tetragonopterin genera, an indication of its probable paraphyletism. This study is an attempt to recognize putative natural groups inside Moenkhausia. Up to this moment, at least one monophyletic group was identified, the so-called M. intermedia group, supported by characters found in the gill rakers and coloration. The paraphyletic condition of the genus Moenkhausia is clearly demonstrated by the phylogenetic status of M. crisnejas, which is probably more closely related to species of Attonitus and Bryconacidnus. Moenkhausia species from upper Rio Paraná basin are commonly referred as M. intermedia and M. sanctaefilomenae, although both species were originally described from Amazon and upper rio Parnaíba basins respectively. Meristic and morphometric analyses revealed that the forms from upper Rio Paraná basin are distinct species.

23017: The depauperate nature of the Mesoamerican primary freshwater fish fauna stands in stark contrast to the diverse ichthyofauna of South America. With the exception of catfishes in the genus Rhamdia there are no examples of adaptive radiation, perhaps owing to the relatively short period of time since primary fishes have colonized Central America, an hypothesis originally put forward by Miller (1966) and Myers (1966). But as noted by Bussing (1985) the extensive geographic distribution of some Mesoamerican freshwater fishes suggests long occupancy in the region, perhaps dating to the hypothetical proto-Antillean land bridge in the Late Cretaceous or Paleocene. We have used DNA sequences to infer the evolutionary history of all Mesoamerican primary freshwater fishes, and to estimate the temporal scale of diversification through reference to molecular clocks. Although molecular clocks can be notoriously difficult to validate, the extreme difference (>50 Ma) in the temporal predictions of the Bussing versus the Myers and Miller colonization models permits a confident test of the alternative hypotheses. For all Mesoamerican primary fish species, our data reject a Late Cretaceous or Paleocene date, in favor of recent colonization associated with the rise of the Panama Isthmus. Nonetheless, the colonization history of Mesoamerican primary fishes appears to be more complex than envisioned by Myers and Miller, and we posit two or three distinct waves of expansion across the Mesoamerican landscape rather than a single colonization event associated with the Pliocene rise of the Isthmus. In sum, molecular phylogenetics permits the strong inference that the species composition of Mesoamerican freshwater fish communities owes principally to evolutionary history and extrinsic biogeography rather than local ecological processes.

23018: Geminate marine species separated by the Central American Isthmus provide a great opportunity to study the molecular evolution of taxa that have been separated approximately 3 millions years. The rise of the Panamanian Isthmus rendered the continuous range of marine taxa into two large populations, resulting in many pairs of closely related marine species. Because they are numerous, phylogenetically diverse, and are thought to have been separated by the same geologic event, the geminate species pairs provide a remarkably array of organisms in which to investigate nucleotide substitution processes and rate variation in molecular clocks. 23021: The nurseryfish has a unique swim bladder morphology that apparently serves as a peripheral auditory organ through a sensory connection via a lateral line branch of the vagus nerve. The swim bladder is encased and tightly bound laterally to the enlarged but thin 5th to 10th ribs. There are the six dorsolateral extended lobes of the swim bladder on each side that cradle precaudal vertebrae. The caudalmost of these dorsoposterior lobes is the narrowest and most dorsally extended. All these dorsolaterally extended lobes are encased and tightly bound to dorsally extended lobes of the ribs. The integument and lateral musculature overlying these rib extensions are also very thin so that light is easily transmitted through both preserved and fresh specimens resulting in four or five apparent "rib windows". There are no anterior lobes of the swim bladder that could articulate with the neurocranium and the large otoliths of the inner ear. Although the lateral line is restricted to high on the anteriormost part of the body, an enlarged branch of the vagus nerve that normally serves the lateral line extends along the side of the body where no lateral line exists. This nerve exits the vagus foramen of the skull and proceeds posteriorly over the distalmost tips of the swim bladder-rib lobes and attenuates posterior to the rib cage. We hypothesize that this nerve serves as the mechanosensory link for the swim bladder to serve as a peripheral auditory structure.

23023: The growth of aquaculture, recreational and ornamental fisheries in the last decade has caused the introduction of several exotic fishes in the Amazon basin. This study focused on documenting the distribution of three exotics species in the region: the common guppy (Poecilia reticulata), tilapia (Oreochromis sp.), and the threespot gourami (Trichogaster trichopterus). These exotic fishes are well adapted to the urban streams (igarapés), where waters are contaminated. Established populations of threespot gourami (T. trichopterus) were found in the Igarapé São Raimundo and São Vicente of Manaus. Threespot gourami has even been traded as “native” ornamental fish from São Gabriel da Cachoeira (850 km up the Rio Negro). Arapaima farms (Arapaima gigas) in Maracapuru and Itacoatiara are rearing gourami as feeder fish. Poecilia reticulata was found in the Igarapé São Raimundo and water discharged the facilities of ornamental fish exporters near Manaus. It has also been collected from the sewage runoffs in Barcelos (400 km up the River Negro). Hybrid tilapias (Oreochromis spp.) are cultivated in local fish farms and recreational fishing ponds. Tilapias were introduced to the lake of Balbina Hydroelectric Dam and found in the Igarapé Mindú of Manaus. Populations of cardinal tetra (Paracheirodon axelrodi) and species of Carnegiella, Apistogramma, and Corydoras have been established in Igarapé Tarumã and Igarapé Acará near Manaus, where they are not native to the area. Brazilian laws currently only have restrictions on cultivation of African sharptooth catfish (Clarias gariepinus), and North American channel catfish (Ictalurus punctatus). The transshipment of indigenous ornamental fishes among watersheds in the Amazon basin is not regulated. Governmental agencies are often advocating exotic species introduction to boost aquaculture productions. (CNPq no. 46.6098/2001-4 & 550367/2001-2).

23024: We studied the effects of the structural habitat, thermal ecology and social environment on the reproductive behavior of eight species of treefrogs in the genus Scinax, a genus that includes species exhibiting great diversity of calling and locomotor behavior during the breeding season. The species included in this study reproduce over a wide range of temperatures and in different types of habitat, which reflect interspecific differences in reproductive season, geographical distribution and spatiotemporal selection of microhabitat. There is significant variation among the eight species in call structure and rates of call production; species in the ruber group produce simple calls at relatively high rates and low to moderate frequencies. These species also tend to use standing water in open areas or forest edges for breeding. Species from the catharinae and perpusillus groups produced calls at relatively low rates, and calls were more complex and higher in frequency. Breeding sites for these species tend to be restricted to forested habitats. A notable difference in calling behavior of the species from the catharinae group was the high proportion of silent males in the chorus. In general, species with high calling rates also had high rates of locomotion, and are active at higher temperatures. One exception was S. crospedospilus, which has an extremely high calling rate, but exhibits among the lowest rates of locomotion and activity temperatures. The outstanding ecological diversity of Scinax seems paralleled by comparable behavioral diversity in which complex calls delivered at lower rates and simple calls produced at high rates represent extremes of the range of calling behavior. We propose that this apparent dichotomy observed in the genus reflects, in part, constraints on sound propagation imposed by structural characteristics of the microhabitats.

23025: Three new troglobitic (exclusively subterranean) trichomycterid catfishes, Ituglanis bambui sp. n., Ituglanis epikarsticus sp. n. and Ituglanis ramiroi sp. n. are described from different cave systems in São Domingos karst area, State of Goiás, Central Brazil. 23026: I studied the evolutionary relationships and parental care behaviors of an assemblage of 19 species of microhylid frogs from a mid-elevation site in Papua New Guinea. 23027: We examined the relative influence of local versus regional environmental factors on fish assemblage structure using a database of fish collections from 170 sites across Texas. Correspondence analysis (CA) was used to compare local fish assemblage structure without the influence of environmental factors. The effect of sub-basin on fish assemblage structure was significant (MANOVA p < 0.001). Canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was performed twice using species relative abundances and either local or regional environmental factors. Non-significant and redundant environmental factors were removed from both analyses, and remaining factors were combined in a subsequent CCA to evaluate relative influences of local versus regional parameters on local fish assemblage structure. Species were classified into trophic (omnivore, herbivore, invertivore, piscivore) and tolerance (intolerant, intermediate, tolerant) groupings based on previously published literature, and relationships with environmental factors were evaluated using CCA. In addition, we used multiple regression to evaluate the relationships between two measures of diversity (Shannon- Weiner diversity and species richness) and environmental factors. 23028: Boa constrictors originating from islands off the coast of Belize have been entering the pet trade since the 1970s. 23029: Juvenile Trachemys scripta callirostris were obtained opportunistically to provide samples for an initial electrophoretic survey. 23030: Frogs belonging to the Bufo margaritifera complex are often highly polymorphic for dorsal color and pattern characteristics. 23031: The genus Rhamdiopsis is a relatively rare Neotropical taxon, until now known only from its type species, R. moreirai, from the upper Rio Iguaçu, southern Brazil, and R. microcephala, from the upper Rio São Francisco, southeastern Brazil. 23032: The unisexual Ambystoma found in eastern North America present a confusing array of diploid and polyploid individuals and populations. 23033: Coccidia are intracellular protozoan parasites of all classes of vertebrates that live in the digestive tract epithelium and other tissues of their hosts. 23034: Trematodes such as frog lung and bladder flukes have complicated life cycles that include 3 hosts: a first intermediate mollusk host, a second intermediate arthropod or vertebrate host, and a vertebrate definitive host. 23035: We studied activity rhythms in six species of balitorid fishes from Thailand. 23036: Estuaries are significant, essential habitat for more than 85% of the fish species that inhabit coastal areas. Many estuaries have experienced a long-term trend of increasing environmental stress due to increasing human activities along their shores. Various environmental stressors have affected fish biodiversity and productivity in these biotopes. Moreover, each fish brings with it a growth history (through its otolith annuli) that can be used to evaluate the impact of suspected estuarine stressors. 23039: The relationship between sensory-bias and the origin of female mating choice was investigated in the pentamorphic livebearing fish, Poecilia parae, because a possible non-sexual origin of female mate choice was recently elucidated for its close relative, the guppy, P. reticulata. Female P. parae chose carotenoid- and pteridine-colored males as mates, preferring yellow and red melanzona morphs when given a choice among the five distinct male morphs, blue, red, and yellow melanzona, parae with a colorful caudal patch, and female-like immaculata matched for size. These preferences may have originated because it enabled female P. parae to obtain high-quality mates. Field and laboratory tests indicated that free-living and wild caught adult P. parae of both sexes, outside a mating context, nibbled more often at orange, red, and yellow discs than at green and blue discs, and never at white and black discs. Our results also indicated that an innate attraction to colored inanimate objects correlated with female mate choice for colorful males in yet another Poecilia species. This is the second study to show both an association between a potential trigger of a mate-choice preference and a sexually selected trait. These results corroborate the sensory-bias hypothesis for the evolution of female mating choice in P. parae.

23040: Most diurnal reptiles in deserts use shelters during nighttime. Nevertheless, Ctenophorus isolepis, an agamid from Australian sandy deserts, sleeps above ground. We investigated in the Simpson Desert three non-exclusive hypotheses to explain this habit: 1. C. isolepis does not have and /or cannot dig burrows. 2. Burrow temperatures in this area are too hot at night and impose heavy metabolic costs. 3. The risk of predation in burrows is too high. From 53 sleeping sites we recorded sand surface temperatures, percent cover of vegetation, a description of the site and the settling time of the lizard. Data were also recorded from C. nuchalis that coexists on some of the dunes, faces similar conditions, yet regularly uses nighttime burrows. A comparison between the two species may point out reasons for their different behaviors. Most C. isolepis settled within 20 minutes of sunset in one of six different types of sleeping site. Most sleeping sites were near, under or on small plants. Observations indicated that C. isolepis, even those that possess daytime burrows, hardly ever use burrows at nighttime. Calculations based on soil temperatures and metabolic rates suggest that for C. isolepis a night in a burrow would cost 24% of its daily energy expenditure, but for C. nuchalis, only 10% of the daily expenditure. The two agamids differ in their habitat too: C. nuchalis mainly inhabits areas that have been recently burnt or that have only low vegetation cover, while C. isolepis is active in more vegetated parts of the dunes, where much higher presence of predators was observed. We conclude that C. isolepis sleeps aboveground not because of a lack of burrows, rather due to a combination of physiological cost and predation risk.
23041: Intertidal fish assemblages of central California and central Chile have no species in common and only two of the twelve represented families in common. These assemblages have similar feeding guild structures despite their taxonomic disparity. The relationship between morphology and diet was examined for 14 species of Californian fishes and 13 species of Chilean fishes (in progress). The purpose of this study was to determine: (1) if there is a relationship between dietary and morphological similarities; (2) if there are unique morphological configurations associated with a particular feeding guild; and (3) the degree of similarity between the morphologies of the Californian feeding guilds and their Chilean counterparts. Twelve morphological measurements of features potentially related to feeding were made: standard length, head length, head depth, head width, eye diameter, head length with jaws protruded, mouth width, mouth height, orientation of open mouth, gill raker number, gill arch length, and gut length. Linear regression revealed no assemblage-wide relationship between dietary and morphological similarities, but a significant relationship between taxonomic relatedness and morphological similarity was found. Principal components analysis of morphological variables relative to body size revealed considerable overlap in morphology between the four Californian feeding guilds: carnivores, microcarnivores, polychaete feeders, and omnivores. The microcarnivorous guild is the most diverse in morphology, and the carnivore guild is the most specialized in morphology. Results from the morphological study of Chilean fishes (in progress) will be discussed and compared to the assemblage of California.

23042: Humans are constantly changing the environment, often by altering and fragmenting habitat. Recently, scientists have become interested in using remote sensing as a tool to quantify habitat change and fragmentation, and examine their potential effects on plant and animal populations. The long-term goal of this project is to correlate habitat change and fragmentation with the health of amphibians in western Kentucky. Amphibians are a potential group of indicator species, which are sensitive to environmental stress. Scientists use indicator species as an early warning system for environmental problems. As a first step, this study focused on quantifying habitat change and fragmentation. Using LandSat 7 ETM+ images and GIS software, I created land cover maps for 1994/95 and 2000/01. Using these maps, I examined change over time and fragmentation. The initial analyses indicated that the majority of the habitat changed from one type to another during the five-year interval. The change has been predominantly of four types: cropland becoming grassland (and vice-versa), cropland becoming deciduous forest, and grassland becoming deciduous forest. Fragmentation analyses showed that there are an increased number of patches (higher fragmentation) in agricultural areas compared to less disturbed areas. In addition, the patches in agricultural areas are smaller with more edge than those in less disturbed areas. After quantifying habitat change and fragmentation, I will compare the results to those on amphibian health to better understand how remote sensing might be used to better manage and conserve amphibian populations.

23043: Smooth puffers (Tetraodontidae) have the smallest genome size of any vertebrate measured to date (0.4 picograms haploid versus 3.5 pg for humans and a mean of 1.0 pg for all non-polyploid teleosts). We used flow cytometry to measure genome size in 15 species belonging to 6 tetraodontiform families. Very small genome sizes (< 0.5 pg) are found only within the smooth puffers, and substantially larger genome sizes (0.8 pg) are found in the two closest outgroups, Diodontidae and Molidae. Parsimony analysis of this pattern indicates that the plesiomorphic condition for Molidae (Diodontidae, Tetraodontidae) is a genome size of 0.8 pg, and the tiny genome size of smooth puffers is a derived character unique to tetraodontids. However, an alternative explanation is that the ancestor of Tetraodontidae acquired a heritable tendency toward decreasing genome size, such as a new or modified deletion mechanism, and that genome size in all of the tetraodontid lineages has been decreasing in parallel since the split from Diodontidae. Previous workers have proposed that the loss of anatomical parts in puffers (no ribs, no pelvis, few vertebrae) might be related to the loss of genetic material in these fishes. Our results do not support this hypothesis because molids and diodontids are missing just as many bits and pieces as smooth puffers, yet they do not have equally small genomes. Within the other families of tetraodontiform fishes sampled, small genome size (< 0.6 pg) appears to have evolved independently in some members of Monacanthidae, and the largest tetraodontiform genome sizes (> 1.0 pg) are found in some members of Ostraciidae.

23044: Reservoirs are ecologically important artificial environments due to the great changes caused by its implantation. The new conditions are either adverse or attractive to fish species which can present several sorts of biological responses. Sorubim lima is an abundant species found in South America reservoirs. Herein we provide the Serra da Mesa reservoir (Central Brazil) as an example of the attraction of this pimelodid fish. The captures with gill nets were carried out on 8 reservoir sites and 4 river sites, from Dec/95 to Dec/02, encompassing the periods: before dam construction - River phase; during the reservoir formation - Filling phase; and after beginning of dam operation - Operation phase. Only 7 individuals of a total of 1907 were captured in the River phase. The abundance values both the Filling and Operation phases were not significant different. Larger specimens were found in the Operation phase in reservoir sites. However, the lowest condition factor (K) was registered in the Operation phase. Most reproductive individuals (97.14%) were captured in the Operation phase. No reproductive individuals were found in the Filling phase. It suggests that this population was growing in the reservoir area but only completed its reproduction cycle in the Operation phase when the stabilization process has began. A non-standardized capture revealed the presence of S. lima in the pelagic area indicating that this species is probably able to cross the reservoir area. The original stretch of the studied Tocantins River was a fast-flowing stream which ran through a narrow river valley. The lentic environment of the reservoir has clearly furnished better conditions to the establishment of a permanent S. lima population. Factors like water flow reduction, increment of prey and shelters availability, due to the vegetation submerging, must have influenced the habitat choice of this carnivorous catfish.

23045: Subfamilial phylogenetic relationships within the family Scincidae, (as well as relationships within the subfamily 'Scincinae') are inferred using partitioned Bayesian analyses of 2700 bp of mtDNA. The analysis includes all three genera of Acontinae, one genus of Feylininae, five genera of Lygosominae (representing the five major clades) and 22 of ~29 genera of 'Scincinae'. Scincid monophyly is strongly supported, as is the monophyly of acontines and lygosomines. However, 'Scincinae' is polyphyletic. The deepest divergence within Scincidae is between East Asian and North American 'Eumeces' (including Neoseps) and all other skinks. This latter clade includes a strongly supported clade of African, Malagasy, and Middle Eastern skinks exclusive of the Lygosominae and the East Asian 'scincine' Brachymeles. Deeper relationships within this clade are not well supported except for: 1) a clade containing 'Eumeces' schneideri, Scincopus and Scincus, and 2) a large clade of Southern African and Malagasy (and surrounding islands) 'scincines', Chalcides, Sphenops, and feylinines. It has been suggested that feylinines are not skinks and warrant recognition as a rank equal to Scincidae, but the phylogenetic analysis strongly rejects the hypothesis of a non-scincid relationship for Feylinia. The monophyly of the acontine 'Typhlosaurus' and the speciose 'scincine' genera, 'Eumeces' and 'Amphiglossus' are strongly rejected The analysis also rejects the close relationship of Gongylomorphus to Janetascincus and Pamelascincus - three 'scincine' genera possessing a derived condition of the secondary palate. The phylogenetic placement of Ophiomorus and the 'Eumeces' schwartzei group remain unclear. Partitioned Bayesian analyses (estimating specific model parameters for different partitions of the mtDNA) result in an improved explanation of the data as measured by mean – lnL. However, how one identifies partitions heavily influences this outcome. Partitioning the protein-coding genes by codon position shows the greatest improvement of the mean – lnL and results in the inference of relationships not supported by other less-partitioned analyses.

23046: The Cerrado is a savana-like vegetation that covers about 2 million km2 of Brazil. Despite the frequent ocurrence of fire in this habitat, the effects of fire on anuran assemblages in the Cerrado are still unknown. We compare pre and post-fire frog diversity at a preserved area of Cerrado (Itirapina Ecological Station; 2.400 ha) in southeastern Brazil. We gathered data for two fire events (July 2000 and July 2001). Frogs were sampled with pitfall traps. Sampling was done for five days twice each month from April 2000 to March 2002. For statistical analyses, the sampling was divided into two periods of time: peridod 1, April 2000 to July 2001; period 2, April 2001 to March 2002. Each 3-month period was treated as a sample. In period 1, a total of 774 individuals of ten species were captured and Physalaemus fuscomaculatus was the dominat species both in burned and unburned areas. In period 2, a total of 356 individuals of nine species were captured and P. fuscomaculatus was the dominant species only in burned areas; Physalaemus gr. cuvieri was the dominat species in unburned areas. Compared to unburned areas, burned areas showed a significant increase in relative abundance of most frog species for a short period (3-6 months) after the fires. Species richness was similar before and after the fire at both periods of study in burned and unburned areas. Fire drastically alters habitat structure, although the vegetation recovers almost completely in a relatively short time (3-6 months). The relative abundance of frogs became similar in burned and unburned areas when the vegetation of burned areas is completely recovered. Our results indicate that fires have no negative effect on Cerrado frog diversity. Funded: FAPESP.

23047: Most information on behavioral ecology of the genus Necturus is based on one species, N. maculosus. Only isolated information concerning the other four members of the genus is available and primarily addresses taxonomic issues. Although the natural history and ecology of N. beyeri have been studied by various researchers, no information about the Texas populations of this species is currently available. As part of a study designed to advance our understanding of the biology of N. beyeri, we have documented the habitat preferences of a population in eastern Texas. Seventy-five minnow traps were placed every ten meters in Hill Creek (Smith Co. TX) and checked once per week from March 2002 to April 2003. Animals trapped were measured, sexed, weighed, and uniquely identified using a Passive integrated transponder (PIT tag). After this process, the animals were released where they were collected. In every trap location, biotic and abiotic variables were recorded for the aquatic environment (dissolved oxygen, temperature, pH, width and length of the creek, current velocity, amount of logjams) and for the surrounding habitat (rainfall, temperature, canopy coverage, shape and angle of the bank). These environmental variables were analyzed with respect to the number of N. beyeri captured at every site using principal components analysis (PCA) and discriminant function analysis (DFA). Preliminary results from the DFA indicate that stream width, depth and substrate were the most important variables for explaining the variation in trap success. These results suggest that N. beyeri has habitat preferences that are similar to those of other Necturus species in the southern United States. More details of the habitat preferences of N. beyeri and differences in habitat use between sexes and ages will be discussed.

23048: It has long been suspected that environmental stressors can increase susceptibility to disease. We designed two experiments to examine the effects of environmental stressors on amphibians in the presence of a naturally-occurring pathogen. In the laboratory, we exposed spotted salamander larvae (Ambystoma maculatum) to the pesticide carbaryl, UV-B radiation, and the pathogenic fungus Saprolegnia and recorded time to mortality. In field mesocosms, we exposed southern leopard frog (Rana sphenocephala) tadpoles and spotted salamander larvae to carbaryl and Saprolegnia and recorded survival, size at metamorphosis, length of the larval period and, for tadpoles, percent lipid content. In the laboratory, larvae exposed to all three stressors died more quickly than larvae in other treatments. In the mesocosms, both carbaryl and Saprolegnia reduced the survival of both amphibian species. Tadpoles exposed to both stressors had the lowest survival. Carbaryl, as well as the interaction between carbaryl and Saprolegnia, promoted greater mass at metamorphosis for tadpoles. This study illustrates the importance of examining multiple factors (both natural and anthropogenic) simultaneously when attempting to determine causes for amphibian declines.

23049: In contrast to other vertebrates, amphibians have diverse modes of respiration. The lungs and the buccopharyngeal surfaces are the internal respiratory structures; however, considerable gas exchange takes place cutaneously in terrestrial amphibian. The breathing occur when the nostrils are open and the buccal floor is depressed, air is drawn into buccal cavity; closure of the nostrils and elevation of the buccal floor concomitant with the opening the glottis forces air into the lung. A respiratory cycle is a single cycle of inhalation and exhalation. In normal breathing of mammalian, the most important respiratory muscles are the diaphragm and the external intercostals. Basically the lungs of amphibians are paired organs with great distension capacity, and the pulmonary membrane is folded to form internal septa, which are highly vascularized and covered with a thin epithelium except along their inner edges where ciliated and mucous cells are present. Fragments of the lung of Bufo ictericus was processed according to the standard histologic technique for paraffin embedding in order to characterize the support tissue of the pulmonary parenchyma. The lung of Bufo ictericus is a saclike structure, and from the external wall septa extends into the lumen. Bundles of smooth muscle wall provide a substantial support to the septa, and can represent an active intrapulmonary diaphragm important in the expiration process of the air for the toad.

23050: Many snakes follow a foraging strategy characterized by the ingestion of relatively large alimentary items after long fasting intervals. In these "sit-and-wait" species, the digestive tract is down-regulated during fasting period and, following meal ingestion, dramatic changes in morphology and physiology occur. In this study we investigate the morphological changes of the small intestine and liver in response to feeding in boa (Boa constrictor) and the South-American rattlesnake (Crotalus durissus terrificus). We used ultrasonography (Sonosite 180, 10MHz linear scanner) to access changes in organ size under fasting and feeding conditions. Moreover, histological examinations of the small intestine and liver were made in fasting and fed (48 hours after feeding) snakes. In both species, the tickness of the small intestine mucosa increased significantly after feeding reaching a maximum increase in the fourth day after feeding. Thus, the morphological changes in the small intestine of boas and rattlesnake in response to feeding reached maximum levels later than previously reported for Burmese python or garter snakes (~48 hours after feeding). The surface of villi did not increase significantly and few lipid droplets were incorporated into the enterocytes following meal ingestion by boas and rattlesnakes. However, these results were probably caused by the premature sampling of tissues (two days after feeding). Cross sectional diameter of the liver increased soon after feeding in both species, but this increase was not significant in either. The good body condition of the experimental animals, even during fasting, may let no room for any substantial increases in organ size following feeding. Indeed, the hepatocytes of both species were found to be still loaded with lipid droplets even after 30 days of fasting.

23051: The phylogenetic position of the superfamily Loricarioidea is one of the most intriguing questions in the systematics of Siluriformes. Loricarioidea is the largest demonstrably monophyletic group of catfishes in the neotropics, and its relationships to other members of the order has potentially important biogeographical and evolutionary implications. Despite some previous proposals, the problem cannot be considered as satisfactorily settled. In order to resolve the issue, a large-scale phylogenetic analysis was conducted, including all major clades of Siluriformes. A total of 331 morphological characters were coded for 114 taxa representing all recent catfish families. Strict parsimony analysis of the data resulted in 96 trees, with CI=0,30 and RI =0,78. The hypothesis strongly supports a sister group relationship between Loricarioidea and the African family Amphiliidae. That idea has been tentatively proposed previously, but on the basis of relatively weak evidence. Here, the group composed of Loricarioidea plus Amphiliidae is supported by a total of 16 character-state transitions, two of which homoplasy-free: a posterior expansion on the second epibranchial, and a unique ventral process on the fifth vertebral centrum. The clade is comparatively robust, with high Bremer support. The clade composed of loricarioids plus amphiliids is the sister group to the superfamily Sisoroidea. This whole assemblage, in turn, is the sister group to most remaining siluriforms. The cladogram obtained also includes a number of additional hypotheses of relationships which are relevant for the understanding of catfish phylogeny, including resolution of the phylogenetic position of Cranoglanididae, Ictaluridae, Doradoidei, and other suprafamilial clades. The sister group relationship between Loricarioidea and Amphiliidae is an obvious South-American/African biogeographical component.

23052: The anterior vertebrae in members of the evolutionarily highly successful Otophysi are modified into a sound transmitting system that forms part of the Weberian apparatus. 23054: Declines in amphibian populations have led to sustained interest in the interactions of possible causal factors such as disease, UV-B and contamination by agricultural chemicals. Chemical contaminants may also interact with biotic and abiotic factors, which could modify their effects on anuran development. Therefore, realistic experimental designs that integrate the interactive effects of different kinds of stressors acting at different phases of an amphibian's life are needed. I reared eggs of the Australian frog Litoria peronii at two different temperatures, maintained the resulting tadpoles at a common temperature, and subsequently exposed them for 95-h to environmentally relevant concentrations of the organochlorine insecticide endosulfan. Endosulfan is used extensively throughout the world and often contaminates aquatic environments. Endosulfan significantly reduced feeding and modified tadpole behavior (this behavior changed with egg rearing temperature). Tadpoles exposed to endosulfan were more vulnerable to capture by dragonfly larvae when tested 24 days later; this response was dependant on egg rearing temperature. Thus, 1) short-term exposure to concentrations of endosulfan similar to those recorded in the field, significantly affected feeding, behavior and predator avoidance; 2) different egg-rearing temperatures altered tadpole behavior and their ability to avoid predators; 3) the effects of egg-rearing temperature and endosulfan were interactive. Consequently, brief contact with endosulfan in natural conditions may also alter future components of fitness. Likewise, the conditions that a tadpole experiences as an embryo (such as minor, short-term shifts in temperature) may potentially alter the effects of some agrochemicals. Thus, it appears that successive exposure to superficially benign conditions can massively impact on subsequent viability. These trials highlight the need to test interactions between parameters of potential ecological importance over the long-term if we are to evaluate possible consequences of anthropogenic contamination in natural communities.

23055: Successful management of herpetofauna relies on integrated management of ecological and physiological research data. In southern California, the Western Ecological Research Center of the US Geological Survey is working with researchers, city, county, state and Federal resource agencies to develop strategies to supply data that meets these management needs. Land managers and regulators rely on access to the most current and applicable research data available in making sound decisions to conserve reptile and amphibian diversity in perpetuity. Integrated data management allows researchers, agencies and consultants to share non-sensitive information regarding their independent research, inventory and monitoring projects. Several data management strategies ranging from local and regional partners to Federal partners from the Departments of Interior, Defense and Agriculture that are collaborating in the national USGS program ARMI (Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative) were examined to determine how to meet needs of the managers. Federal and university researchers and statisticians also contributed greatly to impart study design needs and capabilities and to insure data of highest value. Together, these concepts provided a base on which a strategy could be developed. To develop the data management strategy that is currently being tested by USGS, several goals needed to be accomplished. Stringent database development has provided a backbone structure that can meet the needs of the managers and still provide flexibility for the researchers. Networking solutions have been developed to allow secure access to managers and researchers whether centrally located or at remote locations. Multiple data entry and recall tools have been developed to meet the demands of different study designs, including full digital data collection utilizing hand held computers with standardized forms, queries and reports. Coupled with sound science, this strategy of integrated data management will be of great benefit to the researchers and an invaluable tool to land mangers.

23056: Growth and mortality parameters of liseta Leporinus muyscorum were estimated used length frequency data (ELEFAN) from January to December 2000 (n = 1698). Total length (TL), Fork length (FL) and Standard length (SL) in centimeter and total weight (TW) in gram were measured. The class interval was of 1 cm. The estimated values for asymptotic length (Linf.), growth rate (K) and age at zero length (t0) were 45.7 (± 0.14) cm, 0.29 (± 0.02) year -1 and -0.51 years, respectively, with average environmental temperature taken as 28 °C and 95% confidence intervals. Average performance growth index (prime phi) was 2.78. Total mortality (Z) estimated was 1.82 (± 0.17) year-1 with 95% of confidence intervals, natural mortality (M) 0.71 year-1 and mortality by fishing (F) 1.11 year-1. Exploitation rate (E = F/Z) was 0.61, the mean length at first capture (Lc) 22.4 cm TL and the mean length in the catch 25.8 cm TL. Estimations of asymptotic length and growth rate suggest that liseta is a fish with longevity and growth rate medium, and the performance growth index is closely to another report for Leporinus friderici, an coespecific fish from French Guyana. In this work, 1545 individuals (91%) were captured under the mean length in the catch (31.1 cm TL) established by INPA and the exploitation rates values confirm over fishing. The increase in the catch of this species may be due that liseta is becoming replacement species because of possible scarcity of greater commercial value fishes. The liseta fishery is being supported by very small and very young individuals, therefore over fishing on recruitment and growth is observed and it is inferred that the situation is critical for this species. This should be considered by the fishery assessment agency in order to regulate the fishery in the Sinu river basin.
23057: (1) Salamanders show greater diversity in life histories than other vertebrate taxa of equivalent rank. The biphasic life cycle with a complex metamorphosis is probably the ancestral life-history mode, whereas paedomorphosis and direct development are common derived modes. (2) The larviparous and (especially) pueriparous life histories in the genus Salamandra can be considered the most derived of all urodelan life histories. (3) Larval morphology is correlated with habitat adaptation in salamanders. Larval periods tend to be shorter in pond- than in stream-breeding populations/species, and in low- versus high-elevation populations/species. (4) Salamanders show pronounced variation in age at metamorphosis and age at first reproduction. It seems obvious that these traits have been relatively free to evolve independently. The relationship between the endocrine axes regulating these two important life-history transitions, and the mechanism of disengagement of the two axes in the evolution of paedomorphosis and direct development, are two unresolved questions. (5) Salamanders tend to have greater ages at first reproduction, longer generation times, and greater life expectancies than other small ectothermic vertebrates; these differences are related to behavioral and other adaptations that reduce mortality risks. (6) In oviparous salamanders, clutch size tends to increase with body size in many taxa; the form of the relationship varies with reproductive mode. The general trend suggests the operation of fecundity selection. (7) In conclusion, the extreme diversification in life-history modes in this relatively small taxon is probably related to the lack of morphogenetic and morphological specialization, in comparison with vertebrates generally, and with anurans and caecilians specifically, in a taxon in which the ancestral life history was biphasic.

23058: This presentation evaluates variation in age and body size at metamorphosis in the desmognathine and hemidactyliine lineages of plethodontid salamanders, in the context of several theoretical models of amphibian metamorphosis. The principal models under consideration are those of Wilbur and Collins (1973), Smith-Gill and Berven (1979), Werner (1986), Rowe and Ludwig (1991), and Day and Rowe (2002). In plethodontids the data for testing the model derive mainly from descriptive life-history studies of members of the Eurycea bislineata complex, and from experimental studies of several other species. Reaction norms of age and size at metamorphosis predicted by these theories and the realized reaction norms observed in plethodontids show poor agreement generally. One likely explanation is that biphasic plethodontids are basically stream- adapted salamanders, wherein the larval forms inhabit relatively unproductive yet hydrologically reliable aquatic environments. In contrast, the theoretical models cited above have been formulated primarily for pond-breeding amphibians that utilize habitats that are more productive but less reliable than those of their stream-breeding counterparts.

23059: Virtually no information on the inheritance of the ability to produce sounds exists for fishes. In birds, which usually provide extensive post-hatching parental care, acoustic signals are leaned in some species but innate in others. Almost no fishes provide extensive post-hatching parental care, providing little opportunity to hear and learn sounds produced by the parents (usually the male in fishes). We used a minnow, Codoma ornata, to test whether sound production is learned from the parents or innate. Fertilized eggs of this species were raised in isolation from adults. Upon maturity, these fish were tested for sound production during aggressive and spawning contexts. Fish which had no contact with adults, and therefore no opportunity to hear the acoustic signals of their species, produced sounds that were similar to their parents and produced under the same contexts. Since no opportunity for learning existed, this provides evidence that the ability to produce sounds is innate in this minnow species.

23060: The genus Pareiorhina was proposed by Gosline (1947) to include a single species, Rhinelepis rudolphi Miranda Ribeiro (1911), from the Paraíba do Sul river drainage. Pareiorhina rudolphi is a relatively small species, quite different from the large-sized species of Rhinelepis. While studying the fish fauna of the southwestern portion of the Serra da Mantiqueira in southeastern Brazil, we found an undescribed loricariid species that is very similar to P. rudolphi. The new species is distinguished from P. rudolphi by the relatively wider cleithral width, the presence of a conspicuous papilla located inside the mouth posterior to the upper jaw, the presence of odontoids in the tip of the snout, and the presence of a lateral cusp in the teeth, among other characters. The presence of bicuspid teeth in the new species requires a reevaluation of the characters traditionally associated with the diagnosis of the genus Pareiorhina. We provisionally include the new species in Pareiorhina based on the shared presence of a pair of dorso-lateral ridges in the caudal peduncle. This character, however, is not unique and requires further study of relationships among Pareiorhina, Kronichthys, and undescribed taxa apparently related to Corymbophanes. 23061: The Characidiinae comprise 83 nominal species of Neotropical freshwater fishes, of which we recognize 74 as valid. The group also includes several undescribed species, mostly in the genus Characidium Reinhardt (1866). Phylogenetic relationships within the group were analyzed cladistically by Buckup (1993). Subsequent descriptions of new species and new genera by A. Zarske (Geryichthys), and Presswell, Weitzman & Bergquist (Skiotocharax) led us to reevaluate that hypothesis of relationships. Our analysis includes 42 taxa representing all valid genera. Six new morphological characters were added to the original matrix, totaling 70 characters. A parsimony analysis using cladistic methodology produced 870 equally parsimonious cladograms (CI=0.45, RI=0.80). Differences among these cladograms mostly involve rearrangements among species of Characidium. According to the strict consensus cladogram, Microcharacidium geryi Zarske (1997) is more closely related to a subset of species of Characidium than to any species of Microcharacidium Buckup (1993). Similarities between M. geryi and Microharacidium are more parsimoniously interpreted as convergences, and the species must be removed to the genus Characidium. The analysis also indicates that recognition of Geryichthys Zarske (1997) as a valid genus would render Characidium paraphyletic. Geryichthys sterbai Zarske (1997) is closely related to a group of species of Characidium with incomplete lateral line, and the monotypic Geryichthys must be included in the synonymy of Characidium. 23062: In species of prolonged breeding the males defend their territories through acoustic communication and or you physical combat. The aim of this work was to verify the effect of the density in the spacing pattern among the individuals of Scinax centralis. The observations were made in a creek in the Floresta Nacional (FLONA), IBAMA, municipality of Silvania, Goias. The number of calling males and rate of advertisement calls were larger in the density 8, while, proportionally, there were more calling males of the density 4. The distance for the nearest neighbor decreased with the increase in the density. The pattern of space distribution observed for S. centralis in experimental conditions was not very different from the observed in natural conditions, always tending to uniformity. Though, as the density increases (4 for 8 males/m2), the random pattern becomes more frequent. The maintenance of the uniform space distribution for males of S. centralis indicates that it would be an important resource for the individual reproductive success.

23063: The Turtle Conservation Fund (TCF) was created in 2002. The primary purpose is two-fold: First, to serve as a fund-raising mechanism for turtle conservation priorities, and second, to help prioritize and coordinate communication among the many individuals and institutions that are involved worldwide with turtle conservation activities. Thus, the TCF is not a turtle conservation program, per se. The Turtle Conservation Fund Executive Committee has been assembled with individuals who represent global turtle efforts and demonstrate fund-raising and priority-setting capabilities. Additional representation will be welcomed and added as we are found lacking in certain areas. An Action Plan and Initial Prospectus has been completed and is now available. Three main Components of a worldwide comprehensive turtle conservation plan have been identified: 1) Establishment of Assurance Colonies; 2) Conservation Biology Research; 3) Range Country Capacity Building. An initial prioritization of all tortoise and freshwater turtle species has been made and component needs identified for the highest priority species. Fund-raising efforts are beginning to bear fruit. Seven major regions of the world have been identified as important for tortoise and freshwater turtle conservation: Asia, Africa, Australasia, Mediterranean, North America, Meso-America, and South America. We wish to engage and coordinate with conservation-minded individuals and institutions in all of these regions to advance collaborative conservation actions that will benefit tortoises and freshwater turtles of the world. Should the TCF continue to prosper and grow, we believe that the future will have become significantly brighter for chelonian species.

23064: Pseudoplatystoma is a pimelodid catfish group with 3 recognized species; all reach large sizes and live in tropical and subtropical freshwaters in South America. The individuals of species of Pseudoplatystoma are familiar due to their striking color pattern; often referred to in the vernacular as "Bagre rayado" or "Pintadillo" (tiger catfish/tiger-shovelnose). These catfishes are piscivorous and even eat members of their own kind. The known distribution of Pseudoplatystoma includes the following major river basins: Parana, Amazon, Orinoco, Sao Francisco and Magdalena. None of the nominal species have been reported from the Pacific basin. Species of Pseudoplatystoma are of considerable economic value and most studies have emphasized their general biology. Although studies of the general biology are adequate, there is a paucity of information on the taxonomy and systematics of the group. In fact, the lack of detailed morphological studies has precluded clear species delimitation; doubts still exit on the status of species such as P. tigrinum, which is confused with P. fasciatum by non specialists. Regardless of its wide distribution and differences in the external morphology, different populations (Parana, Magdalena, Amazon, Guyana and Orinoco) have been lumped into one single species, i.e., P. fasciatum. The intention of this study is to propose a phylogenetic hypothesis as the first insight to the history of Pseudoplatystoma. The group forms a monophyletic assemblage of eight species, including the three widely recognized and five new species in the process of description. .
