23065: Distinct intromittent organs were present on three mature male Monotocheirodon specimens collected from three separate localities in Peru. Standard lengths and museum numbers of these specimens were: 30.5mm, MUSM 11250 (MUSM = Museo de Historia Natural de la Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos, Lima, Peru); 38.1mm, MUSM 6756; 33.9mm, ANSP 143791 (ANSP = Academy of Natural Sciences, Philadelphia, PA, USA). The lengths of the intromittent organs, measured from the posterior point of insertion to the distal tip, for these specimens were 2.2mm, 4.0mm and 3.7mm, respectively. Sperm transfer to females was confirmed through histological demonstration of spermatozoa (which in all cases had elongate nuclei) in mature ovaries of females from all three collections. From histological sections, it appears that the intromittent organs develop as extensions of the body wall around the gonopore, since the sperm duct runs the entire length in the center of the structure, opening at its tip. Neither bone nor cartilage is present. Skeletal muscle, which is present throughout, possibly forms a circularly arranged sphincter at the base. More distally most skeletal muscle fibers are arranged longitudinally, although some circular/oblique fibers are present. This is the first documentation of an intromittent organ in a characiform fish.

23066: The digenean endoparasite communities of six northeastern Pacific species of the serranid genus Paralabrax (P. clathratus, P. nebulifer, P. maculatofaciatus, P. loro, P. auroguttatus, and P. albomaculatus) were compared. Six species of digenetic trematodes were identified as parasites of the six fish hosts. The prevalence of five of the parasites was quite low and only two parasite species were shared among species of hosts. Paralabrax clathratus hosted the most digenean species, the highest prevalences of parasites, and different assemblages of parasites at different geographic locations. These parasite assemblages hold minimal information for phylogenetic application (e.g. Hennig's Parasitological Method) but may, at least in the case of P. clathratus, be useful in identifying and tracking isolated stocks of the hosts.

23067: A phylogeny of colubrid snakes in Madagascar is estimated using morphological characters. Outgroups included a sampling of African, Neotropical, and widespread lineages. The results support a dual origin for the Malagasy radiation. One lineage includes only the genus Mimophis, which belongs to a clade of primarily African snakes including Psammophis and its relatives. All other Malagasy colubrids comprise a single radiation whose relationships are with other African colubrids; however, the complexity of the African colubrid radiation precludes a rigorous assessment of precise relationships at this time.

23068: The subfamily Serrasalminae (Characidae, Teleostei) is an endemic Neotropical group of fishes distributed along the Amazon, Paraná/Paraguay and Orinoco Basins. Population characterization of the pacu Piaractus mesopotamicus, found in all major rivers that comprise the Pantanal of Mato Grosso, holds practical implications for fisheries and conservation biology in Brazil. Previous studies, using mitochondrial DNA restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis, revealed a lack of population structure in the Pantanal region and low levels of genetic variability among members of the subfamily Serrasalminae. In order to further investigate population genetic structure within P. mesopotamicus, microsatellite loci were isolated from an enriched genomic library constructed for this species. These markers were used to screen 120 individuals from six different localities (Cuiabá, Paraguay, Miranda/Aquidauana, Taquari, Paraná and Paranapanema rivers. Seven out of the nine loci characterized exhibited greater than 50% heterozygosity and the number of alleles per locus ranged from three (Pme21 and 34) to 18 (Pme28). Genotypic frequencies conformed to Hardy-Weinberg expectations in all but one single locus test (Pme28), probably due to occurrence of null alleles at this locus. Two estimators of the proportion of total genetic variation that occurs between populations (Fst and Rst), which are based on different mutation models, indicated the existence of a single panmictic population of Piaractus mesopotamicus in the Pantanal. However, private alleles were found in the Cuiabá sample. When these primers were tested in other members of the subfamily, different levels of cross-species amplification were obtained. Pme2 amplify only within the genus Piaractus while Pme21 gave positive results even outside Serrasalminae.

23069: The order Characiformes, one of the largest assemblages of freshwater fishes, is distributed in the African continent and in the Neotropics. In Africa, there are circa 150 extant species placed in four families: Hepsetidae, Distichodontidae, Citharinidae and Alestidae. In the Neotropics, there are over 1,200 living species divided in 14 families. The aim of this study is to provide phylogenetic hypothesis to enable the assessment of current biogeographical scenarios. While most previous studies, with a broad taxon sampling, were intended to resolve lower-level groupings, our study is the first specifically designed to resolve higher-level relationships among Characiformes. In the present study we analyzed 135 taxa representing all African and all Neotropical families (except for Curimatidae and Gasteropelecidae) using six different gene regions from both mitochondrial (16S and Cytb) and nuclear (Rag2, Fkh, Sia and Trop) genomes for a total of 3681 nucleotide characters in a cladistic simultaneous analysis, which resulted in 18 most parsimonious trees. The contribution of each gene partition was assessed showing a net positive support from all partitions, furthermore 67% of the nodes presented bootstrap values higher than 70. The strict consensus tree is fully resolved except for rearrangements within Tetragonopterinae and position changes of some Brycinus species within Alestidae. The use of cypriniform and siluriform taxa as outgroups resulted in a monophyletic Characiformes. Neither the African nor the Neotropical assemblages were recovered as monophyletic nevertheless, the monophyly of several morphologically recognized groups such as Distichodontidae, Citharinidae, Alestidae, Cheirodontinae and Serrasalmidae was recovered. Our results point to an early Cretaceous origin of some characiform clades but indicate that it is unlikely that a single vicariant event could explain the current distribution of African and Neotropical taxa.

23070: The Neotropics harbors more species of anurans than any other comparable region on earth, and much of this diversity is found in the Amazon region. Yet, the diversity of this region remains underestimated for several reasons. Much of the region is unexplored, and numerous undescribed species exist in many genera; in addition, numerous species appear to be composed of species complexes. We examined anuran faunas at seven rainforest sites in the Amazon basin. In general, the number of species increased from east to west, possibly in conjunction with moisture gradients and length of dry season. Nevertheless, each site has numerous undescribed species. To demonstrate the extent of this unrecognized diversity, we focus on the dendrobatid genus Colostethus as an example. As recently as the late 1990s, only four species of Colostethus were known from the Amazon region. Our intensive work at various sites has revealed from 2 to 4 distinct species at each site. Since 2000, various authors have described 13 new species of Amazonian Colostethus, and we have at least five others awaiting description. Newly described species include those with interesting biology; for example, one Amazonian species is the fourth known Colostethus with a nidicolous tadpole; this reproductive mode is unknown in other dendrobatid clades. Thus, not only is taxonomic diversity underestimated in the Amazon region, but ecological and behavioral diversity is unknown as well.

23071: Taxonomic status of a recently established gymnotiform genera, Iracema Triques, is discussed. It is first noticed that conditions explicitly pointed out in the original description of Iracema as uniquely derived for this taxon concerning the family Rhamphichthyidae and/or the order Gymnotiformes (namely, external observations referring to its overall color pattern) have been in fact also observed in members of the rhamphichthyid genus Gymnorhamphichthys Ellis. Second, it is argued that additional major features considered "diagnostic" of Iracema, also tentatively used for supporting that genus as valid, are all actually intermediate conditions between those observed in Gymnorhamphichthys and Rhamphichthys Müller & Troschel. This being the case, a general discussion is presented for demonstrating that treating those "intermediate conditions" as "apomorphic conditions" of Iracema, as originally placed, actually relies on specific phylogenetic schemes where homoplasy statements must be favored in transformation series of multistate characters. If, otherwise, also available hypotheses maximizing primary homology presentations are preferred over those mentioned above, that "genus" is left with not a single apomorphic condition and should be viewed as non-monophyletic. At the end of the above demonstration, when no objective supports remain for accepting a generic status concerning Iracema, and as a final result, a taxonomic proposal is made for recognizing Iracema caiana Triques as a member of Gymnorhamphichthys, as Gymnorhamphichthys caianus (Triques), comb. nov.

23072: Coordinated movement has not been reported in crocodilians. However, between 1989 and 1999, 94% of the 525 Caiman crocodilus yacare found walking on land in the Pantanal were in coordinated groups (N=70) walking head to tail and forming almost straight lines. The caimans left pools and initiated terrestrial movements spontaneous, and in response to disturbances by researchers and hunters. The sex ratio of the groups was biased towards males (x=0.8; SD = 0.24), and was similar to that found in aquatic habitats in the study area. Caimans that left pools in response to disturbances buried in mud and in leaf litter in forest.
23073: Diet studies in anurans have used pre-established concepts, based on anecdotal cases, generally developed in assemblages with similar features. Nevertheless, few authors tested such concepts and classifications. It is well known that anuran size is correlated to the size of the ingested preys. Many authors suggest that such relation may express differences in size as much as in the sort of ingested preys, since large individuals would be exposed to certain categories of preys unavailable to the smaller individuals. Eleutherodactylus binotatus was chosen to perform this study because it is largely distributed along the Southeastern Brazil, and species of this genus, with direct development, have different size classes occupying the same environment. Comparisons on stomach contents, based on a variety of measurements parameters, were performed between classes in the same season to determine the variation related to size. Data on the same class and different seasons were compared to determined seasonal variation. Selectivity was verified by comparing the proportions of categories in the diet and environment. Eleutherodactylus binotatus adult females may be considered different from the other classes in size but not in sort of ingested item. The mainly seasonal variation was the selectivity to mites and spiders. The former were preferred in the dry season and avoided in the rainy season, whereas the latter were preferred in the rainy season and avoided in the dry season. We conclude Eleutherodactylus binotatus is generalist, despite avoiding consuming ants, as others Leptodactylidae

23074: We studied factors affecting nest mortality and patterns of human egg consumption of a population of Podocnemis unifilis along a stretch of the Aguarico River located in the Cuyabeno Reserve. The area is inhabited by a hunter and fisher traditional Cofan community which is experiencing a community management plan for terecay conservation. We investigated the spatial distribution of nests and egg survivorship on the most productive beach, Erestinae, mapping each nest the morning after laying with a GPS meter. Pillage was responsible for the loss of 6.5% of all nests while 22.4% were lost due to flooding. Harvesting apparently represents the principal factor of mortality, affecting 28.2% of all depositions found in the area (383). Although harvesting did not occur on randomly selected nests but only on those which would otherwise be lost through flooding, as revealed by the study of the spatial distribution of nests on Eristinae. In fact the Cofans harvested nests placed close to the river shore, or, following the flooding development, on nests at once before the current took them away. Moreover they transplanted part of the nests in imminent risk of flooding to the highest areas of the beaches. Therefore to calculate the effective flooding influences, not biased by human activities, we added up the percentage of nests lost due to flooding (22.4%), harvesting (28.2%) and those which had been transplanted with success (12.5%), with the result of a comprehensive mortality percentage of 63.1% of all depositions. This work suggests that the tarecay egg resource could be completely sustainable by using those eggs that would otherwise be lost due to flooding, a cause of mortality that appears especially important in this Amazonian region.

23075: Boreal toads (Bufo boreas), a widespread species in the Rocky Mountains of the western United States, are among the most susceptible amphibians to infections by the pathogenic chytrid fungus Batrachchytrium dendrobatidis. As a result, this species is a good model species for examining the interaction between this pathogen and one of its hosts. A few museum samples dating from the 1970s are positive for this pathogen, suggesting that the widespread mortalities observed in the 1970s-early 1980s were due to this pathogen. A number of laboratory experiments have been conducted in hopes of learning as much as possible about factors that may promote infection in the wild. Exposure to as few as 20 zoospores for 24 hrs is adequate to cause death in some animals, and an indirect correspondence exists between zoospore dosage (up to 1 M/24 hrs) and the number of days survived. Exposures to 100 zoospores or more are invariably fatal. Boreal toads are differentially susceptible to various isolates of this species, including those taken from other sympatric amphibians. Therefore, although molecular data (obtained by others) support the contention that different populations of chytrids throughout the world are one "species", some specializations to each type of amphibian host may have occurred. Temperature, crowding, and body size play major roles in the time to death following exposure to chytrid zoospores. The pH of the water in which infected toads are held seems to have little effect on survivability of a chytrid infection. Some boreal toad populations appear to be free of the disease, as judged by PCR of skin taken from individuals in various populations, and some individuals appear to persist for some time in an infected state in infected populations. Not all individuals in a population appear to be infected during a given summer. Toads can become infected from zoospores in water that has been occupied by infected toads, and do not require physical contact with infected animals to become infected.

23076: I contrast DNA data from ca. 600 bp of the cytochrome b and ca. 600 bp of the ND2 gene across populations of Proceratophrys gr. boiei that occur in forest remnants of northeastern Brazil. Two questions are addressed: What are the impacts of fragment age on the genetic diversity of the study taxa? What do phylogeographic analyses inform about the history of these species and forests? Samples were collected from rainforest remnants in the states of Ceará and Pernambuco. Two of those are located in the coastal, humid Atlantic Forest domain. Two lie in the transition zone between the Atlantic Forest domain and the adjacent, semi-arid Caatinga. Two are found within the dry Caatinga. While some of these fragments are known to be human-made, being and at most 500 years-old, others are thought to have been naturally isolated thousands of years ago, and are seen as relics of a former connection between Amazonia and the Atlantic Forest. Results show that there is considerable genetic structure among Atlantic Forest populations, reflecting fragmentation events that predate human-driven habitat destruction. Genetic data agree with distribution and fossil data gathered for other organisms, suggesting that mesic forests once occupied the currently arid Caatinga. Populations in older, naturally isolated forests within the Caatinga show lower genetic diversity compared to those in areas recently fragmented by human activity. To investigate the occurrence of deeply divergent haplotypes at one Atlantic Rainforest site in the state of Pernambuco, a side study is conducted with samples collected from four different breeding assemblages connected by continuous forest. 23077: A histological examination of the lateral branch of the vagus nerve reveals a close association with the swim bladder. As in other bony fishes, this nerve connects to the hindbrain and exits the exoccipital through the vagus foramen. Although this branch of the vagus nerve normally serves the lateral line, no lateral line canal extends caudally on the body. Thin bony rods run lateroventrocaudally from the nerve toward the swim bladder. We hypothesize that these bony rods, and the nerve itself, may serve a mechanosensory function. 23078: The Columbus crab, Planes cyaneus is a pelagic crab often found in a wide variety of floating objects such as inanimate flotsam, drifting kelp, the gastropods Jantinha, the cephalopod Spirula and marine turtles, mainly C. caretta. A cleaning association has been suggested between columbus crabs and loggerheads, since it was found that this crab do feed on other epibionts (i.e., barnacle cyprids, parasitic amphipods). This relationship may enhance the survivorship of turtles, reducing carapace weight and improving their hydrodynamic performance. The effect of epibionts may be more noticeable in juveniles loggerheads due to their relatively small size and strength. A total of 18 loggerheads were collected between 100 and 200 miles of La Paloma (Uruguay) between April and October 2002, during operations of uruguayan Tuna Longliners. Once on board, crabs were removed from turtles, labeled and frozen. Before released, turtles were tagged and body measurements taken. Then crabs were fixed for preservation, sexed, and their carapace length and width were recorded. All but three turtles were colonized by P. cyaneus. Fifteen of the 18 observed turtles had at least one crab, eight turtles has two crabs, generally an heterosexual pair, and in six cases only one specimen was found. Only one turtle has three crabs (two males, one female). Two of the crab females were ovigerous while all males were considered mature. In all cases, crabs were found living between the turtle tail and the carapace. Crabs mean carapace length was 17.58 mm (SD 3.4) in males and 20.2 mm (SD 2.23) in females, with no significant differences between sexes. This species have been found in Pacific Ocean (41°N to 35°S), Indic Ocean, southwestern Atlantic (Uruguay y Brazil, west coast of Africa, Santa Helena Island), North Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico. However, this is the first report of turtle-crab association in the southwestern Atlantic.

23079: Ocean sunfish (Mola mola) comprise the largest bycatch component (29% of total catch) of the California drift gillnet fishery for swordfish. We used temperature and depth-sensing acoustic transmitters to quantify the vertical and horizontal movement patterns of ocean sunfish near Santa Catalina Island, California. Eight ocean sunfish were tracked continuously over 24-72 h periods, during which oceanographic data were collected every two hours. Geographical position and depth of tracked fish were analyzed in relation to oceanographic data and time of day. Ocean sunfish traveled a mean distance of 26.7 ± 6.3 km (mean ± SD) per day. Horizontal movements were characterized by a significant decrease in rate of movement during the six-hour period following sunset (0.78 ± 0.26 km h-1) as opposed to daytime periods (1.26 ± 1.16 km h-1). Horizontal movements were also highly directional, with angular concentration values (r) as high as 0.765 over the duration of entire tracks. Nocturnal vertical movements were confined to the mixed layer and thermocline, while diurnal vertical movements were characterized by repeated dives below the thermocline (max. dive depth = 392 m). A significant relationship was found between minimum temperature experienced during a deeper dive and the duration spent in the mixed layer (p<0.001). Ocean sunfish were less active at night than during the day and may behaviorally thermoregulate between deep daytime dives. Depth distribution patterns of ocean sunfish revealed in this study indicate that lowering the depth of gillnets in the water could significantly reduce bycatch of this species in the California drift gillnet fishery.

23080: This study investigated the effects of forest fragmentation on lizard community composition in fragments associated with Amazonian savanna. We constructed an index of community composition, performing two-dimensional ordinations of sites by hybrid multidimensional scaling (HMDS) using data on 11 lizard species. The effect of habitat category (continuous forest versus remnant) on community composition was evaluated by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA). The effects of fragment size, isolation, vegetation structure and food availability were evaluated by redundancy analysis. Community composition differed between fragments and continuous forest and was affected by fragment isolation, vegetation structure and invertebrate biomass. Fragment size did not affected community composition. 23081: Records of cleaning symbiosis between freshwater fish are scarce. Here we report on an instance of cleaning behavior between two freshwater fishes: the juvenile Raphael catfish, Platydoras costatus (Doradidae) and the piscivorous trahira, Hoplias cf. malabaricus (Erythrinidae). Field work was done in São José dos Bandeirantes (13°41′S 50°47′W), Nova Crixá, Goiás, western Brazil, in a clearwater stream tributary of the Rio Araguaia, Amazon Basin, in May 2002. The observations were made using all occurrences and focal animal sampling during 25 min. We observed Raphael catfish moving directly to a nearby trahira, positioning itself on the flank of the host fish and then moving towards the head, where it nibbled the mouth area of the trahira. Then the catfish returned to the back of the trahira moving along the body while touching it with its mouth and barbells. The cleaning behavior recorded for P. costatus is the first instance of a freshwater catfish acting as a cleaner under natural conditions. The armored body of the catfish may provide some protection and so facilitate the cleaning interaction with a potentially dangerous client. The contrasting black and white coloration of young P. costatus may be regarded as a signal that allows for its recognition as a cleaner. Since visual contact appears to be of utmost importance for these interspecific interactions it is likely that new records of cleaning symbiosis among freshwater fishes are to be expected in other clear water, species-rich streams and rivers of the Amazon.

23082: Within a reproductive ecology of Podocnemis erythrocephala project on the lower Río Inírida, Department of Guainía, Colombia, during the low water season of 1996-97, threats to nests and the primary causes of damage to eggs were recorded. 23083: Radiotelemetry was employed to monitor the movements and compare terrestrial habitat use of hatchling and adult wood turtles, Glyptemys insculpta, from 1 August to 15 October 2002 in agricultural and riparian edge habitats along the Delaware River and one of its tributaries in northwestern New Jersey. Post-emergent hatchling and adult turtles distributed themselves differently within the study site. Hatchlings demonstrated a preference for agricultural fields (stands of mature corn) with relatively bare soil substrates while adults showed a preference for meadows dominated by Solidago spp. and substrate covered by vegetation. Within these habitat types, both groups were found at locations with similar relative humidity, air temperature, and soil moisture. However, substrate temperature differed and was significantly lower at hatchling locations. The mean straight-line distance traveled per day was 21.1 m (0-260 m). All hatchlings remained in the agricultural fields for at least 12 to 51 days after emergence from their nests and before entering aquatic habitat. Hatchlings successfully tracked from nest to water entered the home stream or the Delaware River. Hatchlings were observed foraging on small slugs in the agricultural fields on several occasions. One hatchling was observed eating < 24 hrs after emergence. Measurements recorded for individual hatchlings showed that they gained weight and grew in length before entering over-wintering aquatic habitat. No radio-tagged hatchlings were predated during this study. However, numerous predator tracks along field edges and streamsides, suggested that predator levels were high. These observations suggest that agricultural fields provide forage and protective cover for post-emergent wood turtles and that there is high hatchling survivorship in the weeks following emergence. Hatchlings are however at risk if early maturing crops are planted and harvesting equipment enters the agricultural fields before the hatchlings have departed from them. Planting, spraying, and harvesting should be timed for those periods when turtle activity in them is limited. Management recommendations that would serve to reduce mortality include the planting of late-maturing crops and implementation of best farming practices.

23084: Blackwater forest streams in the Colombian Amazon sustain very complex fish communities, as recent works carried on near Leticia put in evidence. The present work has as main objective to produce information about the role played by spatial distribution in the dynamics of fish communities and how it contributes to maintain a high diversity. In order to understand how fishes are distribute in the brook we made 65 diurnal and 10 nocturnal observations with diving mask and lamps, selecting fishing in the different microbiotopes or what we assumed as such, analysis of stomach contents and took in account the external morphology of the different species. In general terms the forest stream is in capacity of sustaining such complex communities thanks to the presence of different biotopes (water column, stream, roots, submerged marginal vegetation, logs and branches of fallen trees, beaches, litter covered bottoms and lateral puddles) offering fishes a wide variety in what concern food and shelter. The optimum use of space at the level of microhabitats require morphological, behavioral and alimentary adaptations of the fishes and we can gather them in different trophic groups (piscivorous, larvae eaters, detritivorous, herbivorous, insectivorous), for which the dietary preferences are not only related to what they eat also to the particular strategies they use for catching those items. 23085: Anthropologists have long recognized traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) as an important component of indigenous resource management. There is a growing recognition of the roles of both TEK and indigenous resource management as tools for confronting water, wildlife, and agricultural management problems. The increasing importance of indigenous tenure rights and biodiversity prospecting has recently brought TEK to the fore in mainstream western scientific literature. Wildlife and fisheries management planning has begun to integrate traditional ecological knowledge in several countries. Some of the benefits of integrating TEK with western science come from the capacity of TEK to provide data on broad temporal and spatial patterns as well as provide a more holistic view of the interactions between people and wildlife. Most importantly, data gathering in western science is often not participatory and the resulting data, and its interpretation, are often alien to those that will be the major users of the information. This paper discusses the integration of traditional knowledge in the stock assessment and management of Arapaima (Arapaima gigas) in the North Rupununi Wetlands, Guyana. The paper examines the involvement of local people in Arapaima research and management and presents stock assessment results from two years of collaborative management. The results suggest that integrating TEK in tropical wildlife and fisheries management in the Neotropics is potentially more cost-effective than other methods of data gathering.

23086: The dental morphology and patterning in sharks has long been used to predict both species and body size, with somewhat limited success. The lack of fit between dental patterns and body size is partially due to monognathic and dignathic heterodonty, as well as varying tooth size along the jaw margins. The ability to accurately predict body size from bite patterns is important for better understanding shark attack on humans and even submarine equipment, both civilian and military. To this end, we measured inter-tooth distance and tooth size for the two anterior and first four lateral teeth on both the upper and lower jaws, as well as jaw circumference, in a variety of carcharhinid and lamnid sharks, and regressed these against total length. Tooth gap distance is an accurate predictor of body size (upper jaw R2 = 0.83) (lower jaw R2 = 0.82) for twelve carcharhinid species as a group. More triangular upper jaw tooth spacing is isometric (m = 1.05) whereas the narrow and more pointed lower teeth (m = 0.89) display negative allometry. Taken individually different carcharhinid species display somewhat variable spacing patterns. Tooth bearing circumference is also isometric and predictive (R2 = 0.94) of total length. White and mako sharks display greater tooth gap spacing for a given length than carcharhinids with high regression coefficients and low variability. These simple measures taken from bitten submarine equipment and organisms allow quick assessments of shark size. This research continues with collection of additional data on potentially hazardous or commercially destructive species and identification of species specific damage patterns.

23087: Inter and intrafamilial relationships of the Prochilodontidae were investigated based on information from osteological and soft anatomical systems. 23088: Henochilus, a characiform genus endemic to the rivers of eastern Brazil is reviewed. 23089: The study was made in a sustainable management zone inside the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve (RDSM) in the dry seasons of 2001 and 2002. The main goal of this study was to test the hypothesis that the system of lake management employed, which consists in the differentiation of lakes according to its use by local communities, affects the density of Colossoma macropomum. 5362 individuals from 10 different lakes (2 preservation lakes, 4 subsistence lakes and 4 commercial lakes) inside the RDSM area were marked. An estimation of abundance was obtained by mark and recapture experiments. The density was obtained calculating the area of those lakes and the abundance estimations. The results show that the density of C. macropomum is not related to the management systems of the lakes in RDSM, but the mean size of the individuals captured was significantly different in the categories of lakes studied. 23090: Ohio has three major rivers (Great Miami, Scioto, Muskingum) that run from the upper one-third of the state south 200 kilometers to the Ohio River. One of the rivers (Scioto) is free of barrier dams for 100 km upstream from its mouth. This river has been sampled for fishes on an annual basis for more than 70 years. Over that time span a number of fish species have moved north in the system, some about one degree of latitude. Two southern species in particular, the spotted bass, Micropterus punctulatus, and the dusky darter, Percina sciera, have established self- sustaining populations well north of their distribution limit, circa 1930. Other species such as ghost shiner, Notropis buchanani, and smallmouth buffalo, Ictiobus bubalus, show similar latitudinal changes in distribution. Additional forms like gravel chub, Erimystax x-punctatus, steelcolor shiner, Cyprinella whipplei, and river carpsucker, Carpiodes carpio, are part of the group. Some of these same species (Ictiobus bubalus, Notropis buchanani, Percina sciera) have been introduced into northern Ohio where they are not native (Lake Erie or its tributaries at 41 degrees 20 minutes N latitude) and have become well established. Another southern species, the mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) has moved up the Ohio River and was recorded for the first time in the Scioto River during the last decade. The movement of fishes to higher latitudes in the state of Ohio may reflect, in some cases, improvement in water quality but also suggest in the case of certain species a correlation with warmer average annual temperatures and possibly reflect the influence of global warming in this area.

23093: Geological reconstructions proposed for the Greater Antilles fit into two major categories, each with different biogeographic consequences. 23095: The purpose of this work is to examine some of the conclusions emerging from the work of Patterson and Johnson (1995) on the evolution of intermuscular bones. On the basis of the presence of these peculiar bones and the location of the first ribs in two flatfish families (Bothidae and Samaridae), Patterson and Johnson (1995) suggested that these families might be closely related and insisted on the value of intermuscular bones and ligaments to assess interrelationships amongst flatfish clades. Intermuscular ligaments, identical in shape and position with intermuscular bones, have been found in all flatfishes. However, when considered within a global phylogenetic analysis, it appears that the ossification of ligaments in bothids and samarids is the result of convergence, not common ancestry. A second character that was suggested as a possible synapomorphy of samarids and bothids was the location of the first ribs on the second abdominal vertebrae. Our survey shows that the location of the first rib is highly variable within and among flatfish families. Nevertheless, the global examination of these structures has revealed some interesting phylogenetic information: ribs are present on the fifth abdominal vertebra in poecilopsettids while they are entirely absent in species belonging to the Achiridae-Soleidae- Cynoglossidae clade.

23096: Latouche’s frog, Rana latouchii, and central Formosan toad, Bufo bankorensis, are the most abundant ground-dwelling anuran species in Najenshan forest, Taiwan. 23097: Fishes of Rio Negro have been documented by A. R. Ferreira, L. Agassiz and A. R. Wallace since the turn of 19th century. Recent studies have found ever-increasing species richness in the nutrient poor waters of the basin. This study is to test and adopt a rapid assessment protocol (RAP) to compile fish diversity and ecological information from tributaries and floodplain of the middle Rio Negro basin, where the rich diversity has contributed to a flourish ornamental fishery for five decades. We tested RAP in three watersheds: Rios Cuiunizinho-Alegria (01°07′39″ S, 64°14′06″ W), Rios Paudauary-Preto (00°08′24″ S; 64°06′67″ W) and Igarapé Zamula (00°50′24″ S; 62°45′67″ W). We used collapsible cylinder trap, cacurí trap, rapiché and dip-net to sample along the margins of forest stream (igarapé) and flooded forest (igapó); also used beach seines, gill nets and bottom trawl along the riverbanks and in the deeper channels. Each RAP survey takes 3-5 days fishing effort in a designated radius of 5-10 km. The first RAP at Cuiuni site, a darker water river, yielded 91 species from the igarapés and 18 species from six bottom trawl hauls. The third RAP at Zamula site where water was slightly tinted, we registered 144 species from floodplain and 49 species from six trawl hauls in the river channel. The predominant groups from all RAP surveys are Characiformes (43-55%), Siluriformes (13-23%), Gymnotiformes (5-12%) and Perciformes (19-23%). Characiformes are most dominant in the igarapés (54-63%), followed by Perciformes (24-26%) and Siluriformes (7-13%). Bottom trawl hauls caught more Siluriformes (30-51%) than Gymnotiformes (13-38%) and Perciformes (6- 17%). Previous fish surveys in the Igarapé Zamula registered about 150 species from the floodplain, and 27 from bottom trawl. First RAP survey at the Igarapé Zamula has increased the record of floodplain species to 218 and trawl haul species to 59. This protocol is a more efficient and economic means to conduct fish surveys in the undocumented waters of the Amazon basin. (CNPq no. 46.6098/2001-4 & 550367/2001-2)

23098: The impact of deforestation in the Amazon has been well documented and linked to broader concerns such as the global warming and rapid loss of biodiversity. In spite of the great diversity and socio-economic value of fishes and aquatic systems, fishes are not often included in the conservation and sustainable development projects in the region. Our goal (Project Piaba) is to generate baseline information on the diversity and ecology of fishes in the Rio Negro basin to help maintaining a sustainable live ornamental fishery, which is a way to preserve rainforest and alleviate poverty in the region. Ornamental fishery has been a principal subsistence for riverine communities in the middle and upper Rio Negro basin, since the discovery of Cardinal tetra (Paracheirodon axelrodi) in the 1950’s. Over 40 million live tropical fishes are extracted and exported annually from the region, including 70 species and nearly 90% are the endemic Cardinal tetra. Major findings of Project Piaba are: (1) Cardinal tetra is the indicator species for the ornamental fishery, any significant changes in their stocks can alter the socio-economic orders of the riverine people as well as the fate of rainforest and river system. (2) Species richness is much greater than previously documented, the role of river channel as a barrier and refuge of floodplain fish distribution is evident. (3) El Niño events have strong influence on fish distribution and the ornamental fishery. (4) Problems on mortality rate of live fish transport processes have been identified, but the issues cannot be solved by technology alone. (5) Training local people and involving the ornamental fish collectors, traders, hobbyists, and regulatory agencies in the conservation of Amazon fishes have made notable progress. Understanding the fish diversity and its socio-economic value can be a key to conservation in the Amazon basin.

23099: Ostional beach is a massive nesting beach of olive ridley sea turtle Lepidochelys olivacea. Since 1970 this population had been studied by the Department of Biology of the Universidad de Costa Rica. The nesting activity is year around, with ranges of 5000 to 400,000 sea turtles per month per kilometer of beach. However the hatching success presents high variability throughout the year. From February to June the production of hatchlings is close to zero, during the rest of the period production can reach several million per month. The ENSO seems to have influence in the variation in the hatching success between years. The hatching success also varied throughout the platform. The nests incubated near vegetation present poor hatching success. The mouth of the estuaries and the zone near the ocean have a high production of hatchlings. The overdigging by the same sea turtles, the erosion by the ocean waves and estuaries, the predation by dogs, raccoons and humans are all very important in explaining the nest mortalities. The non-viability eggs explain the 30% of the mortalities during incubation; the hatching success is close to 30% in the nest survival, but the remaining 40% of the mortalities of nest that survive the incubation period is not explained at present
23100: Primary male was referred to the male of a protogynous species, which never had a female function in its life history. Additionally, some secondary males of this species were discovered that the process of sex reversal occurred earlier or faster than the gametogenesis carried out, so those female would translate to be a small but functional male which were the same as the functional primary male described in other normal protogynous species.

23101: In a number of studies, William A. Gosline considered the evolution of jaw structure and function in atheriniform fishes. In these studies, Dr. Gosline considered that jaw evolution and associated mechanics were influenced by phylogeny and ecology. In this presentation, we consider the structural, morphometric and biomechanical evolution of the heads and jaws of atherinopsid fishes belonging to the tribe Membradini. Membradin silverides are primarily neotropical, inhabiting freshwater, estuarine and marine habitats. The fishes range in body shape and food preference from herring-like planktivores to pike-like piscivores. We use the phylogeny based upon all membradin species as a framework to interpret morphometric and biomechanical patterns of evolution. We are particularly interested in similarities due to convergence. We will also examine the biomechanical constraints on shape change in the heads of these silversides.

23102: Age and growth of Orectolobus sp. A was studied using micro-radiographs of sectioned vertebrae and laboratory growth studies with two fluorochrome marker dyes, calcein and oxytetracycline. Vertebrae from 182 individuals were examined for length at growth band formation. The relationship between total length (cm, TL) and centrum radius (mm, CR) was linear: TL = 15.92CR + 10.65 (R2 = 0.9, n = 68). Growth bands were difficult to interpret and final counts were obtained from 98 (53%) individuals with a size range of 63 to 146cm total length. The formation time of growth bands in the vertebrae of captive animals varied, with no predictable pattern, indicating that these bands may not form annually. Growth band formation is thought to be influenced by non-periodic changes in centrum or somatic growth rather than with time. Von Bertalanffy growth parameters estimated from vertebral analysis for both sexes combined were L = 146.5, K = 0.12, t0 = -1.45. Growth parameters estimated from back-calculated length at growth band formation did not agree with those estimated from observed length at growth band formation. Individual growth rates/year of Orectolobus sp. A for the period of captivity (423-472 days) varied considerably, ranging from 3.5cm/year to 13.8cm/year in total length (mean = 7.03cm/year ± 1.15cm SE) and from 0.42kg/year to 3.07kg/year in weight (mean = 1.81kg/year ± 0.25kg SE). The rates of growth in total length/year for captive animals were similar to growth rates estimated from the von Bertalanffy growth curve.

23103: Plethodontid salamanders of the tribe Hemidactyliini exhibit a wide range of reproductive and life history modes that include paedomorphosis and subterranean dwelling, the latter accompanied in some species by extreme morphological modifications associated with cave habitats. We provide the first comprehensive phylogenetic hypothesis for the Hemidactyliini, including all genera, all species groups, and nearly all described species, plus outgroups representing all other major lineages of plethodontid salamanders. Phylogenetic analyses based on nuclear and mitochondrial sequences (1500+ bp of the nuclear recombination-activating gene 1, RAG-1, and 1500+ bp of mitochondrial cyt b and ND4), plus morphology and other characters, indicate that the Hemidactyliini is monophyletic, except that placement of the enigmatic genus Hemidactylium remains problematic. Both paedomorphosis and cave dwelling have evolved independently in several distantly-related lineages of hemidactyliines. All cave dwellers, including the genera which display the most extreme cave-associated morphologies, Haideotriton, Typhlomolge, and Typhlotriton, are phylogenetically nested within primarily surface-dwelling taxa that are (or until recently have been) considered wide-ranging species. Paedomorphosis appears to have reversed to metamorphosis at least once, in some central Texas hemidactyliines. Although several cave- dwelling species are obligate paedomorphs, this association is not absolute; evolution of this combination of traits appears to be governed by diverse factors, including developmental mode of the surface ancestors, habitat characteristics, occurrence of aquatic predators, and possibly competition. We will test hypotheses regarding ecological and other factors that have shaped habitat use and developmental evolution in the group, including habitat availability, climate, interspecific interactions, and phylogenetic inertia versus "predisposition" to different life history strategies.

23104: Several studies have implied that fish might have the capacity of dispersing seeds in the flooded forests. Thus, our aim was to determine the potential for seeds from six species of Amazonian trees (shiringa Hevea brasiliensis, guayaba Psidium guajaba, punga Pseudobombax munguba, camu-camu" Myrciaria dubia, pijuayo Bactris gasipaes and ñejilla Bactris concinna) to be dispersed by Colossoma macropomum, an endemic fish of the Amazon, and if the dispersal is itself affected by fish size. From June to October 2002 a study was conducted at IIAP facilities in Peru. Three individuals of C. macropomum for each weight-group (1 kg, 3 kg and 5+ kg) were placed in ponds in randomly assigned cages (6 m3). Fish were starved for two days until they had released their gastric contents. Later, fish were fed fruits and seeds (one of each of the six species at a time) until satiation. After verifying fish seed consumption, fish were placed into individual tile-bottom tanks to collect their feces. Seeds were collected from feces by separating whole from broken seeds. Later, whole digested seeds and undigested seeds from the same tree (control) were sowed into sterilized humus (120 °C for 24 h) to determine their viability and germination rate and placed under similar conditions (light intensity, photoperiod, temperature and moisture). Data were analyzed using one-way Anova. Guayaba, camu-camu and punga seeds (small-size seeds) germinated after passing through the C. macropomum digestive system, hence proving their viability. In contrast, pijuayo, ñejilla and shiringa seeds were broken during ingestion, likely because of their large size, and thus did not germinate. Also, fish weight did not have a significant effect on seed germination rate (Guayaba P = 0.6503, Punga P = 0.2856 and Camu-camu P = 0.4369) Our results indicate this fish is an active seeds dispersing agent, and likely plays an important role disseminating seeds of many tree species through the flooded forest.
23105: Eastern tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum tigrinum) populations are becoming increasingly fragmented in eastern North America. These populations are now known to represent an evolutionary lineage that is genetically distinct from western populations. I have been studying the demography of the only remaining population in the Appalachian Mountains for the past four years - in natural sinkhole ponds at an isolated site in the Shenandoah Valley, Virginia, USA. I captured adults and dispersing metamorphs at drift fences constructed around three breeding ponds situated 350-400 m apart. The marked animals include 650 adults and 1,122 juveniles with 2,572 total captures to date. I performed a multi-state analysis of capture-recapture data using MSSURVIV to generate maximum likelihood estimates of survival, movement, capture probabilities and the probability of skipping breeding. The most parsimonious model indicated that adult survival varied among local populations within years and within local populations across years. Adults showed high fidelity to breeding ponds and suffered high mortality in dry years. Recruitment into the juvenile age-class by metamorphs was highly variable across years due to variable weather patterns and also varied among ponds within years due to differences in individual pond hydrology. I took a matrix modeling approach to construct population projections with the goal of evaluating extinction risks that these populations face under different long-term weather regimes. I will discuss sensitivity analyses conducted to identify which vital rates are most critical to the viability of these remaining populations and should, therefore, be the primary targets of future conservation efforts.

23106: Fire has long been a part of the landscape in the Missouri Ozarks. However, in recent times fire suppression has changed the face of the landscape dramatically. Of the savanna and open woodland, once prominent in Missouri, now less than 1% of its original extent remains in similar condition. This is largely due to fire suppression with resulting woody encroachment and dense undergrowth. One of the remaining examples of savanna in the state has been managed with prescribed fire for the last two decades. This site represents a unique opportunity to investigate differential use by the herpetofauna in the areas that are burned annually, biennially, and those that are only affected by occasional wildfire. Reptile and amphibian abundance and species richness were sampled with cover boards and time-constrained searches along transects representing these different fire histories. Results indicate that fire is an important component of savanna management for maintaining reptile and amphibian species diversity and abundance.

23107: A large nearly complete premaxilla from the upper Miocene Ituzaingó Formation of eastern Argentina near Paraná is identified as a new distinctive serrasalmine characid. This extinct species had seven premaxillary teeth in a compressed, zig-zag row – an arrangement that is somewhat intermediate between the double row of pacus and single row of piranhas. Three teeth of the fossil are well-preserved and complete; one is fragmentary; the three others are known by their well-defined attachment surfaces. The complete teeth are triangular and compressed with long, finely-serrated cutting edges suggestive of a biting carnivorous diet. The fossil shares with true piranhas (Pristobrycon, Serrasalmus, Pygocentrus, Pygopristis) a compressed tooth row, compressed tooth crowns with well-developed cutting edges on crowns, and the dorsal margin of the premaxilla is concave lateral to the ascending process. However, the fossil has seven premaxillary teeth, not six as in adult piranhas in which the distal-most elongated tooth may be compound. Also, the fossil lacks the single row of interlocking teeth that is characteristic of piranhas. If the fossil serrasalmine is a proximate outgroup to true piranhas, the arrangement of its premaxillary dentition suggests, following the lead of William A. Gosline, the following evolutionary rearrangement. The primitive inner-row symphyseal tooth shifted to a symphyseal (medial-most) position in the outer row, and the primitive second inner-row tooth shifted forward in between the original first and second outer row teeth. The "megapiranha" reported here is the first record of an extinct serrasalmine.

23108: The studied zone is located on the lower Caqueta river, Colombia Amazon, in the surrounding area of the Ameru Indigenus community, and the captures correspond to fishing preferences and methods used by the indigenous community fishermen, and also torrent conditions for captures. A total of 3362 individuals were captured summarizing 82 fishes species, reunited on 5 orders, 16 families and 55 genera, during the upstream migration period (from July 18 to August 15 of 2001) on the “Chorro de Cordoba” torrent. Not all captured species have migratory habits, but they can be associated to river torrents zones where they spent most part of their biological cycles. In terms of number of individual and biomass, the most abundant species on captures belong to the genus Brycon (Brycon cephalus, Brycon falcatus and Brycon melanopterus), having an abundance peak between July 24 and August 4, which correspond to their migratory period. On general, a dynamics or change through time can be observed on the migration of fishes from this torrent, taking on account that not all traveling species do migrate at the same time or at the same velocity, but each one shows differences on migratory patterns, possibly responding to environmental, reproductive or dietary factors. Most of the analyzed species are omnivorous and depend on allochthonous material, eventually feeding on some of the autochthonous material. This can be due to the fact that, as other Amazon rivers, the Caqueta river presents cyclic variations its water levels, causing the quantity and quality of food offer to respond to these fluctuations. 23109: A total of 170 species of amphibians and reptiles were identified over a four-year period at the Tiputini Biodiversity Station (TBS), Ecuadorian Amazonia. TBS protects approximately 650 hectares of primary rainforest. 23110: The herpetofauna of the Rio Guajalito Protection Forest, northwestern Ecuador, was studied over a period of four-years. The species richness and relative abundance of the amphibians and reptiles was determined through the application of ‘inventory multiple methods’ (visual encounter survey transects, leaf litter plots, larval survey, and random sampling points). A new species of frog of the genus Phyllonastes endemic to the area, several restricted-range species of the genus Eleutherodactylus (Amphibia), Dipsas and Atractus (Reptilia) are present at the forest. Using data obtained since the late 70’s, several changes in the composition and relative abundance of species have been observed. At least three taxa of amphibians are extirpated or extinct and some local declines have been detected on anurans and lizards. The extinctions and declines at the area could be related to several factors working synergistically: habitat destruction, introduced species, diseases and local climate change. However, the patterns of changes of the community of amphibians and reptiles at the Rio Guajalito Protection Forest are similar to those reported for Monteverde, Costa Rica, not just for the herpetofauna but for birds as well, suggesting a link to recent climate changes. Issues concerning the conservation of the amphibians and reptiles of the region are discussed.

23111: Ecuador has the biggest number of amphibian species per unit of area in the world (427 species in 276,840 km2). Glass frogs (Centrolenidae) with 30 species, constitute 7.06 % of the Ecuadorian anurans. However, the current state of knowledge of this family in Ecuador is still very basic. Several species of glass frogs are currently undescribed, confused with previously described taxa, not yet reported from the country but present in local museum collections, not yet discovered in Ecuador, or even described under two different names. The genus Hyalinobatrachium is poorly known in the country (four species), but at least three undescribed taxa are present in the western lowlands of Ecuador. Among the genera Cochranella and Centrolene, at least 6 new species are known from tropical and subtropical areas in western and eastern slopes of the Ecuadorian Andes. Several characters such as the patterns of skin, eye, peritoneum and pericardium color, the prepollicall spine, the nuptial pad, and the presence of the bulla are discussed, especially around its taxonomic potential. At least one undescribed taxon from western lowlands of Ecuador is critically endangered, if not extinct. In the last decade, conservative estimates indicate that at least 26 species of Ecuadorian amphibians have declined or gone extinct, two of them belong to the family Centrolenidae. The reasons for this crisis are not clear but have been related to habitat destruction, climate change, and fungal disease such as the chytridiomycosis

23112: The gopher tortoise has been the focus of a number of conservation strategies. Of these, relocation has been one of the most controversial. Concerns stem from potential impacts on social structure, genetic mixing and spread of infectious disease. A post-relocation movement study was conducted to better understand tortoise behavior following relocation and to improve relocation success. Adults and juveniles relocated from McIntosh County, Georgia, to Aiken County, South Carolina, were separated into experimental groups then penned for varying lengths of time in 1 ha enclosures. All groups were overwintered between capture and release. Release group 1 was released shortly after emerging in the spring of 2002. Release group 2 was released in July 2002. Release Group 3 was released in September 2002. Movement and diffusion of tortoises were monitored during the first active season. Animals that established a burrow within the compartment and regular home range areas were generally considered successful. Failures characterized by a number of factors including straight-line movement, failure to establish burrows, movement outside dispersal boundaries and repeated dispersal were more common in the first release group. Release group 1 showed the lowest success rate (30.7%), while release group 3 showed the highest success rate (91.7%). Release group 2 had an intermediate rate of success (61.5%). Long-term penning of multiple tortoises may significantly improve relocation success. Additionally, information is now available on site selection for burrows, density changes from pre-relocation conditions and tortoise interaction following relocation.

23113: In Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, we have observed site-attached juveniles of Pholidichthys leucotaenia leave their burrows at dawn and return at dusk. During the day they feed on plankton as far as 50 m from their home burrows. Swarms from a single burrow vary from 30 to over 10,000 juveniles. We are raising groups of juveniles that have grown in eight months from 2 to 15 cm TL in two 80-gallon aquaria: (1) the "reef tank" is a "control" with 18 cm-deep coral sand and large coral stone formations; and (2) an experimental aquarium with less than 2 cm sand depth and a fiberglass tunnel, open-sided against the aquarium glass. Juveniles in aquaria also form loose swarms in their limited space. At night they go into shallow burrows they have made in the sand under rocks in the "reef tank." 23114: Many predators capture their prey through ambush. In order to effectively ambush prey, a predator must locate a site wherein profitable prey are likely to return. One means by which predators evaluate potential ambush sites is by recognizing high-use areas through chemical cues deposited by their prey. I examine the selection of ambush sites by timber rattlesnakes exposed to trails made from chemical extracts of the integument of various prey species. I evaluate the role of feeding experience by comparing ambush site selection before and after timber rattlesnakes have experience with prey items. Timber rattlesnakes are more likely to select ambush sites adjacent to chemical trails from prey they have feeding experience with. However, only snakes feeding on relatively large prey showed an increase in responsiveness. Furthermore, increased responsiveness after feeding experience was only exhibited in trials using integumentary extracts of mammals (the natural prey of timber rattlesnakes), and not fish. These findings show that timber rattlesnakes can learn to recognize chemical cues present on the integument of food items, and use that knowledge to modify their ambush hunting strategies.

23115: The human exploitation of the Amazonian floodplain has caused major landscape alterations, primarily due to logging, cattle farming, agriculture and commercial fishing. The flooded forest of the white waters rivers are the feeding ground for many organisms, specially fish. The aim of this study was to verify the relationship between the consumption of forest litter (seeds, fruits, leaves and also canopy insects) and the amount of flooded forest in floodplain lakes in Central Amazon, Brazil. Fish were collected in July 2000 in 11 lakes, using a set of 13 gill nets, in a 24 hour period, at each lake. The stomachs were analyzed using occurrence and point methods. The amount of flooded forest was estimated using radar images (SLAR). The abundance, biomass and richness of fish species that fed on allochthonous items were related with the flooded forest, using simple linear regressions. The richness of species that fed on allochthonous items varied between 5 and 19; their abundance range from 9 to 119 individuals and their biomass range from 972 to 24,845 g. The biomass of fish feeding on allochthonous items was positively (R2=0.045; N=11; p=0.04) related with to amount of flooded forest, which suggests that the conservation of the flooded forest is important for fish production and consequently the Amazon fisheries.

23116: Some years ago an unknown bythitid fish was photographed in a limestone cave in Tomia, an island off southeastern Sulawesi. Subsequently a ripe male from the same cave was sent to us for study. We identified it as an undescribed species of the bythitine genus Grammonus. This is the sixth known species of Grammonus, which occurs in the warmer parts of all oceans. The new species differs from the other Grammonus species in size of head, numbers of anal fin rays and vertebrae and its unique otolith. 23117: Embryos of the cypriniform fish, Rivulus marmoratus, were maintained either in a static container or rotating cell culture system (RCCS) to assess the effects of prolonged exposure to RCCS conditions. The RCCS is used to simulate ground-based microgravity conditions analogous to those experienced in space. Experimental embryos were placed in the RCCS shortly after fertilization and maintained until hatching, approximately 21 days later. Survival of viable embryos was 100% in both experimental and control groups. Control post-hatchlings exhibited normal morphology and locomotory movements associated with swimming, as well as successful visual tracking and prey capture of live Artemia nauplia. In addition, they were highly responsive to tactile stimuli. In contrast, experimental fish exhibited extensive curvature of the axial skeleton, abnormal elongation of the lower jaw and marked postorbital cranial depression. Experimental fish were also unresponsive to tactile stimuli and failed to visually track or capture live prey. All experimental fish died within 7 days of hatching. A subsequent histological examination of the brains of both experimental and control individuals revealed a conspicuous lack of neural aggregations within the white matter regions of experimental animals, as well as a reduction in ventricle volume. In addition, among experimental fish, retinal layers of the eye were expanded resulting in either the lack of development, or occlusion, of the vitreous humor region, rendering image formation impossible.

23118: Hypsophrys nicaraguense, a cichlid native to Costa Rica and Nicaragua, has long been known to be unique among substrate spawning neotropical cichlids because of its nonadhesive eggs (other substrate spawners lay eggs with adhesive threads that attach the egg to a hard substrate). 23119: Due to the high pace of habitat destruction in Neotropical countries, the collection of biodiversity data from poorly sampled areas became a priority. Many sampling methods are currently available to herpetologists, but detailed comparisons of their strengths and weaknesses in neotropical regions are scarce. We compare the effectiveness of haphazard sampling versus a combination of pitfall traps and drift fences in Amazon Rainforest at Guajará-Mirim, Rondônia, Brazil. Haphazard sampling was conducted during 90 days by experienced collectors, whereas 75 sets of pitfall traps were used during 33 days. Each set consisted of 4 plastic buckets arranged as an Y and connected by 5m of plastic fence; sets were placed approximately 10m from each other. We produced species accumulation curves based on 10,000 randomizations (with replacement) using the software EstimateS. We used non-linear regression analyses to find the best fit of the data among the Clench, Linear, and Exponential models. The Clench model provided the best fit for both anurans and lizard accumulation curves. For lizards, models indicate that richness estimates are the same using either sampling method, but the rate of species accumulation is higher with pitfall traps. In general, Gymnophthalmids were collected more effectively with pitfall traps, whereas Polychrotids and Tropidurids, with haphazard sampling. For anurans, richness estimates using haphazard sampling were approximately twice those from pitfall traps. This resulted especially from the poor performance of pitfall traps in sampling hylids coupled with the high diversity of this group in the region. The inflexion point of all curves is reached only after approximately 30 days of collecting. Our results indicate that short-term herpetofaunal inventories in the Amazon may grossly underestimate richness and that a combination of different sampling techniques is the best strategy to obtain reliable estimates.

23120: Early studies of amphibian metamorphosis focused mainly on understanding the physiological mechanisms that controlled transformation from an aquatic larva to a terrestrial form. Studies of how the environment might influence the process were generally limited to abiotic factors like temperature or concentrations of elements like oxygen or iodine. The latter, for example, was suggested as a possible explanation for the delay or absence of metamorphosis under some circumstances. Experiments were usually done in the laboratory and were designed to uncover the proximate causes of metamorphosis. Models of population dynamics prior to the 1970s generally assumed that all individuals in a population were alike. Natural historians knew that the assumption was wrong, but it was needed to simplify the mathematical models. Individual variation is no longer dismissed as easily since there is now sufficient evidence suggesting that intraspecific specialization has important consequences for population dynamics. In the mid- 1970s an interest in testing how individual variation affected population dynamics and some 50 years of research into the causes of amphibian metamorphosis intersected. Ecologists began analyzing amphibian metamorphosis as a context-dependent process; transformation was envisioned as a function of an individual's performance within a group of congeners, and by extension, other species. Investigators combined models with laboratory and field experiments to elucidate the proximate and ultimate causes of metamorphosis. Research over the last 30 years has demonstrated how growth, morphology, larval performance, and trophic level are functions of population and community dynamics. We still, however, have not adequately connected population dynamics and physiological mechanisms. I will review how a range of studies that integrate phenotypic plasticity, size-structured populations, and amphibian metamorphosis exemplify what some are calling eco-devo, or ecology and development.

23121: Pathogens are among the suspected causes of declining amphibian populations, but studying pathogens in small, threatened populations is ethically and experimentally problematic. We need model host-pathogen systems in which sample sizes are large enough for good designs, but the pathogen does not threaten the host with extinction. We report on viral geographic variation, persistence, and differences in host susceptibility of a model salamander-virus system. Insights from this system are helping us understand the ecological and evolutionary interactions that may threaten amphibian populations. Our model pathogen is Ambystoma tigrinum virus (ATV), which causes recurrent epidemics in tiger salamander populations in western North America from southern Canada to southern Arizona. ATV is a large cytoplasmic dsDNA virus that causes systemic infections. The genome of ATV is sequenced, and an analysis of structural and functional genes reveals geographical relationships among viral isolates from Canada to Arizona. We studied ATV persistence in tiger salamanders (Ambystoma tigrinum). The virus is transmitted via direct contact, feeding on infected tissues, and in water with high viral titers. ATV degrades quickly in pond water and dry mud, precluding long-term persistence in the environment; alternate syntopic hosts are unknown. ATV is usually lethal within 2-3 weeks, although some salamanders lose overt symptoms of infection and survive indefinitely. In one experiment ATV was re-isolated from 40% of these survivors, and transmission to uninfected salamanders occurred. Sublethal infections also occur in natural populations and appear to be the means by which ATV persists between epidemics. Lastly, a cross-infection, laboratory study of two Canadian population clusters separated by 800 km revealed significant differences in susceptibility to viral isolates. The causes of the differences are unknown, but several hypotheses are being tested.

23122: The Rio skate is an endemic species from the Southwest Atlantic. It is abundant off Argentina and Uruguay, which may make it an important benthic predator. However, the feeding habits of Rioraja agassizi are unknown in the region. We analyzed the feeding habits of the Rio skate from two areas: the La Plata River estuary (LP, 34-37° S) and off Blanca Bay (BB, 39-41° S). We examined 140 specimens, of which 114 had prey into the stomach. The specimens were sorted into four groups: juveniles from LP (15), juveniles from BB (42), adults from LP (18), and adults from BB (39). Cumulative prey curves as a function of sample size were constructed in order to estimate the minimum sample size for describing accurately the diet of each group. All curves showed that the sample size was large enough as to describe the diet of each group. Prey importance was quantified through the percent index of relative importance (IRI). Also, the prey- specific importance index (Pi) was calculated. The IRI gives information about the population feeding habits, while Pi brings individual-based information on foraging strategy. In general, decapod crustaceans were the most common prey (IRI = 55.5%). The diet of juveniles from both areas was composed mainly of amphipods (IRILP = 65.1%, IRIBB = 42.5%). Adults of both areas were mostly specialized in the consumption of decapod crustaceans (IRILP = 88.6%, IRIBB = 64.8%). Polychaetes and cephalochordates were consumed more often in BB than in LP. Pi showed that most juvenile individuals (43.1%) were specialized in the consumption of amphipods (Pi = 66.5). In contrast most adults (58.9%) consumed mainly decapod crustaceans (Pi = 76.3). This ontogenetic shift in diet could be due to several causes such as changes in mouth structure and dentition, changes in energetic requirements and/or prey availability.

23123: We studied demographics of the Yazoo shiner Notropis rafinesquei, a species endemic to the upper Yazoo River system, in three northern Mississippi streams. We sampled each population approximately monthly from March 1993 to October 1994. Preliminary analysis of length- frequency distributions suggests several life history features. Spawning, as evidenced by appearance of young-of-year in samples, occurred twice each year (late spring-summer and fall) in all streams. Recruits from spring spawning reached 10-20 mm standard length by July-August, and by October are large enough to potentially participate in fall spawning. Length-frequency distributions were similar at all sites in both years. However, animals appeared to live 2-3 years in Buckhorn and Cypress creeks, but only 1.5-2 years in Hotopha Creek. Maximum adult size was lower in Hotopha Creek. Our results show that the Yazoo shiner shares life history traits with related species, particularly the orangefin shiner Notropis ammophilus. Further analysis of life history strategies of the Yazoo shiner and comparisons among close relatives will allow discriminations of ancestral characteristics from species-specific adaptations.

23124: Exotic invasive species established may become pests, outcompeting or eliminating local species, especially endemics, when developing highly similar niches. Competition levels have been reported in many places worldwide, either for food, breeding places, or shelter, and comes usually from predation, interbreeding, or parasitizing. Mexican nation-wide reports are known only in freshwater fishes, and show an increase from 54 in 1984 to 100 in 2002. Several localities with long recorded history of collections disclose reductions of 15 to 100% of native species, as compared to invasives. International programs by USF&W and FAO are also responsible for most introductions or training, combining with national programs to produce food for people, usually disregarding native species. Exotic amphibians and reptiles in Mexico are poorly recorded, only 16 are reported herein. Fishes have shown indications of replacement, competition, or hybridization with native species in Mexico, whereas amphibians and reptiles show no similar evidence. Differences between responses in ichtyological and herpetological groups may be due to their biological properties, collecting methods and deficiencies or lack of interest of specialists. Research in their presence, distribution and impacts is needed on the relationships between invasive and native species, to develop strategies for protecting Mexican biodiversity.

23125: The Mesoamerican region contains a large diversity of fresh water environments. Their understanding is urgent due to the apparent deterioration. Their utilization as sources of water and dumping sites for domestic, farm and industrial refuse represents the main anthropogenic threat to their physical and biotic integrity. However, it is also evident how little attention they have received from planning processes and environmental legislation to support their protection and conservation. In this contrasting context, between the imperative need for resource conservation and management toward the future, through the Mesoamerican Biotic Resources Network we have integrated a task force to initiate a discussion among Mexico and the Central American countries to point out and systematize the knowledge of fresh-water ecosystems that has been accumulated in the region and the perspectives that multiple use, planning and legislation permit for its adequate use, and to establish a starting point toward integrated discussion of the strategies that allow conservation and sustainable management in these ecosystems based not only on its large biodiversity, but also on the quality and quantity of environmental services furnished to the Mesoamerican inhabitants. We have defined fresh water fishes as our indicator species in terms of (1) the vast knowledge we have on them with respect to other aquatic organisms, and (2) they are easy to collect and identify. As an outcome of a workshop held on July of 2002 at the Universidad Autonoma de Queretaro, Mexico, an ample number of ideas, proposals and recommendations regarding research needs, public policies, conservation and management strategies were gathered. As well as an evaluation of the current status was also obtained, where the impact of exotics, habitat loss and environmental degradation in general, has led to the extinction of numerous species, a situation that is most severe in Mexico where 19 fresh water fish species have been lost.

23126: Damselfishes (Labroidei, Pomacentridae) constitute a diverse group (>340 sp.) of marine fishes that have been thought to exhibit little trophic diversity. Despite widespread interest in labroid feeding, the morphological and functional variation of pomacentrid jaws has not been quantified. We combined morphometric analyses of the oral jaws of damselfishes with biomechanical models of jaw function in order to measure the functional diversity of pomacentrid jaws. Biomechanical modeling generated estimates of jaw functional parameters that are strongly associated with trophic habitats. Results show that accounting for muscle morphology and physiology yield different estimates of jaw mechanics than bone lever ratios alone. We compared the functional diversity of damselfish oral jaws to those wrasses (Labridae), another species rich lineage of marine fishes. Results show that the morphological and functional diversity of damselfish oral jaws was greater than expected. The hypervolume of shape space occupied by damselfishes is similar to that occupied by wrasses although the two groups have different functional specializations. The lower jaw lever of many pomacentrids confers a high mechanical advantage (0.15-0.70) and is extreme in the coral eating species Cheiloprion labiatus. Surprisingly, the bite of C. labiatus is estimated to have a mechanical advantage (0.70) greater than those predicted for parrotfishes (0.50). A significant finding of the study was that the hypervolumes of shape space occupied by wrasses and damselfishes are completely independent. We reject the hypotheses that the low degree of trophic diversity reported for damselfishes is associated with low functional and morphological diversity of their oral jaws relative to other fish clades.

23127: Developmental rates of young of the year fish may be influenced by temporal and spatial variability of physicochemical factors within a nursery area. To elucidate the relationship between developmental state and environmental variation, we collected larval and juvenile Brevoortia patronus from unique habitats within an oligohaline estuary. Over 22,000 B. patronus (19-88 mm TL) were collected by beach seining from five stations in the Lake Pontchartrain estuary, Louisiana from February to June of 2001 and 2002. The majority of the specimens were collected from the lower estuary near freshwater tributaries or in low salinity and turbid waters. Relative to total length, specimens directly associated with the tributaries had higher weights, a deeper keel, and a more sophisticated gut. Specimens collected outside of the tributaries immediate influence were more likely to retain a shallow keel and a simpler gut over a wide range of total length. Habitat dependent variation in morphological development may convey a survival advantage to young of the year B. patronus associated with Lake Pontchartrain's tributaries.
