23362: In each vertebrate stock (agnathan, chondrichthyan, actynopterygian and tetrapod) the brain had separate evolution, even similar tendencies can be found. Considering their brain/body weight ratio several batoids match birds and mammals, and surpass the other vertebrates. In mammals and birds astrocytes predominate and large brain areas are nearly devoid of GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein, an astroglial marker), where, however, astrocytes can be visualized by the immunostaining of glutamine synthetase or S-100 protein. In reptiles, however, the ependymoglia xhibit GFAP immunopositivity in every brain area. For the present study, a spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) was used as a representative of the less advanced elasmobranchs. Batoids have a more advanced brain. Of them a skate (Raia erinacea), and rays of Myliobatiformes: Dasyatis pastinaca, Urolophus halleri, Mobula japanica, Potamotrygon sp. were processed for immunohistochemical detection of GFAP, and, in some cases, Gln synthetase and S-100. In the spiny dogfish ependymoglia were found, which displayed GFAP immunopositivity in almost even distribution. The meningeal surface was lined by endfeet of radial glia, and the perivascular glia also consisted of fibers. In the skate brain, however, radial ependymoglia occurred only at a few segments of the narrow ventricular system. The meningeal and perivascular glia were composed mainly from astrocytes, but their positions to the surface was different from that seen in either mammals or birds. Rare but huge astrocytes appeared in the diencephalon, mesencephalon and cerebellum. To enhance the resemblance to the glial structure of mammals and birds, extended areas of the skate brain displayed a lack of GFAP immunopositivity. S-100 protein and Gln synthetase immunostainings detected astrocytes in these areas. The distribution of astrocytes did not correlate strictly with the thickness of the brain wall, in contrast to the classical supposal of Horstmann (1954). The data obtained on the rays proved to be congruent with these observations. Further observations suggest that in batoids the glia/neuron ration is similar to those of mammals and birds, but the satellite cells are more numerous. Further studies are required to see if the findings also apply to galeomorph sharks.

23363: The conservation and sustainable exploitation of the world's shark populations has been a concern among marine fisheries biologists for decades. However, highly variable molecular markers suitable for investigating population structure and other aspects of molecular ecology are available for few shark species. In this study, we characterize 1 monomorphic and 15 polymorphic microsatellite loci isolated from the blacktip shark, Carcharhinus limbatus, and present results of cross-species amplification in 11 Carcharhinus species, 4 additional genera from the family Carcharhinidae, and 2 species from the genus Sphyrna. An unenriched library of 2,304 cloned fragments produced only 36 (1.6%) colonies positive for dinucleotide repeat motifs, indicating microsatellite loci are relatively scarce in blacktip sharks as in other carcharhinid species. We subsequently produced an enriched library with a much higher (48%) fraction of positive clones. Heterozygosities of polymorphic loci ranged from 0.04 to 0.96 with 2 to 22 alleles per locus in 28 blacktip sharks tested. Amplification products were observed at 9 to 13 loci in 10 Carcharhinus species with 5 to 11 loci polymorphic per species. All of the other species examined were polymorphic at 1 to 8 loci. The range of variation and widespread cross-species amplification of these microsatellite loci demonstrate their potential utility for investigating the population structure and molecular ecology of numerous shark species.

23364: The French Guiana river system regroups rivers and swamps. The ichtyofauna of the rivers is characterized by a strong endemism. The swamps shelter a particular ichthyofauna. One finds there species adapted to slow and stagnant waters and able to resist to weak concentrations in oxygen. Such are " atipas " (Hoplosternum littorale), catfish presenting the peculiarity of power to inhale atmospheric air through their intestine, or " the eel tété " (Lepidosiren paradoxa) South American Dipneuste, who possesses two lungs and sinks into a hole when the swamp dries out. An effort of inventory of three years on the swamp of Kaw was made on more than twenty sites: main bed of the river of Kaw upstream to the village; downstream till the middle way of the mouth; tributaries on the upstream sector; ponds and varied puddles. Different techniques of fishing (trammel nets, gillnets, seine, castnet, handnet) allowed to collect more than 110 species, what, considering knowledge acquired by our predecessors, increased the specific richness of the swamp up to 156 species on this area. Among these 156 species, about sixty are recorded for the first time to Kaw and 3 or 4 of them could be new for the science. The swamp of Kaw has a specific richness equivalent of some river drainage of French Guiana. Nevertheless, the structure of the swamp (a coastal plain surrounded with reliefs rising until 350-400 m of height) is very original. It is a drainage basin without the characteristic intermediate fauna of the medium course of rivers: one cross from upstream species to upper lower streams and swamps species. The ichthyofauna is diversified and contrasted because of the heterogeneity of biotopes between the coastal plain and the mountain. 4 types of fish community can be found. Fish communities of the swamp of Kaw are fragile. The swamp represents besides, with the peninsula of Cayenne, the limit West of distribution of several amazon species (black caiman, dipneuste). These communities are also subjected to fishing pressure. Some species as Atipa are the object of a more or less commercial fishing and require the implementation of plans of management even of protection.

23365: Some aspects of the biology of Zagros tooth-carp, Aphanius vladykovi, an endemic species from Chahar-Mahall-va-Bakhtiari province in central Iran, was studied by regular monthly collections and direct observations in aquaria during a full year. The main objective of the study was to reveal its biology for rearing it in aquaria. Specimens from Modar-Dokhtar spring of Gandoman were collected and biometric and biological features were measured on the specimens. The gut content was mostly consisted of freshwater shrimp and the relative length of gut (RLG) was 0.7, in average; an indication of a carnivorous diet. The eggs were large with an average diameter of 1 mm. The average working total fecundity was 110 eggs and the working relative fecundity was 73 eggs/g of the body weight. The Gonadosomatic index (GSI) indicated that the reproduction period of the species was in March-May with a high peak in the middle of April. The species was euryhaline and eurythermal and preferred neutral to basic waters. Though tolerant to hyperoxia, it is found in well oxygenated waters. Considering its small size, beautiful color, well tolerance to different physiochemical conditions of aquaria and its adaptation to aquarium fish foods, this fish is a suitable species for keeping in aquaria.

23366: Vertebral variation in fishes may be influenced by genetic and environmental factors that affect individuals during embryonic development. Nevertheless, vertebral counts have value in systematics below, at and above the species level and for species identification, especially of juvenile specimens. We are investigating vertebral count variation in the morphologically diverse Pimelodidae, a family comprising 30 genera and over 110 valid species. Other meristic characters associated with the post cranial axial skeleton are also investigated and defined. Vertebral and other counts were obtained from dry or cleared/stained material, and radiographs of ethanol preserved specimens representing 82 species (N=740). Total vertebral counts in Pimelodidae ranged between 36-73. Within species the mean vertebral count range was 3.3 (maximum 8 for species with N>5, not including Hypophthalmus). We present vertebral count data within the available phylogenetic framework and contrast cases where these serve well or not as phylogenetic characters. At the species level we illustrate a possible case of species discovery in a widespread pimelodid, Sorubimichthys, between the Amazon and Orinoco basins. High and variable vertebral counts in Hypophthalmus are problematic for distinguishing variation.

23367: The River Continuum Concept (RCC) suggests that longitudinal changes in the physical characteristics of a river channel can have predictable effects on the distribution of habitats and biota. The objective of this study was to investigate the influence of spatial variation on the distribution of habitats and the structure of fish communities in headwater streams in the Jau National Park, in Central Amazonia. A series of physical, chemical and biological parameters were measured in 34 independent headwater streams during the months of November - December of 1998. A total of 66 fish species from 24 families were collected and classified into seven trophic guilds: allocthonous insectivore, autocthonous insectivore, general insectivore, piscivore, detritivore/algivore, detritivore/insetivore and insectivore/piscivore. Four significant correlations were found between bottom substrates, one positive (log-clay) and three negative correlations (rock-leaf, leaf-sand and rock-log). These correlations were linked primarily to differences in geology and geomorphology, independent of stream size. Three ordinal axes were created from the physico-chemical variables including bottom substrate coverage. Significant relationships (linear regression) were obtained between the stream size axis (E1) and the biomass of allocthonous and autocthonous insectivores and piscivore numbers, as predicted by the RCC. The biomass of piscivores and detritivore insectivores varied significantly with the sand-leaf axis (E2), the former being associated with sandy bottoms and the latter with leafy bottoms. The biomass of piscivores and number of autocthonous insectivores varied significantly along the leaf-root/rock axis (E3), both groups being positively associated with root/rock substrates. However, a highly significant relationship was encountered between substrate diversity and fish species diversity. Variations in the distribution and diversity of bottom substrates, independent of stream size, were the most important factors influencing fish community structure in these systems.
23368: There is a growing literature on patterns of skeletal development in both fishes and amphibians. Most studies rely on the staining of cartilaginous mucopolysaccharides with Alcian blue and bony calcium deposits with alizarin red. Consistent and biologically meaningful evolutionary trends have been revealed through such comparative studies. There is also a growing understanding of the developmental mechanisms that underlie cartilage and bone formation. Key genes have recently been described that regulate both cartilage and bone differentiation in several model organisms, including zebrafish, mouse, and the domestic chicken. Surprisingly, many of these genes have been cloned and their expression patterns characterized in early stages of the Xenopus laevis embryo, yet few have been examined in the developing amphibian skeleton. I am interested in synthesizing the information gained through morphological studies of skeletal development with current molecular models of skeletal differentiation. I present here the preliminary results of in situ hybridizations of several RNA probes from genes implicated in cartilage and bone formation in the developing skull of Xenopus laevis. This work will elucidate the conservation and variation of developmental models, and begin to characterize the molecular basis of bone and cartilage formation associated with amphibian metamorphosis.

23369: Atmospheric testing of thermonuclear devices during the 1950s and 1960s created a global radiocarbon (14C) signal in the ocean environment. The bomb-generated radiocarbon signal retained in fish otoliths can be used as a permanent, time-specific marker of the radiocarbon present in ambient seawater, making it a useful tool in age validation of fishes. The goal of this study was to determine radiocarbon levels in otoliths of the age-validated yelloweye rockfish (Sebastes ruberrimus) to establish a chronometer for radiocarbon in the waters of southeast Alaska and to validate age of the quillback rockfish (Sebastes maliger) using this chronometer. Radiocarbon values from the first year's growth of 43 yelloweye rockfish otoliths were plotted against estimated birth year to produce a radiocarbon time series for southeast Alaskan waters from 1940 to 1990. Radiocarbon measured in quillback rockfish otoliths, with estimated birth years from 1950 to 1985, was similar to values recorded for the yelloweye rockfish during the same period. The agreement between the rockfish records successfully validated the age estimates for the quillback rockfish and the ageing methodology of otoliths for this species. The establishment of a radiocarbon chronometer in the waters of southeast Alaska, and the successful age validation of the quillback rockfish based on this chronometer provides a valuable tool useful for future age validation of marine fishes in this region. 23371: Several degraded Carolina bay wetlands on the Savannah River Site have been subjected to experimental management in an effort to functionally restore these valuable habitats. This project evaluates responses of amphibian populations to this restoration effort. Carolina bays are important habitat for pond-breeding salamander and frog species. Sixteen bays were monitored: three reference bays (functionally intact), three control bays (with active drainage ditches), six treatment bays, and four intact bays near two of the treatment bays (in effect creating two meta- populations). The first year of the study was a pre-restoration year, the bays were then restored during 2001, and 2002 was a post-restoration year. Restoration activities included harvesting pine trees, replanting wetland vegetation, and plugging drainage ditches. Each bay is partially encircled with drift fences and pitfall traps. Amphibians at each bay were captured, batch marked, and released between January and July, 2000-2002. Individuals were given visible implanted elastomer batch marks that designated the year and bay of capture, the age (adult or juvenile), and for salamanders, whether it was captured entering or leaving the wetland. More than 25,000 amphibians of 22 species have been captured to date. Comparisons of population estimates and species diversity between the treatment groups over time shows that after the bays were restored, the amphibian community changed. At least two of the restored bays are supporting a larger number of amphibians than any of the other bays, including the reference bays. Of more than 6,000 salamanders captured during this study, 13% have been captured more than once, while 8% of more than 20,000 anurans have been recaptured. Drought conditions in 2002 caused a 64.1 % decrease in amphibian captures at the control bays and a 62.5 % decrease at the reference bays; however, the restored bays experienced a 4.7 % increase in captures.

23372: The subfamily Colubrinae has approximately 600 species distributed in 87 genera, with 14 genera known for South America. They are relatively well defined by their hemipenial morphology: their hemipenis is non-symmetric with a simple sulcus spermaticus and, when bilobed, the sulcus runs along the right lobe (Zaher 1999). We analyzed a total of 30 species representing all 14 South American genera (Chironius, Dendrophidion, Drymarchon, Drymoluber, Drymobius, Leptophis, Masticophis, Mastigodryas, Oxybelis, Pseustes, Rhinobotryum, Simophis, Spilotes, and Stenorrhina) and 84 species representing 33 genera from other continents. We failed to find hemipenial characters exclusive for the South American genera. The simplest hemipenial pattern found in Chironius, Drymoluber, Mastigodryas, and Rhinobotryum consists of a non capitated hemipenis with a single lobe ornamented by papilated calyces and a body ornamented by spines. The base of the organ is either naked or with spines and shows a basal naked pocket that varies in length and depth. On the other hand, Drymarchon shows a significantly different hemipenial pattern, with a slightly bilobed, triangular form, and a lobe ornamented by spinulated calices and a body covered by uniformly small spines. The distal surface of the lobe retains a naked area, depressed in the middle. This hemipenial pattern is unique among the South American genera, being similar to some Neartic species. Dendrophidion shows a hemipenis with a capitular groove around the edge of the lobe which is ornamented by papilated calices that tend to form horizontally directed flounces through the fusion and development of their horizontal walls. Similarly, Stenorrhina shows flounces ornamenting the hemipenial lobe. Pseustes and Spilotes has a hemipenial pattern different from all other analyzed genera, yet similar between them: both sulcate and asulcate surfaces are naked; the lateral surfaces of the lobe show large calices at their base, which diminish in size toward the distal portion and gradually fade toward the center. This feature is here interpreted as a putative synapomorphy uniting these two genera.

23373: The tegu lizard Tupinambis merianae possesses a post-hepatic septum (PHS) which divides its body cavity into two parts: the cranial cavity contains lungs and liver, and the caudal cavity, the remaining viscera. Despite being a simple, transversely orientated membrane and containing smooth muscle, the PHS is of demonstrated importance for breathing in the animals. In tegus with surgically removed PHS, stomach and intestine are displaced cranially, thereby reducing the space for the lungs significantly. This results not only in reduced resting and maximum lung volumes but also alters the compliance of the respiratory system. During locomotion on a treadmill, tegus without PHS are not able to increase tidal volume but increase breathing frequency to compensate for the reduced ventilation. Tegus without PHS, however, are not able to reach the values of minute ventilation shown by tegus with intact PHS during slow locomotion. These results demonstrate that the PHS is of eminent importance for respiration in tegus. Its main function is to prevent a cranial displacement of the viscera but because of that the PHS reduces the work of breathing in tegus and facilitates the inflation of the stiff lungs. This accessory breathing structure is unique among lizards and may explain in part the dominance of tegus as predatory lizards in the neotropics. Furthermore, the PHS of Tupinambis may shed some light on the evolution of an analog structure: the mammalian diaphragm.

23374: The UNISINOS Fish Ecology Laboratory works since 1997 in the Lagoa dos Quadros with the objective to develop a plan of management for this lagoon. Fisheries of inland waters are regulated by Brazilian federal laws, Portaria no. 466 Nov.1977 and annual legislation of protection period. The use of gill and trammel nets is restricted to mesh sizes higher than 35 mm (70 mm stretched mesh size), hook and line with the maximum number of 100 hooks for fisherman are permitted, maze gear, drag nets, among others methods are forbidden. The adjusted sustainable management of the fishing resources is made difficult by the current law, where the access to the resources is not limited, therefore all fishing permitted by IBAMA or associates of fish Federation can fish. During the period of 1997-2001 four species had dominated the captures: viola (Loricariichthys anus), biru (Cyphocharax voga), tambicu (Oligosarcus robustus) and traira (Hoplias malabararicus). Considering that the length of the first maturation corresponds to the average value for 30 mm mesh in the gill and trammel nets, L.anus (29,4/30,2 cm), C.voga (18,7/18,8 cm), O. robustus (23,9/23,6 cm) and H. malabaricus (26,0/28,7 cm), the mesh sizes reduction would not negatively interfere with the natural reproduction of larger sized and dominant species but would increase captures at a rate of 17% - 130%. Our proposal for future management is to reconsider existing regulations. We recommend that the sizes of mesh and the use of fyke and trap nets should be more flexible, based on the results of scientific monitoring. A precondition for all future management plans is a restriction of the access to fisheries resources where only local communities should obtain licenses for fishing.

23375: Gonadal cycles of pleudodire turtles are less studied than those of cryptodire turtles. I investigated gonadal cycles of Chelodina oblonga, C. steindachneri and Pseudemydura umbrina (Chelidae) in South-western Australia and of Erymnochelys madagascariensis (Podocnemidae), Pelomedusa subrufa, and Pelusios castanoides (Pelomedusidae) in Western Madagascar. The gonadal cycles of the Chelidae in South-western Australia are generally similar to those of many cryprodire turtles. However, the cycles of the Pelomedusidae and Podocnemidae in Madagascar show some peculiarities. For example, despite producing several clutches per reproductive season, ovaries of Pelusios and Pelomedusa do not show staged size classes of growing, vitellogenic follicles that represent subsequent clutches of eggs at the beginning of the reproductive season as shown by many other turtles that produce multiple clutches per reproductive season. It seems that follicles for subsequent clutches only start growing after the completion of the previous clutch. Erymnochelys females have a biannual reproductive cycle and an extended nesting period from September (late dry season) until April/May (end of wet season). This pattern seems to differ from that of its closest relatives, the South American river turtles of the genus Podocnemis. In contrast to the other species studied here that show postnuptial spermatogenesis, Erymnochelys males have a pre-nuptial spermatogenetic cycle. The gonadal cycles of Erymnochelys are reminiscent of sea turtles rather than of typical freshwater turtles.

23376: With seven endemic chelonians (Geochelone platynota, Heosemys depressa, Lissemys scutata, Morenia ocellata, Kachuga trivittata, Nilssonia formosa, Chitra sp.) Myanmar has the highest chelonian endemism of Southeast Asian countries and the highest chelonian diversity with at least 26 non-marine species. Of the seven endemic species, the softshell turtles N. formosa and Chitra sp. and the Roofed Turtle K. trivittata are large-bodied, highly aquatic river turtles. Morenia ocellata and L. scutata are also highly aquatic, but of smaller adult size and not restricted to the main river channels. A turtle survey at the upper Chindwin River and the Myitnge River in July/August 2002 revealed that all large river turtles are declining and many populations are heavily depleted, with K. trivittata today being the rarest and most endangered of all river turtles. No live specimens of K. trivitatta had been recorded between 1935 and 2002. The major threat to K. trivitatta and other river turtles seems to be over-exploitation of the turtles and their eggs for human consumption and trade. Kachuga trivitatta populations collapse and disappear much faster than those of the large softshell river turtles Nilssonia formosa, Chitra sp. and Amyda cartilaginea. Despite being specifically targeted for exploitation, the large softshell turtles persist longer under exploitation pressure. Kachuga trivittata has not been recorded in any protected area, but in February 2003 Nilssonia formosa, Chitra sp. and Amyda cartilaginea were found to occur in Lake Indawgyi, a newly created wildlife sanctuary. Relict populations of K. trivittata can still be found at the upper Chindwin and upper Myitnge (or Dokthawady) Rivers. One male and two female K. trivittata are currently at the zoo in Mandalay and form the basis of an assurance colony for the species.

23377: Potential hybridization between the endangered pallid sturgeon, Scaphirhynchus albus, and the sympatric shovelnose sturgeon, S. platorynchus, has been reported within the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, with most purported hybrids from the lower Mississippi River Basin. Because no studies have examined the extent of morphological variability within either species in the lower basin, identification of hybrids is problematic. Principal components analysis (PCA) has been a useful tool in differentiating between these parental species and known hybrids from the upper Missouri River. Previous attempts to distinguish between these species and to identify hybrids with unique genetic markers have been unsuccessful, in part due to the lack of vouchers to verify specimen identification. We used a series of microsatellite loci known to be polymorphic within Scaphirhynchus to identify useful genetic markers for differentiating between these taxa and their purported hybrids. Either a specimen or a photo voucher is associated with all tissues used in the molecular study. Meristic and morphometric data analyzed with PCA from these vouchers is useful in differentiating between these two sturgeon species and their hybrids. Accurate specimen identification, associated with genetic variability, is essential for researchers to collect valid data useful in the management of the endangered pallid sturgeon and forensic identification of caviar and flesh products.

23378: Northeastern Rio Grande do Sul lies in the subtropical warm temperate zone. In this region where various vegetation types with different macrohabitats meet, i.e., Araucaria forest and grassland (campos) on the volcanic plateau (Planalto), Atlantic rain forest in the Serra Geral, deciduous forest and campos in the lowlands, and dune vegetation in the coastal zone, a very high anuran species diversity is found, even in comparison with tropical regions. Combined data from both field work since 1995 and bibliographical records revealed 71 anuran species from six families in an area of about 300 km2 extending from sea level to 1200 m altitude. The tree frogs (Hylidae) with 29 species in six genera (Aplastodiscus, Hyla, Phrynohyas, Phyllomedusa, Scinax, Sphaenorhynchus) and the whistling frogs (Leptodactylidae) with 27 species in twelve genera (Adenomera, Cycloramphus, Eleutherodactylus, Hylodes, Leptodactylus, Limnomedusa, Odontophrynus, Physalaemus, Pleurodema, Proceratophrys, Pseudopaludicola, Thoropa) are the most speciose families, in addition to ten species of toads (Bufonidae: genera Bufo, Dendrophryniscus, Melanophryniscus), two narrow-mouthed frogs (Microhylidae: genus Elachistocleis), two harlequin frogs (Pseudidae: genus Pseudis), and one introduced true frog (Ranidae: genus Rana). About 25 % of these species are endemic either to the Planalto, to the Serra Geral or to the coast, and a few species are not yet described. This remarkable anuran diversity might be caused by the high and regular annual precipitation, the variety of different macrohabitat types and the availability of numerous spawning sites. In the highlands of Rio Grande do Sul, a spatial segregation exists between anurans of open campos (40%) and forest (35%) habitats, few species (25%) are generalists that occur in both habitat types. During the breeding season, most anurans use permanent and temporary standing water bodies; about 25% of the species use small streams for reproducing.

23379: Elasmobranch fish maintain solute and acid/base balance by regulating transepithelial transport across the epithelia of the gill, kidney and rectal gland. Another possible regulatory site is the epithelium surrounding the coelomic cavity that secretes fluid into that space. Coelomic fluid in many lower vertebrates including elasmobranch fish can exit the body via paired abdominal pores, two slit-like openings adjacent to the cloaca. Analyses were made of solutes (Na+, K+, Cl-, protein, urea) and pH in coelomic fluid (CF), plasma (PL), and in surrounding seawater of male and female euryhaline, Atlantic stingrays, Dasyatis sabina, adapted to full-strength and dilute Charleston, SC Harbor seawater. The PL and CF osmolality values were nearly at unity with the full-strength (≈ 900 mOsm) seawater. Concentrations of cations and anions in CF and PL were approximately 25-50% less than in the surrounding full-strength seawater. Urea concentrations in CF and PL were nearly at unity. CF pH was acidic (5.1-5.4) compared to PL (7.1-7.3) and seawater (7.6-7.7). Transfer of rays to diluted seawater (451 mOsm) for 24 hrs reduced CF and PL osmolality (17% and 20%, respectively), and concentrations of Na+, Cl-, and K+ in PL and CF. Urea, a major osmolyte in marine elasmobranchs, decreased only 5% and 8% in PL and CF, respectively. The CF pH remained markedly acidic (pH 5.7) in dilute seawater conditions. These results suggest that the coelomic epithelium may act as a selective transport site of solutes and hydrogen/bicarbonate ions to maintain the acid base and solute homeostasis in stingrays in concert with coelomic fluid excretion through the abdominal pores.

23380: Historically, researchers have relied mainly on tooth and mouth structures and body shape to determine the taxonomy of cichlids. More recently researchers have also included behavior, genetics, ecology, and scale morphology and squamation. While much work has been done in detailed analysis of scale morphology and squamation using a scanning electron microscope, a complicated and expensive investigative method, there has not been a practical and economically feasible technique developed. My study involves the analysis of cichlid scales for the purpose of species identification and the testing of feasible methods. The immediate motivation for this project comes from the need of researchers in Lake Malawi National Park, Africa to understand the diets of Lake Malawi's native otter populations. Scales were taken from five species of cichlids commonly found in the park, three from the genus Metriaclima, one from Labeotropheus, and one from Pseudotropheus. I have evaluated different staining, mounting, and photographic techniques with respect to technical difficulty and ability to discern scale characters. Distinct characteristics were determined for each species by comparing scales at low to medium magnification using a phase contrast compound microscope. This study also investigated squamation pattern of each species as a determination of the validity of findings using scale morphology. This study shows that efficient and cost-effective techniques can be used to identify cichlids using only the scales. In the future, a scale identification key will be constructed for the 10 most common genera found in Lake Malawi National Park, for use by Lake Malawi researchers.

23381: This work describes the reproductive biology of a population of Bryconamericus iheringii from rio Vacacaí and of a population of Bryconamericus stramineus from rio Ibicuí, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. The reproductive period and fecundity are characterized. Possible interactions of the reproductive period with biotic (stomach repletion and hepatosomatic indexes) and abiotic factors (rainfall, day-length and temperature) are investigated. Collections were made monthly from April/2001 to March/2002 with seine net, and physical and chemical parameters of the water were registered. The individuals were preserved in formalin 10% in the field. In laboratory, the total weight, standard length and gonad, stomach and liver weights were registered. The reproductive period of the species was established through the analysis of 195 females and 209 males of B. iheringii and 209 females and 166 males of B. stramineus, occurring from September to February in both species (spring and summer in Southern Hemisphere), as described for other characids of the same area. The averages of absolute and relative fecundities for B. iheringii were 933.71 oocytes and of 0.36 oocytes/mg of total weight; for B. stramineus the values were of 371.3 oocytes and 0.35 oocytes/mg of total weight, respectively. Correlations between the monthly variation of the means of GSI values and the variation of the biotic and abiotic data were inexistent in the studied species (except between the day-lenght and GSI of males of B. stramineus).

23382: The Neotropical cichlid subfamily Geophaginae is composed by 14 described genera (Acarichthys, Apistogramma, Apistogrammoides, Biotodoma, Biotoecus, Crenicara, Dicrossus, Geophagus, Guianacara, Gymnogeophagus, Mazarunia, Mikrogeophagus, Satanoperca and Taeniacara). The phylogenetic relationships within the subfamily are addressed from a cladistic approach. An analysis with 31 terminal taxa (21 from the ingroup, including all Geophaginae genera of the subfamily except Mazarunia and Apistogrammoides and 10 from the outgroup, covering all Neotropical cichlid subfamilies) and 80 osteological characters was performed. The resulting hypotheses regarding relationships of the geophagine fishes suggest: the Geophaginae is a monophyletic taxon without the inclusion of Crenicichla, in contrast to recent total evidence analysis result; a new interpretation of the character states supporting its monophyly indicates that character states related to the presence of the epibranchial lobe are sinapomorphic to the subfamily, in contrast with the previous morphological analysis and; the confirmation of the non- monophyletic condition of the genus Geophagus.

23383: The species of the neotropical characiform family Hemiodontidae are distributed along the basins of Amazonas, Orinoco, Parana-Paraguay, and the rivers of Guyana, Suriname, and French Guiana. Anterior phylogenetic analyses involving hemiodontid taxa have dealt only with genus level, and besides few comments involving groups of species, nothing is available about species relationships. A phylogenetic hypothesis is presented for most of the species included in the family. A matrix with 110 characters, and 30 taxa (20 hemiodontid species, and Alestes and Astyanax as outgroups) is analysed; all characters were treated as unweighted or, in the case of multistate characters, also as unordered. Maximum parsimony analysis was performed using the heuristic search method in PAUP; random addition sequence and tree-bisection-reconnection branch swap options were carried out. Three most parsimonious cladograms were found (241 steps, CI= 0.56, RI= 0.79, RC= 0.45); differing just in a conflicting-node with some of the Hemiodus species. In order to choose among the hypotheses for that conflicting-node, characters were successively weighted and computed three times, until weights stabilization. The three successive weighting processes and computations always produced the same result, which was identical to one of the three initial cladograms. This cladogram had 108.9 steps, CI= 0.81, RI= 0.93, and RC= 0.75; support for it was assessed by performing 1000 simple heuristic bootstrap replications. The results show that all hemiodontid genera are monophyletic, and corroborate an anterior hypothesis for relationships of the genera. Hemiodus immaculatus is the sister species of all other Hemiodus species, that were divided in two clades, one with the larger species, with small and numerous scales, and another with the smaller species, with large scales. Bivibranchia protractila is the most generalized Bivibranchia species; its sister group was composed by two clades: B. velox plus B. notata, and B. bimaculata plus B. simulata.

23384: Our principal objectives were to prepare a global overview of the fish diversity of the Guiana Shield and propose areas for conservation and future research. One of the outstanding results of this work was that we able to delineate for the first time the biogeographic limits of the Guiana Shield in terms of its ichthyofauna. The southern limits are marked by the waterfalls or in the case of the Río Negro by a prominent rocky constriction. The Amazon is not included in the Shield. At the mouth of the Orinoco river, we only include the southern tributaries of the Delta. We identified 25 priority areas: nine are in the eastern basin, ten are in the north central part of the Shield and six in the south western portion. On all of these 25 nominated areas, we are covering six different ichthyofaunistic areas, which are: 1) Areas of the Guiana in the eastern zone from the Essequibo to the Oyapock. 2) Areas in the north central part that drain into the Orinoco. 3) Río Ventuari Basin in the north west of the Orinoco. 4) River basins in the south western extension that includes the region of Chiribiquete. 5) Upper and middle Río Negro and Trombetas area. 6) A series of inter-basins headwater areas that drain off large mountain and tepuy areas. The fish species richness of the different countries of the Guiana Shield are distributed as follow: Colombia (800 species), Venezuela (1000 species), Guyana (700 species), Suriname (450 species), French Guiana (475 species), Brazil -Río Negro basin- (750 species) and at least 600 species for other Brazilian basins.

23385: Questions about species diversity remain central to ecology despite decades of enquiry. By dissecting components of diversity, we hope to understand how and why communities are structured and learn what factors maintain biodiversity. If we understand the pattern and process of diversity, we should be able to, among other things, develop effective conservation strategies. Species diversity is best understood by examining its three components: alpha (α) diversity – the number of species occurring together at a site (species richness); beta (β) diversity – the turnover in species due to habitat change; and gamma (γ) diversity – the replacement or addition of species from distant sites within the same habitat type. We examined diversity components of the amphibians and reptiles from 14 well-inventoried sites in Costa Rica. Alpha and β-diversity within and among the sites was quantified, with special attention given to analysis of species turnover along the Pacific coast. Alpha diversity was highest in the lowland rainforests of the southwest and Caribbean versant, and lowest in the tropical dry forest of the Northwest. Beta diversity was low between nearby sites, but high between the Atlantic and Pacific versants and along the Pacific coast. Interestingly, β-diversity was not explained solely by distance. Correlates to diversity components including climate, vegetation, landform, and history will be discussed.

23386: The Area de Conservación Guanacaste (ACG) stands as a model for tropical conservation due to a long-standing commitment to both conservation and the biological study of the area. For this reason, it is one of the best studied areas in the country. However, much of this effort has focused on the tropical dry forest. The ACG's eastern region, comprised of premontane and very humid rainforest, has received less attention. This is the case for the area's amphibian and reptile species. Although there is an existing species list for Parque Nacional Santa Rosa (Sasa and Solórzano 1995), the herpetofauna of the eastern sector is poorly documented. We report on surveys of amphibians and reptiles of the eastern portion of the ACG inclusive of the Rincon Rainforest area. We observed 37 amphibian and 53 reptile species between mid June and August 2001, based on visual encounter surveys, road cruising and time constraint searches at four sites in this area. These included 1 caecilian, 1 salamander and 34 frog species, as well as 2 turtle, 19 lizard and 33 snake species. We report additional information on species' abundances, habitat use and distributions throughout the area.

23387: Fishes of the Superorder Osteoglossomorpha (the bonytongues) are sometimes referred to as Jurassic fish because of their ancient origin. While the first fossil assigned to this group dates to the Late Jurassic, the modern osteoglossomorphs are a highly derived and morphologically heterogeneous group of basal teleosts. This group includes 199 described extant species unequally distributed among five families: the Osteoglossidae, including Pantodon buccholzi (five genera, eight species), the Notopteridae (four genera, eight species), the Hiodontidae (one genus, two species), the Gymnarchidae (one species), and the Mormyridae (18 genera, 180 species). For thirty years, interrelationships among osteoglossomorph taxa have been fiercely discussed, due in part to the considerable morphological diversity among the families that makes difficult the identification of shared derived characters. In this study, we present a novel phylogenetic hypothesis for this group, based on the analysis of more than 4000 characters from five molecular markers (the mitochondrial cytochrome b, 12S and 16S rRNA genes, and the nuclear genes RAG2 and MLL). Our taxonomic sampling includes one osteoglossomorph representative of each extant non-mormyrid genus. Within the monophyletic family Mormyridae, we sample only one taxon. We select four outgroups within the basal Teleostei to root our tree. The maximum parsimony analysis of combined and equally weighted characters from the five molecular markers provides a single tree. The Superorder Osteoglossomorpha is found monophyletic. Within this group, high bootstrap proportions and high Bremer support values support each clade. The tree topology is the following: (Hiodon alosoides, (Pantodon buchholzi, (((Osteoglossum biccirhosum, Scleropages sp.), (Arapaima gigas, Heterotis niloticus)), ((Gymnarchus niloticus, Mormyridae), ((Notopterus notopterus, Chitala ornata), (Xenomystus nigri, Papyrocranus afer)))))). To assess the quality of our results, we analyze the role of parameters that may affect the reliability of our tree (e.g. nucleotide base composition, heterogeneity of base substitutions, incongruence between markers). Finally, we compare our results with previously published phylogenetic hypotheses based on morpho-anatomical data.

23388: I studied the anurans on the beaches of Jamaraquá and Pindobal in Belterra, Pará, Brazil, from June to October 2001. The objective was to define which species of anurans occur in localities near the Tapajós River Basin where almost nothing has been documented in the literature due to the difficulties of doing research in the Amazon Basin. The nocturnal registers include both visual and auditory searches. The individuals were located, captured and maintained alive. The following day the 1033 specimens collected were identified, measured, weighed and returned to the site of capture. Those specimens that were not easily identified, 4.25%, were sacrificed in 15% alcohol, and fixed in 10% formalin and later stored in 70% alcohol with date and locality data attached to the specimens. During 10 expeditions, 5 in each locality, I identified 10 species in 3 families. Since the height of the reproductive season is at the high water level it is most likely that more species will be documented from these sites.

23389: The superorder Squalomorphii includes the Hexanchiformes, Pristiophoriformes and the Squaliformes. The Squaliformes are grouped into 6 families, 22 genera and roughly 87 species; however, there are several taxonomic uncertainties regarding this group. Representatives for 13 out of the 22 known Squaliform genera were sequenced for the mitochondrial genes NADH-2, NADH-4, Cytochrome B, and the nuclear gene rag1. These sequences were used in phylogenetic analysis. Hypotheses for inter-generic relationships supported by our data will be discussed and compared with previous morphological and molecular hypotheses.

23390: Detailed examination of the male reproductive tract of specimens initially identified as Parauchenipterus galeatus revealed morphological differences that suggest the occurrence of two syntopic species at the Catalão Lake, Xiborena Island, herein referred to as "dark" and "speckled" morphotypes. Specimens were collected over a 26 months period, at various stages of gonadal development. The number of the finger-like lobes in each side of the anterior portion of the reproductive tract is about the same (13-20) in both morphotypes. This number is similar to the one reported for specimens of Parauchenipterus from rivers of French Guyana and much lower than that reported for Trachelyopterus from the La Plata system. The finger-like lobes are attached to two testicular ducts that join in a medial large chamber. In each side of this chamber, the "dark" morphotyte possess a series of numerous small lobes followed by a very large one, whereas the "speckled" morphotype possess two large lobes followed by 5-6 smaller ones. In specimens in reproductive activity all lobes and the medial chamber are thicker than in resting males. The two species also differ in the length of the cleithrum, which is longer in the "speckled" morphotype, and in the color of the corner of the mouth, which is dark in the "dark" morphotype and whitish in the "speckled" morphotype. These observations suggest that Parauchenipterus galeatus may be a species complex, as previously hypothesized by other authors, and that comparative studies on the morphology of the male reproductive tract can be an useful tool for taxonomical purposes.

23391: Temperature-dependent sex determination was studied in the loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta) nesting on two Georgia barrier islands from 2000-2002. Nest temperatures were monitored with temperature dataloggers to predict hatchling sex ratios. Both in situ (n = 27) and relocated nests (n = 53) were studied on Blackbeard Island and Wassaw National Wildlife Refuges. Nests were monitored throughout the nesting season to determine seasonal changes in sex ratios produced. No difference in sex ratios produced or hatchling size (SCL, SCW, and height) was detected between in situ and relocated nests. Female loggerheads in the northern subpopulation of the Western Atlantic are producing up to 6 nests and laying nests throughout the entire nesting season. Hatchling sex ratios for these Georgia beaches were predicted using average nest temperatures during the thermosensitive period of sex determination. These predictions were based on previously reported pivotal temperatures for loggerhead sea turtles. Our results show that nests laid during the first third of the nesting season (May 1 - June 4) will be male and nests laid during the remainder of the season (June 5 - August 10) will be predominantly female. Sex ratios, based on gonadal histology of dead hatchlings collected from nests post-emergence, were compared with the predicted sex ratios. Female loggerheads nesting on Georgia barrier islands appear to be producing mixed sex ratios of up to 75% females.

23392: Two minnow species, the bridle shiner Notropis bifrenatus (Cope) and ironcolor shiner Notropis chalybaeus (Cope) were listed as state endangered in 1999 by the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission. Both species were historically widespread but now occur in only one stream in eastern Pennsylvania. Objectives of this restoration program are to; 1) culture 6,000 fry of each species, 2) identify suitable habitat in Brodhead Creek Watershed (BCW) to reintroduce these species, 3) mark cultured fry with calcein (SE-MARK®), 4) reintroduce cultured minnows, and 5) monitor populations for reproductive success and population growth. Propagation techniques for the bridle and ironcolor shiner were developed at the Pennsylvania State University fish laboratory during 2000-2001. Preliminary work included habitat surveys to select suitable reintroduction sites. Introductions of cultured fishes will be limited to areas where genetic stock of these fishes existed historically. Pilot populations were marked before release with calcein, which permits identification of fishes as laboratory-raised or wild offspring in the field without sacrificing them. The first laboratory propagated specimens were released during late spring 2003. Pilot populations were monitored by snorkel and video. After a wild spawning period, shiners will be collected and identified as laboratory-raised or their wild offspring. Collections will be made again during spring 2004 to determine if populations survived over winter. Introduction success will be determined by monitoring experimental populations' growth, survival, and reproductive success. Non-game fishes have never been released into streams and monitored in Pennsylvania. This restoration program is the first of its kind and will contribute to the conservation and potential enhancement of the current endangered Pennsylvania populations.

23393: Frogs of the genus Phrynopus are distributed from Colombia to Bolivia where they inhabit cloud forests, páramos and subpáramos (1000 to 4000 m elevation). Most of the montane forests of the eastern Andes have been under-sampled, and we are therefore unable to estimate the number of species of Phrynopus or other anuran genera in this region. Currently 22 species of Phrynopus are recognized in Perú, nine of them were described only recently. The highest regional species density of Phrynopus (six species) is documented in the central Peruvian Departamento de Huúnuco. An introduction to the Phrynopus of Huánuco along with ecological observations is provided. Whether the high regional number of Phrynopus in central Perú is the effect of intensive sampling or reflects a center of speciation, cannot be answered until larger parts of the eastern Andes have been more thoroughly sampled. For most species of Phrynopus, ecology and reproduction are still unknown, but these aspects must be studied before the forests in the eastern Andes are destroyed.

23394: In a recent paper, Goodwin et. al. (1998, Proc. Roy. Acad. Sci., Lond., Series B 265:2265-2272) produced evidence for the multiple independent origin of mouthbrooding reproductive behavior in the family Cichlidae (Teleostei). We have extended and expanded this study by creating a phylogeny of 9 South American Geophagine cichlids of the genus Geophagus (Heckel 1840), a clade exhibiting ancestral substrate brooding, larvophilous ('delayed') mouthbrooding, and ovophilous ('immediate') mouthbrooding, using PAUP and a 316 bp segment of the mitochondrial cytochrome b gene, and then layering behavioral observations over it. The clustering of species and reproductive behaviors suggests that mouthbrooding has arisen at least twice in the genus Geophagus (currently 11 nominal species). And when the study was expanded to include 11 species of other closely-related genera that exhibit mouthbrooding behavior (e.g. Satanoperca, "Geophagus", Gymnogeophagus), a total of 20 species examined, the distribution of species and behaviors suggests that, at a minimum, mouthbrooding has arisen at least 5 times in the Geophagine cichlid clade.

23395: The Espinhaço Mountain Chain encompasses highlands above 800 m that separate the watersheds of São Francisco river and the river basins of the Atlantic coast, as well as the Atlantic Forest from the open areas of Central Brazil (Cerrado/Caatinga). It has a great ecological importance due to the complexity of its relationships with other Brazilian morphoclimatic domains and its apparent richness of endemic taxa. The Serra do Cipó is located in the State of Minas Gerais, at the southern portion of the Espinhaço Mountain Chain, separating the São Francisco river basin, at west, from the Doce river basin, at east. Due to the greatest influence of the Atlantic Forest at the eastern portion, it would be expected that some species typical of these formations occurred just at one slope. In this study, we aimed to compare the composition and some zoogeographical aspects of anuran assemblages at two close sites, each one at one slope of the Serra do Cipó. The western slope has, according to previous studies, 40 anuran species occupying montane meadows (campos rupestres) and gallery forests, while 36 species have been registered at the opposite slope hitherto. The similarity between the two studied sites is high: 21 species in common. Part of the differences observed may be due to a higher availability of forest habitats at the eastern side. Most of the species registered only at the western slope are typical of open sites, while most of those registered only at the eastern slope use forests to reproduce.

23396: The genus Phasmahyla encompasses a group of Phyllomedusinae with restricted distribution within the Brazilian Atlantic rain forest. Phasmahyla jandaia is the only known species of this genus that inhabits the gallery forests from the Espinhaço mountain chain. This is a threatened species and is the focus of the present study, that aims to follow changes in population structure during larval stages. A population that lived in a stream backwater created by a small artificial dam was chosen because of the impossibility of dispersion of the individuals. This population was monitored every other week from July of 2002 to January of 2003. All larvae were captured, had their developmental stage determined and were released after data collection. The initial number of individuals were 213, and at the last inspection this number decreased to 104 due to overflows that occurred in September and November, carrying some tadpoles out of the dam. Otherwise, population increased in August and October due to recruitment of 15 and 30 new individuals, respectively. In the last month, a strong flood pulse killed all tadpoles. In July and August, at the end of the dry/cold season, there were no tadpoles in advanced stages and a large number of individuals in less developed stages was found. When temperature raised and rainfall increased, in September, the tadpoles began to reach more developed stages, enabling them to leave the water and complete metamorphosis. This indicates a negative influence of low water temperatures or other habitat factors on the tadpoles developmental rate. Alternatively, this may also suggest the presence of some endogenous mechanisms that control the larval developmental rate of this species avoiding complete metamorphosis during unsuitable seasons.

23397: HOX genes play a key role in specifying the body plan in a large range of animals and therefore are essential in explaining patterns of evolutionary diversity. Indeed, changes in number and regulation of these genes have strongly influenced the diversification of metazoan body plans. Tetrapods have four gene clusters, each containing up to 13 paralog group members. The loss of some of the HOX genes in several vertebrate lineages may have been accompanied by the secondary loss or simplification of appendages. In amphibians, each of the three orders has a very specific, conserved body plan, with different types of limbs (frogs versus salamanders) or no limbs at all (caecilians). In this preliminary study, we screened a representative of each of these orders for the presence of paralog groups of HOX genes (HOX 9, 10 and 11) that are involved in limb development.

23398: Turbulence is a ubiquitous phenomenon that fishes commonly encounter. The proclivity of lotic fishes to use topographical features as flow refuges has been well documented in the field and laboratory, though the mechanism of this behavior has not been fully explored. Specifically, their ability to capture energy from meso-scale turbulence to save in the cost of locomotion has been proposed, but never demonstrated. I use the periodic wake behind a simple geometric object to investigate the effect of vortices on swimming fish. Under controlled laboratory flow conditions, rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) synchronize their tailbeat frequency to the expected vortex shedding frequency behind a cylinder. During this novel mode of locomotion, which I term the Karman gait, the body translates laterally with large amplitudes, resembling the motion of a flag flapping slowly in the wind. Electromyograms recorded along the axial body show little, regular red muscle activity and no white muscle activity during the Karman gait, indicating a largely passive method of station holding despite high downstream flows. When present, red muscle activity is most prevalent in the anterior myomeres, suggesting that corrective movements are established by the head when necessary. Simultaneous imaging of the trout and the flow behind a cylinder (using Digital Particle Image Velocimetry) reveals that trout slalom around, rather than pass through, the core of each oncoming vortex. The mechanism of the Karman gait may be analogous to tacking in sailboats, whereby the lift force is resolved into thrust by the angle of the sail relative to the incident wind. Preliminary fieldwork suggests that trout may take advantage of the Karman gait only in situations when saving locomotory cost is at a premium and flow regimes are favorable.

23399: We describe the reproductive characteristics of three syntopic dendrobatids (Colostethus caeruleodactylus, C. nidicola and a not yet described Colostethus sp.), that share an area of primary terra firme tropical rainforest in the Castanho municipality, south of the Amazon river, approximately 40 km from Manaus (Amazonas, Brazil), and were studied through intensive monitoring of all individuals found inside 12 replicates of 20 x 20 m plots located in patches of high abundance of one or more species throughout the rainy seasons of 2000/2001 and 2001/2002. All adult males and females were individually marked through toe clipping and measured. All relocations, courtships and ovipositions observed within the plots were recorded. All three species presented sexual color and size dimorphism (females larger than males). C. caeruleodactylus started vocalizing 2-3 months later than C. sp. and C. nidicola. Male C. caeruleodactylus and C. sp. defended territories 5-26 m2 in size, while C. nidicola was less clearly territorial, with males forming aggregates and shifting territories throughout the reproductive season. Female C. nidicola held territories about 17 m2 in size. Courtship was fast (about 1 hour), with a cephalic amplexus for C. sp., but was more elaborate and lasted about 12 hours for the other two species. C. nidicola also performs a cephalic amplexus, while C. caeruleodactylus has no amplexus. Females of the three species were observed to oviposit with different males. One to eight ovipositions per female were observed for C. sp. Clutch size varied from 7-16 and 9-27 for C. caeruleodactylus and C. sp., which carry their tadpoles to the water, while C. nidicola laid 3-6 larger eggs, which develop directly in the nest. Male C. caeruleodactylus obtained a maximum of 10 clutches/season, while C. sp. males obtained up to 20 clutches, which was probably related to the later onset of the reproductive season for C. caeruleodactylus.

23400: The large rivers of the Amazon Basin are classified into three categories (black, clear and white waters). Black and clear water rivers drain geologically old areas, that are poor in inorganic nutrients comparing to the white water rivers, that have more recent geological origin and carry large amounts of mineral nutrients. Previous research indicated that some characiform fish migrate from black and clear water rivers to spawn in white water rivers. In this work we considered larval and juvenile fish occurrence in nine different rivers, to determine whether this spawning tactic is a general pattern for the Amazon basin. The rivers sampled were the Madeira, Juruá and Purus (white water), Tapajós, Trombetas and Nhamundá (clear water), Negro, Urubu and Tefé (black water). Each river was surveyed once, during the rising water phase of years 2000 and 2001. Larval fish was collected with ichthyoplankton net (0.35 mm mesh size) tied to a boat moving at ca. 1m/s against the current in the river channel. Juvenile fish was sampled with hand net on vegetated marginal habitats. A total of 26144 larvae and 951 juvenile characiforms were collected. Mylossoma aureum, M. duriventre, Colossoma macropomum, Anodus elongatus, Triportheus elongatus, Brycon cephalus, Semaprochilodus spp and Prochilodus nigricans spawned in white water rivers only. Total larval abundance and concentration of suspended solids were positively related. Species composition of juvenile characiforms in white water rivers was different from clear and black water rivers. This work strongly supports the hypothesis that nutrient rich rivers and associated floodplains function as spawning and nursery grounds for these migratory characiforms. Furthermore, it indicates that the white water rivers are source habitats, and black and clear water rivers are sink habitats for these species.

23401: The genus Hyphessobrycon Durbin is a speciose assemblage of small characid fishes, comprising about 98 valid species. The genus is distributed from southern Mexico to Río de La Plata in Argentina, achieving its highest diversity in the cisandean northern South America. The systematics of the genus is still largely unresolved; even the monophyletic status of Hyphessobrycon is highly doubtful. Three new species of Hyphessobrycon (Characiformes: Characidae) were recently discovered in the previously ichthyiologically poorly explored upper Rio Araguaia basin, and are described. Hyphessobrycon sp. n. 1 distinguishes from all its congeners by the presence of a well-defined, round humeral spot; a reticulate color pattern; a broad, horizontally-elongated caudal peduncle blotch; and a midlateral dark stripe relatively wide and faint. Hyphessobrycon sp. n. 2 distinguishes from its congeners by the absence of humeral and caudal spots; by the presence of numerous dark chromatophores on sides of body, intensely concentrated on ventral region from pelvic-fin origin to the end of caudal-fin base; dorsal, adipose and caudal fins with carmine red pigmentation in life; and the presence of 7-11 maxillary teeth. Hyphessobrycon sp.n.3 distinguishes from its congeners by the combination of two humeral spots and a general dark color pattern. These three new species, along with Creagrutus molinus (Characidae), Aspidoras velites (Callichthyidae), an undescribed Hypostominae (Loricariidae), Cnesterodon septentrionalis (Poeciliidae), and a new Simpsonichthys (Rivulidae), all of which are apparently endemic of the upper Rio Araguaia, indicate that this area is a previously unrecognized area of endemism.

23402: The Rio Tiquié is a tributary of the Rio Uaupés flowing throughout southeastern Colombia (Departamento Caquetá) to northwestern Brazil (Estado do Amazonas). The Rio Tiquié, was, as several others relatively large tributaries of the Amazon basin still are, virtually unknown ichthyiologically. Tukano and Tuyuka indians, which inhabits its margins are renowned for their expertise on the fishes living within his domains. One of the purposes of the joint MZUSP/ISA/FOIRN/ATRIART project "Peixes e pesca do alto rio Tiquié" was the assembling of a representative fish collection of its upper course in Brazil (above Pari-Cachoeira to the frontier). The primary objective of this collection was to vouch the informations supplied by the Tukano and Tuyuka indians. Two ichthyological expeditions undertaken during the years 2000 and 2002 resulted in a small, but significative collection amounting to 134 fish species. Almost all fish species (131) bears a specific name in both Tukano/Tyuyka. Even considering that fish is by far the main proteinic source to these indians, the accurate and detailed knowledge of the fish diversity and natural history cannot be seen simply as a pragmatic aspect of the Tukano/Tyuyka lore. For example, they apply different names for three species occurring in the area and additionally, its mythology records different origins for each of them. A second outcome of the project was the discovery of several fishes unknown to science. Rio Negro is probably the best sampled in the Amazon; a published list of the fishes from the middle and lower Rio Negro basin recorded 450 species occurring in the area. A comparison between the lists showed that several species occurring in the Rio Tiquié are not known from the Rio Negro, a result that suggests that we are still far from reaching an adequate knownledge of the fish diversity of that basin.

23403: The aim of this study was to analyze the fish diversity in Corumbatai River (a small Brazilian stream) in order to compare two sites (located within 22°12′-33″ S and 47°37′-41″ W) with distinct pollution levels. Fish were collected, identified, counted and weighed during two years, along twelve standardized samples. The river water was analyzed, using a PCA, referring to the following variables: total and faecal coliforms, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, P, Mn, Zn, Pb, Al, Ba and Fe. The fish diversity in each site was estimated using the Shannon Index and the log normal and broken stick models. In each site were collected 31 species (23 common to both), 2,194 specimens and 80,304.10g of fish. Individuals abundance and biomass were higher in site A (respectively 57.57% and 58.26%), but the Shannon Index did not show significant difference between the sites (H′A = 1.97 0.48, H′B = 2.35 0.46, p = 0.0631). The broken stick model did not fit to any site and the log normal, besides fitting to sites A (p = 0.0768) and B (p = 0.7699), was more appropriated to the latter. The water of the site B, though not heavily polluted, presented a higher pollution (due mainly to total and faecal coliforms, conductivity, Al and Ba). Though the Shannon Index has not shown a significant difference between the sites, there is a tendency to higher diversity in site B, and this can be corroborated by the log normal model. However, the higher abundance and biomass verified in site A probably indicates that it offers better conditions for the fish assemblage. Such facts raise a question about the use of the diversity measures as indicators of environmental health, mainly in moderately polluted systems, in which an increase of evenness may occur as a consequence of the reduction of individuals (mainly of the most abundant species), without a significant alteration of species richness.

23404: The flood pulse is a known important abiotic timer in the Amazonian system. The water level oscillation reaches 8 m in the lower Trombetas River region. From 1979 to 1989, the Batata Lake had been silted up by bauxite clay effluents. The bottom lifted up 5-6 m, and transparency and oxygen values decreased. The establishment of large stands of wild rice has been favored in the silted up area during the dry period, followed by its decomposition in the filling period. Trimester samples of several abiotic and biotic features, from March/2001 to March/2002, were related to fish distribution, diversity, abundance and biomass in silted up (S) and natural (N) areas of the Batata Lake. We verified daily and seasonal instability in dissolved oxygen and temperature in S comparing with N (t test, p < 0.05). Fifteen from thirty dominant species presented higher abundance in S during the filling, flood and drawdown period, and higher values in N during dry periods. Six species always maintained the highest abundance in S. The diversity was higher in filling and high water periods in S (Hutcheson, p < 0.05). Access to igapó forest resources, depth, transparency and wild rice presence were the main factors affecting spatial segregation of fish species in the filling/flood period. Fish abundance and biomass values were higher in areas with lower transparency and depth, and were positively related to wild rice presence (multiple regression; p < 0.05). We recognize two patterns: 1) shallow areas, intermediate transparency and high wild rice productivity sustain higher fish abundance and biomass (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05); 2) positive relationship among 21 fish species and intermediate transparency (multiple regression, p < 0.05). The increasing water level in the filling period acts as an intermediate disturbance in the silted up area, increasing fish diversity, abundance and biomass.

23405: Map turtles (Emydidae: Graptemys) are a diverse group of freshwater turtles that are of ecological interest due to their extreme sexual size dimorphism (with females larger) and their diversity in trophic morphology, particularly in females. I used comparative analyses (correlation analyses and GLM analyses using phylogenetic independent contrasts as input data) to examine hypotheses regarding the evolution of body size in the genus. Body size of both males and females was positively related to latitude. Trophic morphology (relative head width, expressed either as a continuous or a discrete variable) was not an additive source of variation in male body size, but was for female body size, primarily due to the large body sizes exhibited by the mesocephalic, southern species that comprise the pulchra clade (G. pulchra, G. ernsti, G. gibbonsi, and G. barbouri). Status as allopatric or sympatric to other species of Graptemys was not an additive source of variation in female body size. Sexual size dimorphism increases with body size of females, also due primarily to the large females of the pulchra clade; this result means Graptemys is an exception to Rensch's Rule. These results, together with the relative lack of dietary diversity among male map turtles, argue against the hypothesis that character displacement of body size was important in the radiation of map turtle species, and instead suggest a functional relationship whereby degree of molluscivory in females covaries with female body size.

23406: The settlement of reef-associated temperate fishes was monitored during the summer and fall of 2002 at King Harbor, Redondo Beach, California. King Harbor is a man made harbor composed of rock reef and sand habitats. A total of eight settlement traps were anchored on the bottom at depths between 2 and 7 meters to provide a standardized form of structural shelter for settling larvae. During the study period divers conducted weekly and bi-weekly retrievals of these traps and all larval fish collected within the traps were preserved for identification and analysis. A total of 126 new settlers were collected throughout the study, consisting of four different species; Gobiesox rhessodon (59%), Paraclinus integripinnis (20%), Hypsoblennius jenkinsi (18%), Ruscarius creaseri (3%). Settlement pulses were then compared to physical anomalies such as moon phase, sea surface temperature, and sub-surface temperature. The influx of new settlers was positively correlated, on a daily basis, with abrupt changes in temperature (∆T; r = 0.77, p < 0.05). Preliminary results indicate that the majority of these reef-fish settlers are being transported inshore by processes that, in turn, also cause large temperature fluctuations in the water near the bottom. In this case, the observed temperature fluctuations were consistent with the occurrence of tidal bores.

23407: Bristlenose catfish (Ancistrus sp.) get their common name from their distinguishing morphological feature, fleshy tentacles on their snout. Tentacles of adult males are larger and more dispersed over the snout than those of females or juveniles, and their function is a mystery. Since the tentacles have taste buds on them, it has been suggested they are used for chemoreception. Recently a hypothesis was proposed to suggest tentacles are larval mimics used by males to convince females that they are good fathers. Untested, this theory arises from the fact that Ancistrus are one group of fish that exhibit solely paternal care where male Ancistrus build cave-like nests then guard the embryos and newly-hatched larvae. Histological sections and histochemical studies on snout tentacles revealed thousands of goblet cells in the epithelial layer of Ancistrus tentacles, and that the contents are likely to be high-energy glycoproteins. Hence we proposed a hypothesis that male Ancistrus provide nutrients to their young via secretions from their tentacles. Electrophoresis and glycoprotein detection methods were used to further delineate the chemical composition of the secretion. Further investigation examined male-juvenile interactions, and stomach contents of juveniles were analyzed.

23408: Amphibian populations are declining on all continents on which they occur, but not all species are equally affected. Populations of some species are extirpated, others decline but survive, some populations do not obviously decline, and some are increasing. If amphibian populations at multiple sites were affected by the same factors, then surviving species should share traits that promote persistence, while declining species should share traits that promote susceptibility. Identifying those traits can help diagnose potential causes and thus direct conservation actions. Using logistic regression, we quantified the vulnerability of amphibian populations in four areas in Central America. We analyzed a species-specific database of taxonomic identity, geographic and elevational range, elevational distribution, adult and larval habitat, activity period, and maximum adult body size. We show that 1) all four sites exhibited the same pattern of decline (there were no interactions between site and other variables), 2) declining populations shared aquatic habitats, restricted elevational ranges, and large body sizes, and 3) there was an interaction between body size and elevational range. The most significant variable in the model was lifetime aquatic index, a factor not related to demographic vulnerability, and which therefore might indicate the potential causative agent(s). These results provide a predictive model to assess potential causes of population declines in other areas, and we have generated a list of species predicted to decline at a currently unaffected site in central Panama.

23409: The importance of vision remains unknown in many species of elasmobranchs. Here, we examine the morphology and distribution of both photoreceptor and ganglion cell populations in the retina of a range of species, in order to assess their spatial resolving power and strategies for localising both prey and predator. The retinae of five species (the ornate wobbegong, Orectolobus ornatus, the white tip reef shark, Triaenodon obesus, the great white shark, Charcharodon carcharias, the epaulette shark, Hemiscyllium ocellatum, and the eastern shovelnose ray, Aptychotrema rostrata) representing a range of lifestyles (benthic, pelagic, diurnal, nocturnal) were investigated and morphological and topographic characterization of both cell populations revealed marked variation. Anatomical measures of visual acuity ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 cycles per degree in regional specialisations (areae and horizontal streaks) mediating acute vision. The retinal location of these acute zones varied, emphasizing the relative importance of vision in different parts of each species' visual field. The distribution of both ganglion and photoreceptor cell populations were analysed in the same eye in each species and specialised areas of increased density were found to lie in register. However, differential analyses of rod and cone densities revealed localized differences in distribution suggesting different parts of the visual field may be more important during diurnal (cone-dominated) and nocturnal (rod-dominated) vision. Two and three localized retinal regions mediate acute vision in the frontal and lateral parts of the visual field in O. ornatus and T. obesus, respectively, while an elongated region of increased cell density extends horizontally across the retinal meridian mediating acute vision across a much larger and panoramic part of the visual field in H. ocellatum and A. rostrata. The retina in C. carcharias is unique and possesses a single and localized area for mediating increased visual acuity.

23410: The ten extant families of Tetraodontiformes putatively form a monophyletic group based on several well-defined morphological characters (e.g., ≤ 21 vertebrae; absence of anal fin spines; absence of extrascapular, parietal and nasal bones in the skull; absence of pleural ribs; a restricted gill opening; and ≤ 12 principal caudal rays). Traditionally, Tetraodontiformes has been divided into three suborders: Triacanthoidea (Triacanthidae + Triacanthodidae); Balistoidea (Balistidae + Monacanthidae + Aracanidae + Ostraciidae); and Tetraodontoidea (Triodontidae + Tetraodontidae + Diodontidae + Molidae). For a preliminary molecular phylogenetic investigation of this group, I made a comparative study of the 12S locus of the mitochondrial genome, a locus that has helped to elucidate interrelationships of actinopterygians at several taxonomic levels. I extracted DNA from tissue samples preserved in 95% ethanol using standard phenol-chloroform methods. I amplified 12S using new primer designs based on my alignments and analyses of published sequence data. PCR reaction products were purified and then sequenced using the amplification primers and an ABI Prism 377 Automated DNA Sequencer (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). Fragments were assembled using Sequencher (GeneCodes, Ann Arbor, MI) and sequences were aligned using ClustalX. I reviewed and fine- tuned the alignments by eye using SeaView. My preliminary analysis of 600 base pairs from ten species affords strong support for a monophyletic Balistoidea, as well as monophyletic families Balistidae and Monacanthidae. Other groups are not nearly as well supported, but the addition of taxa and more sequence data may help to clarify these relationships. Supported by DEB-0075460 and the Jane H. Bemis Fund for Research in Natural History.

23411: The genus Leiarius Bleeker, 1862 and its nominal species have never been examined in a comprehensive taxonomic study. A necessary revision is underway based on the examination of type material, images, and several non-type specimens. 23412: Heightened threat to the many populations of the Colombia Spotted Frog, Rana luteiventris, in western North America has spurred questions as to the effects of connectivity of habitat on survival. Rana luteiventris move through lotic and lentic corridors in high mountain basin forests. The importance of water corridors becomes more important in drier areas where down-cutting and drought deplete the area of moist habitat. We surveyed the population dynamics of the Columbia Spotted Frog in the Toiyabe Mountains of Southern Nevada to locate natural dispersion corridors. Our survey included five pasture areas along a dry mountain valley. Corridors were identified between the first and the second and between the third and the fourth pastures going north to south. The other pastures were connected enough to be considered a continuous habitat. Late summer movement was most constrained to the wettest habitats suggesting that the drying out of corridors prevents frogs from returning to over-wintering sights. This suggests that an improvement of corridors between the populations would insure free movement to preferred over- wintering sites and slow down the decline of Spotted Frog populations in this area.
