23413: The testes of Odontesthes bonariensis and Cnesterodon decemmaculatus, two atherinomorph freshwater species from Argentina, are examined. O. bonariensis (Order Atheriniformes) is an externally fertilizing, oviparous silverside. C. decemmaculatus (Order Cyprinodontiformes) is viviparous, fertilization being internal. Although these species possess different fertilization modalities, they share the same basic testis morphology. The testes are unfused, paired organs running laterally along the body wall on either side of the gut. Primary spermatogonia are restricted to the distal termini of the testicular lobules just beneath the tunica albuginea, thus conforming to the typical atherinomorph testis type. In restricted testes, there is a maturational progression of germ cell stages towards the efferent ducts. Unlike the unrestricted testis type, a lobular lumen never develops. The only lumina present are those of spermatocysts, which do not qualify to the definition of germinal epithelium. Then, males never develop a germinal epithelium; rather the germ tissue is epithelioid. In O. bonariensis, mature sperm are released into the efferent ducts, which empty into a single longitudinal main duct in each testis. C. decemmaculatus package sperm in the form of unencapsulated sperm bundles or spermatozeugmata. Spermatozeugmata appear to be formed before spermiation within the lobules. Unlike other cyprinodontiform fishes, each spermatocyst releases a single, large spermatozeugma. PAS+ testicular secretions help maintain the integrity of the sperm packets once they reach the efferent and main testis ducts.

23414: The Lagoa do Peixe National Park (LPNP - 31°S; 051°W) is a large (30 km long; 2 km width) coastal lagoon located in southern Brazil, which is characterized by a diverse ichthyofauna. Although with a National Park status, this site has a long-established artisanal fishery composed of about 168 fishermen. In spite of its ecological and commercial relevance, there is a lack of information about its ichthyofauna. Based on an extensive field collection and bibliography were provide a taxonomic list. Seasonal samples were taken during 2001 winter and spring and 2002 summer and fall with several fishing gears that characterize different habitats. Sampling effort was higher during summer when the by-catch of the pink shrimp fishery was included in the data. Pink shrimp is captured at LPNP by a channel-net. All samples were fixed in situ and then processed at the Ichthyology Laboratory located at the Rio Grande Federal University (FURG). Freshwater species (S=32) showed higher frequency of occurrence in northern and southern sites of LPNP. We captured 25 marine species that were distributed in its majority at the estuarine zone of the lagoon adjacent to the intermittent entrance. 23415: The Lagoa do Peixe National Park is located in south Brazilian coast (31ºS; 051ºW). The lack of information about local herpetofauna makes the present study very important. The goal of this investigation is to provide the first faunal list of this group. The richness of species composition was different for each environment, being greater in plains and swamps (13 amphibians and 15 reptiles) which can be explained by the local environmental characteristics, such as high humidity rate that supplies the metabolic and physiological requirements and high abundance of food that makes this environment favorable to adaptation of the herpetofauna. In the coastal dunes we found seven species of amphibians and four species of reptiles. 23416: Feeding motivation is an important factor when an animal determines whether to forage or not. Here we compared the performance of hatchery-reared normal and growth hormone transgenic coho salmon feeding on surface drifting edible and inedible novel prey items in various social environments. With transgenic fish reared on the same amount of food as satiated normal fish, both genotypes were of the same age and size. With an inherently higher appetite, we expected transgenic fish to be more willing to try to feed on novel prey, and that they would learn faster to feed on edible prey. Transgenic and normal fish were equally willing to attack both the edible and inedible prey, but transgenic fish were more persistent. Transgenic fish were more efficient and managed to seize the edible prey after fewer attacks compared with normal fish. However, the final consumption of prey took longer for transgenic fish. When encountering the inedible prey, transgenic fish were again more persistent and interacted longer with the prey compared with normal salmon. The number of individuals attacking decreased with repeated exposures, as did the time spent interacting with the prey. These responses were stronger in transgenic fish, partly explained by generally low response in normal fish. The observed differences in feeding behaviour are most likely the consequence of elevated levels of growth hormone generating a higher feeding motivation, stronger reinforcement capacity, and stronger reward sensation in transgenic fish. We have shown that transgenic fish learn to feed on a novel profitable prey faster than normal fish. However, elevated growth hormone levels may limit the consumption rate of transgenic fish, possibly because of altered allometric growth, partly counteracting their better seizing performance. Transgenic fish are also willing to waste more time and energy when interacting with novel unprofitable prey so that in the wild, the overall performance of transgenic fish may depend on the type, and relative abundance of edible and inedible prey.

23417: Nesting burrow conditions have been significant to the embryological development of several turtle species which use burrows for egg incubation and have temperature dependent sex determination (TSD). Desert tortoises, Gopherus agassizii, of the western Mojave are known to use multiple burrows throughout the year for thermoregulation, hibernation, and nesting. Juvenile desert tortoises have been shown to select burrows with optimal temperature environments, choosing burrows oriented to the northeast with some associated shrub canopy. Maternal selection of nesting burrows with specific microhabitat characteristics (i.e., depth, temperature, orientation, vegetation and substrate) may be deterministic in egg development, sex determination, sex ratios, and hatchling survivorship. We hypothesize that adult, female desert tortoises (with TSD) will use similar strategies in nesting burrow selection to optimize egg survivorship. Using radio telemetry, we tracked 15 wild, female desert tortoises to their nest sites and collected microhabitat data on nesting burrows during the 2002 nesting season. Nest site data included orientation of burrow mouth, proximity of burrow to vegetation, and oviposition site characteristics. Based on these preliminary findings, we will conduct a manipulative experiment during the 2003 nesting season to determine what affect these variables may have on embryo development, sex, and survivorship. We will collect eggs from wild females using oxytocin injections and place these eggs in pre-selected burrows of varying orientation. In addition to egg nests, we will place data loggers in pseudonests at varying depths to construct temperature profiles within burrows.

23418: In the course of a study aimed at determining the phylogenetic relationships of the sharks of the family Triakidae, we discovered a partial duplication of the cytochrome b gene in the mitochondrial genome of members of two different triakid genera: Mustelus and Hemitriakis. In both cases, the duplicated sequences are located downstream of the cytochrome b gene and upstream of the control region. The large amount of change evident in the region immediately downstream of the functional cytochrome b gene indicate that the Threonine and Proline transfer RNAs normally occupying this position are no longer encoded at this site. Phylogenetic analyses of the duplicated sequences and the functional cytochrome b gene strongly support two different origins for the duplicated sequences. The two duplication events show remarkable similarities in location and gene region affected. The duplicated regions begin 51 and 59 bases downstream of the cytochrome b gene and include sequences that would encode the last 166 and 184 amino acid residues of cytochrome b. The duplicated region of Hemitriakis has acquired a considerably greater number of mutations than that of Mustelus when each is compared to its putative parent sequence. This disparity may be due to differences in the rate of substitution or in the time of origin. Documented cases of changes in the organization and content of mitochondrial genomes of vertebrates remain relatively uncommon; however, the few reports on mitochondrial sequence duplication reveal interesting commonalities. The characteristics of the duplication events we have discovered in triakid sharks correspond well with many of those common features and thus strengthen the case for a common mechanism of origin.

23419: I tested the monophyly of the putative subfamily Geophaginae, and attempted to resolve the genus-level relationships within the group. 72 characters of external morphology, 649 base pairs of the mitochondrial gene ND4, and 950 bp of the nuclear gene RAG2 were analyzed both separately and in a combined data set. The ingroup included 15 genera and 26 species of geophagines (sensu Kullander 1998) and 4 species of Crenicichla included to test whether this genus is sister to Cichla or belongs in the Geophaginae. One species each of the genera Cichlasoma, Hoplarchus and Mesonauta were included to contrast geophagine synapomorphies with characters of its sistergroup Cichlasomatinae; Retroculus, Astronotus, and Cichla were used as outgroups. Data were analyzed by maximum parsimony using PAUP*; support was determined by bootstrapping and Decay Indices. Each of the three partitions alone failed to characterize a geophagine clade, but the combination of external morphology, ND4, and RAG2 provided a better-resolved topology than the independent data sets. Genus-level monophyly was confirmed in all cases except that of Apistogramma. A monophyletic Geophaginae, including Crenicichla, was well supported, as well as a monophyletic Cichlasomatinae. Although with poor resolution at the base of the tree, 3 groups were distinguished within the Geophaginae. The first subclade included the genera Satanoperca, Apistogramma, Apistogrammoides and Taeniacara. The second subclade included Dicrossus, Crenicara and Biotoecus, and coincided with the tribe Crenicaratini proposed by Kullander. The third group included all other genera except Acarichthys and Guianacara. Despite high levels of homoplasy, in a total evidence context, external morphology improved the resolution and support of the topology, and revealed arrangements that molecular data alone did not recover. These results constitute a first approximation of geophagine internal relationships. An additional set of 99 osteological characters is being tested, and will be added to the global analysis with the intention of improving resolution and support of geophagine relationships.

23420: In order to determine if Eastern Pacific green turtles (Chelonia mydas) exhibit feeding preferences within the region of Bahía Magdalena, samples of recently ingested food items were collected by conducting gastric lavage of 15 live-captured turtles (obtained as part of a monitoring study conducted by Wildcoast). The consumed food items were compared to the food resources available in the marine environment. Vegetation transects were conducted seasonally in order to provide information of food resources available to sea turtles within the Bay. Results indicate that green turtle diet consists largely of algae, but that the turtles also occasionally feed on marine invertebrates in larger proportions than previously reported. Unlike many studies of this species in other parts of the world, the eelgrass Zostera marina did not make up a major component of the diet of the turtles in this region. Green turtles in our study selectively consumed diet items, with Codium amplivesiculatum and Gracialaria textorii as preferred species. Differences in the consumption of species were found across seasons and were consistent with changes in the availability of different algae species in the environment. The study shows that the diet of C. mydas is made up of a diversity of food items but demonstrate preferences for some food resources which were consumed in much larger quantities with regard to their availability in the environment. Based on these results, it is recommended that sea turtle conservation plans along the Baja California Peninsula include Pacific coastal mangrove channels with a high diversity of algae species as priority areas for protection.

23421: The three species of mudminnows of the genus Umbra of esociform fishes present intriguing variability in genome size and karyotypic arrangement. While these traits in the European U. krameri are not dissimilar to those in other esociformes, the two North American species (U. limi and U. pygmae) posses a much larger genome and a distinct karyotype that consists of 22 large metacentric chromosomes. The data suggests that this population of transposons is more active in the genomes of Umbra than in those of the outgroups, where conserved translation products were scarce. The sequence variants in Umbra represent at least two distinct groups with unequal abundance. Hybridization and PCR experiments indicate a significantly greater number of these elements in the genomes of the North American species of Umbra. I present a comparison of the elements identified in this study with those reported in the literature and discuss this findings in the context of hypotheses of genome evolution that invoke a role for repetitive sequences in shaping large-scale genome characteristics, such as genome size and karyotypic stability. I focus attention on the difficult question of determining causal relationships between multiple factors that undergo simultaneous change on a phylogenetic reconstruction.

23422: Atelopus is a species-rich genus of Neotropical bufonids. Currently, about 75 species are described, most of which occur in the northern Andes. 23423: The bay pipefish, Syngnathus leptorhynchus, inhabits estuaries along the eastern Pacific from Alaska to Baja California. This pipefish is elongate, slender, and cryptic in its protective eelgrass habitat. Fishes of this species are specialized because females deposit their eggs directly into the brood pouch of a male, where they are fertilized, nourished, and protected until they hatch as free-swimming juveniles. Extensive morphometric and meristic variation has been found across the range of this species, causing both difficulty in identification and distinction from other pipefish species. Due to this morphological variation, specialized reproductive strategy, and affinity to eelgrass habitat, it is hypothesized that S. leptorhynchus may also exhibit both marked genetic variation and geographic structure. Using both mitochondrial control region sequence and microsatellite data, this study examines the intraspecific variation and genetic structure of individuals of S. leptorhynchus from locations from southeast Alaska to southern California. Preliminary data suggest both genetic variation and geographic structure within the species.

23424: Annual fishes (Rivulidae) are an important component of the Neotropical Icthyofauna. Among them, Cynolebias is a specious genus that occurs from northeastern Brazil to northeastern Argentina and southern Uruguay. Cynolebias luteoflamulatus inhabits the eastern lowlands of Uruguay and previous reports indicate that this species is highly variable along its distributional range. In the present work we studied the morphological variation in C. luteoflamulatus using meristic and design characters analyzed with univariate and multivariate analysis, and morphometric characters analyzed with a Geometric Morphometry approach. For analysis purposes specimens were grouped according to their corresponding drainages: Rocha, Castillos, and Merin Lagoons. Due to strong sexual dimorphism, males and females were analyzed separately. Our results showed that morphological variation in this species is associated to a geographical pattern. In the case of meristic and design characters, the strongest discrimination occurred in males while females showed to be more similar among different drainages. Males from Rocha exhibited the strongest discrimination from the others. The number of dorsal fin rays and stripes on the flank were the characters that contributed most to this segregation. It has to be noted that this species is the only annual fish in this drainage. When morphometry was considered, the three populations analyzed could be well discriminated from each other in both sexes. Some of the characters that contributed to this pattern were: dorsal fin origin, position of eyes, and length of snout. Since a design variable and some characters of dorsal fin in males were involved in the discriminations observed sexual selection could also be playing an important role in the differentiation of populations of this species. This species presents a restricted distribution and thus requires conservation efforts. As potential different evolutionary units, conservation policies on this species should consider the three populations found in this study.

23425: We investigated population differentiation and haplotype richness among seasonally fragmented populations of 3 stream fishes in the Ouachita Mountains, Arkansas. Within intermittent streams, riffles may dry during summer, resulting in nearly to completely isolated pools. We sampled Lepomis megalotis (longear sunfish), Etheostoma whipplei (red fin darter), and Fundulus olivaceus (black-spotted topminnow) from 5 isolated pools in the Alum Fork of the Saline River (above Lake Winona) and 2 spring-fed, perennial tributaries in the Saline River system (downstream from Lake Winona) during September 2001 and 2002. We assessed variability of the control region of the mitochondrial DNA on polyacrylimide gels with use of temporal temperature gradient electrophoresis (TTGE). We found temporal population differentiation (between years) for L. megalotis and F. olivaceus. Lepomis megalotis populations also were spatially differentiated along the stream gradient, but populations of F. olivaceus and E. whipplei were not. Haplotype diversity did not differ spatially for any species. After combining data for populations above Lake Winona, we observed significantly higher haplotype diversity below the reservoir for F. olivaceus and E. whipplei. Therefore, stream fragmentation appears be associated with reduced haplotype richness for some species. Spatiotemporal patterns of population differentiation were most obvious for L. megalotis, but less evident for F. olivaceus and E. whipplei which are putatively better dispersers than L. megalotis. Thus, stream fragmentation influences gene flow which appears to be correlated with species-specific dispersal capability.

23426: Several clades of Neotropical freshwater fishes are derived from marine lineages. These marine- derived taxa offer unique opportunities for inter-habitat comparisons of rates and patterns of molecular evolution. Such comparisons involve three steps. First, well supported phylogenies for clades containing marine and freshwater taxa must be generated. Second, molecular changes can be inferred from optimizations of DNA sequence data on the phylogenies. Third, a variety of methods can be used to interpret the inferred patterns of molecular evolution in freshwater and marine lineages. Investigation of three marine/freshwater transitions (two needlefish clades, and one stingray clade) suggests that rates of molecular evolution are higher in freshwater lineages. Analysis of synonymous versus non-synonymous changes reveals that selection does not appear to be the force driving these rate increases. Other possible explanations for the phenomenon are discussed.

23427: Itirapina Ecological Station (IES, 2300 ha; 22°00′ e 22°15′ S; 47°45′ e 48°00′ W) is one of the few remnants of protected Cerrado in the State of São Paulo, southeastern Brazil. It encompasses grasslands, shrubby grasslands, shrubby grasslands with trees, gallery forests, and swampy areas. Leptodactylus fuscus and L. furnarius were significantly more abundant in gallery forests, whereas L. mystacinus seemed to be more abundant in shrubby grassland with trees. Seasonal activity was concentrated in the rainy season (October-March). Leptodacylus fuscus was more abundant in the first half of the rainy season, whereas L. mystacinus and L. furnarius were more abundant in second half of the rainy season. Although differences in temporal and spatial distribution among closely related species may help in avoiding overlap in resource use (e. g., food, breeding sites), we found no evidence of limitation in resources at the study site. 23428: The bluefish Pomatomus saltatrix and the striped weakfish Cynoscion guatucupa are two of the most important commercially exploited species in southern Brazil. 23429: Hypopygus lepturus is a widly distributed Amazonian species with a maximum length of about 8cm. Like all gymnotiform species, Hypopygus lepturus possesses primary electric organs that together with the genus-typic subdermal auxiliary electric organs enable it to produce discharges in the magnitude of about 100mV. Being considered a nonmigratory species, Hypopygus inhabits the leaflitter in small, slow-flowing rivers (igarapes). Preliminary data from the electric organ discharges collected during the field trip indicate differences between individuals from different igarapes. Special regard was given to sampling pairs of opposing igarapes. This preliminary study analyses the molecular variability in DNA-sequences of the mitochondrial control region and tries to identify potential genetic flux between both margins to corroborate the idea that big rivers act as effective dispersal barriers. To do this, two pairs of opposing igarapes were subsampled, one from each extreme of the sampling area. Since the taxonomy of Rhamphichthyidae is not entirely understood, an objective of this study is to find evidence for possible new species or subspecies of the Hypopygus group. DNA was extracted from muscle tissue and amplified via PCR. The purified PCR products were sequenced on an automated sequencer. DNA-polymorphism, parsimony and maximum likelihood analyses were applied to the resulting data. The results of these analyses are discussed.

23430: It has been hypothesized that Southwest Atlantic school sharks Galeorhinus galeus migrate seasonally between southern Brazil and northern Argentina for mating and pupping. Lack of data on life history of school sharks from Argentinean waters precluded the test of this hypothesis. In this study, the reproductive biology, seasonal occurrence, and embryo growth of school sharks from off Argentina are described. A total of 411 school sharks (123 males and 288 females) were examined. Female size at 50% maturity was 124.72 mm total length (TL). Fertility was, on average, 1.77 pups smaller than fecundity. Differences between fecundity and fertility were not dependent on mother size. The largest embryos were found in late October and November in coincidence with ovulation. This indicates that gestation lasts about 12 months. Embryo growth was described by the Gompertz model (with Linf = 29.77, k = 0.021, and a = -1.171). Four groups of females were recognized: juveniles up to 129 cm TL, with translucent-to-white ovarian follicles (<19 mm wide); mature non-ovulating females with yellow ovarian follicles (17.5-27.5 mm wide), low gonadosomatic index (GSI), and empty uteri; mature ovulating females with larger yellow ovarian follicles (42-57.5 mm wide), high GSI, and uteri empty or with recently ovulated eggs; and pregnant females carrying term embryos, with minute ovarian follicles. These observations give support to the 3-year-long reproductive cycle proposed earlier. Males dominated the catches in October and April (63-71% of examined specimens). Females were more abundant than males from November to March (67-100%). The pattern of occurrence and reproductive condition of school sharks in northern Argentina are complementary to that from southern Brazil. This supports the hypothesis that there is a single large population of school sharks in the Southwestern Atlantic that performs reproductive migrations between southern Brazil and northern Argentina.

23431: The tribe Cnesterodontini Hubbs, as currently defined, comprehends four genera (Cnesterodon Garman, Phalloceros Eigenmann, Phalloptychus Henn and Phallotorynus Henn) which are distributed along southern South America. 23432: Takydromus formosanus, closely related to T. hsuehshanensis in the high mountains and T. wolteri in northeastern Asia, is one of the four endemic Takydromus species occurring in Taiwan. 23433: The climatic oscillations at the global scale have played a prominent role in determining the biodiversity of earth lives. It greatly influences the evolutionary process of organisms, including extinctions, speciation, and the lost or gaining of genetic lineages. However, little researches are accomplished in eastern Asia, especially in subtropical regions. In this study, sequence variation of the mitochondrial cytochrome b gene fragment from 178 specimens was used to reconstruct the phylogeographic pattern of the grass lizard Takydromus stejnegeri endemic in Taiwan. Existence of deep lineages in various phylogenetic trees, indicates allopatric differentiation between different refugial areas. According to the inferences from the nested clade analysis, the apportioning pattern of haplotypes in most clades reveals strong tendencies of post-glacial range expansion. Another consequence of geographic expansion is the growth in population sizes. Such demographic expansion history is supported by significant negative Tajima's D values due to existence of excessive singletons over nucleotide sequences. This research highlights the importance of concerned studies in searching the refugial regions with rugged topologies in southeastern Asia, and will provide useful information for making correct conservation policies in the very near future.

23434: During the 1990s the US-Brazilian Calhamazon Project conducted ichthyological exploration of the Amazon River main channels. Four expeditions covered more than 3,500 km of the Brazilian Amazon-Solimoes mainstem and the lower reaches of 14 of its largest tributaries: Tocantins, Jari, Xingu, Tapajós, Trombetas, Madeira, Negro, Purus, Coari, Tefe, Japurá (Caquetá), Juruá, Jutaí, and Iça (Putamayo). Benthic samples were taken with 3 x 1m bottom trawls; midwater collections were made with plankton, neuston, and midwater-trawl nets. The collections are deposited at ANSP, MZUSP, INPA, USNM, MCP, FMNH, and MNRJ, and most are available for study through institutional curators. Auxiliary products include a database of identified specimens with georeferenced locality/habitat information, hundreds of photographs of fishes and habitats, sonar graph bottom profiles of bottom-trawl samples, and EOD recordings of gymnotiforms. More than 360 fish species are represented in the "Calhamazon" collections including deep channel and pelagic residents and sporadics. The benthic fish fauna contains >210 species dominated by siluriforms (68%) and gymnotiforms (22%); at the family level these are mostly pimelodids, loricariids, doradids and apteronotids. Several species of potamotrygonids, sciaenids and achirids are also common. The pelagic fish assemblage of the channels contains several auchenipterids (especially Ageneiosus spp.), pimelodids (Hypophthalmus spp. and juveniles of other species), and several engraulids, clupeids and belonids. Notably absent from or very rare in the channels are: cyprinodontiforms, characiforms, cichlids, and some otherwise common lowland catfishes and electric fishes including pseudopimelodids, callichthyids, scoloplacids, gymnotids and Electrophorus. This report will illustrate the most common and novel fish species of the Amazon channels including newly or yet undescribed species, and the Amazon channel fauna will be compared to that of the lower Orinoco.

23435: The identification of larval istiophorid billfishes inhabiting the Western Atlantic Ocean has long been problematic. Here, a molecular technique was used to positively identify 27 larval white marlin (Tetrapturus albidus), 96 blue marlin (Makaira nigricans), and 591 sailfish (Istiophorus platypterus) from the Straits of Florida and the Bahamas. Nine morphometric measurements were made on each of a subset of the known-identity larvae, and lower jaw pigment patterns were recorded on a grid. A form of discriminant analysis (partial Canonical Variates Analysis, CVA) was used to reveal the extent to which the combination of morphometric, pigment pattern and month of capture information was species-diagnostic. Linear regression revealed species-specific relationships between snout length versus standard length (SL) and between snout length:eye orbit diameter ratio versus SL. Confidence limits about these relationships served as defining characters for sailfish > 10 mm SL and for blue and white marlin > 19 mm SL. Pigment pattern analysis indicated that 40% of the pre-flexion blue marlin examined possessed a characteristic lower jaw pigment pattern and that 62% of sailfish larvae were identifiable by lower jaw pigments alone. An identification key was constructed based on pigment patterns, month of capture, and relationships between SL, snout length and eye orbit diameter. The key correctly identified 69.6% of 283 (blind sample) larvae used to test it. One fish was mis-identified by the key. Of the 85 larvae that could not be identified by the key, 75 (88.2%) were correctly identified using CVA. The remaining larvae could not be identified by either technique. While distinguishing certain larval specimens may always require molecular techniques, we are encouraged that the majority (96%) of those that we examined were ultimately identifiable from external characteristics.

23436: Amphidromous gobies of the subfamily Sicydiinae exhibit long marine planktonic larval stages prior to recruitment into adult freshwater habitats. The length of larval life (LLL) has important implications for speciation, population connectivity and conservation of sicydiine gobies. LLL was evaluated for two species of the genus Stiphodon common in Pohnpei streams. Daily growth increments of sagittal otoliths were counted using digital photographs taken at 400x magnification with polarized light. Significant differences in mean LLL were determined for Stiphodon caeruleus (86.6 ± 1.35 days) and Stiphodon cf. elegans (65.6 ± 3.0 days). Stiphodon cf. elegans demonstrates the lowest mean LLL yet determined for any sicydiine species. The margin of difference (21 days) between the two species is greater than any previously recorded differences among sicydiine species within an island group or among sicydiine congeners.

23437: For almost a quarter century, we have grown accustomed to think of Santa Cecilia, in eastern Ecuador, as the richest single locality for frogs and toads (86 species). The forests just north of Leticia would seem an unlikely place to find an even larger fauna. Based on fieldwork beginning in April 2001 and terminating in February 2003 (117 days), my students and I have taken 95 species of frogs and toads in this patch of forest (seven bufonids, one centrolenid, five dendrobatids, 52 hylids, 25 leptodactylids, four microhylids, and one pipid). Seven other species have been collected in these forest patches by other investigators in other years. Why so big? I suggest the following, with some caution, given that Ron Heyer was quite correct when he suggested that our knowledge base, especially for hylids, was weak: that Leticia is positioned geographically in such a way that it is the biogeographic equivalent of an ecotone where three or four regional faunas overlap in space. Although Duellman has long-advocated the diurnal terrestrials, nocturnal terrestrials, and arboreal frogs as ecological components of these faunas, I am inclined to divide the fauna in a different way-into four components: (1) aquatic frogs, never stray from bodies of water, (2) terrestrial frogs, combining the time series, (3) frogs of the sotobosque, living in the shallow layer that herpetologists walk and work, and (4) the canopy fauna. Initially, I decided to use rough frequency of encounter as a means of separating sotobosque and canopy species (many canopy species breed at ground level). Except for the gramalote (floating meadows there are no nonforest frogs in this fauna although some species abound in pastures. Fieldwork in January and February included use of pitfall traps, bromeliad surveys between 5 and 25 m above ground, nocturnal searches of trails and ponds, and felling of trees. The latter technique, and to some respect, the first technique, call into question some of my initial sorting of the fauna because we have obtained canopy records for some aquatic species (Sphaenorhynchus carneus – to 15 m), found a Scinax confined to bromeliads 6 m or more above the water, found Scinax funerea up to 40 m above ground, and taken Adelophryne and Syncope up to 10 m above ground.

23438: Estuaries are dynamic, ecological systems in which environmental conditions can fluctuate widely over the short (i.e., daily tidal influence, local weather conditions) and long (i.e., global climatic events, anthropogenic changes) term. Many fish species depend upon estuaries as nursery habitats during their young-of-the-year and juvenile life stages. As they grow and mature during these early life stages, many species experience the highest growth rates of their lives and undergo major habitat and dietary shifts. The Alafia River, an estuary located in west central Florida, discharges into the northeast portion of Tampa Bay. The river is 487 km long, has a watershed of approximately 1,092 km2, and until recently, had been relatively unaffected by water withdrawals. Between 1996 and 2001, monthly fish samples were collected by the Florida Marine Research Institute's Fisheries-Independent Monitoring (FIM) program to address fishery and water management mandates. Sample sites, which were selected by stratified-random sampling design, were distributed from the river mouth to 15 km upstream, a point where limestone sills restrict further saltwater intrusion. Using 21.3-m seines (788 hauls) and 6.1-m otter trawls (293 hauls), FIM staff collected 863,348 fish representing 106 taxa, with more taxa unique to seines (42) than trawls (8). A single species, Anchoa mitchilli, was present in over 50% of the seine and trawl hauls and composed over 70% of the total catch in each gear type. Preliminary analyses of select species indicated that species-specific distributions along the salinity gradient were dependent upon fish size. As fish size increased, the abundance for some species peaked in higher salinity waters whereas the abundance of others peaked in lower salinity waters. Analyses of fish habitat should consider fish size to account for the dynamic nature of the environment and its inhabitants.

23440: Amphibian diversity in the Neotropics is very rich, contrasting sharply with the relative absence of ecological studies of this group. The biology of the majority of species is unknown, and the species that have been studied are still understudied. In the southern Brazilian state of Parana, studies of amphibians are mostly confined to descriptions of new species and new occurrences for the state. In the last few decades the face of Parana has changed drastically: human activities have reduced the original forest cover of the state to 3% of its original extent. Biological studies of amphibians, therefore, become much more important in the face of this environmental devastation. Because of their diversity and abundance, amphibians can be important as models for understanding inter- and intra-specific interactions, habitat selection and conservation. Also, amphibian models may inform current interest in forest fragmentation and corridors. To this end, anuran amphibians were studied in a region with 16 areas where anurans reproduce, within an area with a mosaic of natural (Araucaria angustifolia) and exotic (Pinus spp., Eucalyptus spp.) reforestation. This region also contains natural savannah and is a transition zone between the Atlantic Mixed Rain Forest and the seasonal semi-deciduous forest of the middle Tibagi River watershed, near the municipality of Telemaco Borba. In all habitats, monthly sampling was done from October 1991 to December 2001, and bimonthly in 2002, in which all vocalizing species were recorded. Vocalizations were recorded of 40 species distributed among six Families (Bufonidae, Centrolenidae, Hylidae, Leptodactylidae, Microhylidae and Ranidae). We anticipate encountering an additional five species because of historical records. Species segregate spatially (macro- and micro-habitats) and temporally (seasonally). The greatest activity periods, however, occur during the wettest and hottest periods of the year. Fragmentation of this habitat may have important repercussions for amphibian reproductive dynamics and success.

23441: We studied the diet, feeding behavior, reproduction, growth and activity patterns of Liophis poecilogyrus during 30 months (July 1998 - December 2000) in the sand dunes of the North Coastal Plain of the state of Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil. Our results are based on 171 findings (140 captures and 31 recaptures), 52 individuals born in captivity, and dissection of 59 preserved specimens from the region. Anuran amphibians (present in 97.1 % of the individuals with prey) and fish (present in 2.9 %) were the only types of prey recorded. L. poecilogyrus is an active hunter that forages mainly on the ground. Mature females attain mean snout-vent length (SVL) greater than mature males (413 mm and 342 mm, respectively). The reproductive cycle is seasonal, with clutches and hatchlings occurring during the hot months of the year (October to January). The clutch size ranges from 3 to 9 eggs (mean = 6, SD = 2, n = 12). Males reach the sexual maturity nearly at the end of the first year, with approximately 260 mm of SVL, while females reach maturity nearly in the middle of the second year, with approximately 335 mm of SVL. The growth in both sexes is negative allometric and shows seasonal variation, with higher growth rates during the hot months. The temperature seems to be the most important factor on determining the activity patterns of this population. The annual activity is seasonal and unimodal, with higher frequencies of active individuals during the hot months, and the daily activity is bimodal along most of the year (except during the cold months), with higher frequencies of active individuals in early morning and late afternoon. The activity, reproductive and growth patterns appoint a strong influence of ecological factors, mainly temperature, in the natural history of the species.

23442: Studies of frogs in the Manaus region have contributed much to our understanding of anuran community ecology. Studies of the relationships among predators, and tadpoles and eggs of different species of anurans have demonstrated the importance of predators in structuring aquatic communities and contributing to Beta diversity. Subsequent studies in other areas within Amazonia, and on other continents indicate that the patterns are general. Studies of diet and foraging mode have shown the importance of ontogenetic variation in size and behavior in reducing resource-use overlap. Experiments have confirmed the lack of competition between individuals of different sizes within the same species. Studies of population dynamics have revealed the limitations of short term studies and long-term studies that cover small geographic areas. The research summarized covers a period of over 20 years and many researchers. The major sites within the Manaus region have now been included within the only long-term ecological research (LTER) site in the Brazilian Amazon, opening the possibility for more detailed long-term studies.

23443: Leatherback nesting occurs on the shores of tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide. Trinidad, in the southern Caribbean, is tropical and hosts the second largest leatherback nesting aggregation in the Western Hemisphere. It is estimated that 4000 turtles nest annually in Trinidad. Far fewer leatherbacks nest on the subtropical beaches of Florida and the first nest was discovered there in 1947, in Flagler County. The beach near Melbourne, Florida, in South Brevard County, has supported about 3% of leatherback nesting in Florida in recent years. Greatest production on record occurred in 2001, when 39 nests were documented. Hatching success, a measure by which leatherback nesting beach productivity can be compared on different beaches, was studied at Matura beach and Grande Riviere beach in Trinidad abd in South Brevard County, Florida, in 2001. Hatching success for undisturbed nests (33%) was significantly smaller on the Florida beach than on Trinidadian beaches (Matura; 64%, Grande Rivere; 62%), but far more nests were disturbed by predators and erosion in Trinidad (41% of the nests at Matura and 56.4% of the nests at Grande Riviere) than in Florida (8%). Biotic factors such as clutch size of the leatherback turtle nests were compared between Florida and Trinidad. Also, abiotic factors such as incubation temperature, water content and relative gas exchange were compared for nests laid on the Trinidad and Florida beaches.

23444: Kurtus has historically been placed in the Kurtoidei, , a monotypic suborder of the Perciformes. Ichthyologists have previously hypothesized a relationship to beryciforms, pempherids, and apogonids. Due to this vagueness, molecular tools have been employed to aid in the resolution of Kurtus phylogeny. Mitochondrial genes are frequently used to infer phylogeny but questions remain about their ability to elucidate deeper nodes in fishes. Appropriate nuclear genes may better help resolve this problem. The recombination activating gene 1 (RAG-1) has shown promise in determining higher level relationships among fishes. RAG-1 is a single copy, nuclear gene that aids in immune cell production. The present study utilizes the RAG-1 gene to explore the interrelationships among Perciform suborders and families. Specifically, the purpose of this study was to elucidate the previously vague placement of the family Kurtidae among fishes. Initial studies using 500 base pairs of the RAG-1 gene and a limited number of taxa have shown its placement within the Perciformes and relation to the Percoidei. Futher investigation utilizing 1500 base pairs of the RAG-1 gene and increasing the number of relevant taxa to include all suborders within the Perciformes has clarified the placement of Kurtus.

23445: The genus Kolpotocheirodon was described by Malabarba & Weitzman with a single species, K. theloura, from Central Brazil. The genus was diagnosed mostly by the presence of an unique specialized caudal organ at the proximal region of the ventral caudal-fin lobe of males, consisting of hypertrophied elongate dermal flaps attached along the fin rays and series of relatively flat tabs and papillae attached along the exposed border of those flaps. These structures were unknown in other inseminating or externally fertilizing species of characids. A second species collected in the rio Pratinha, Iraquara, Bahia, Brazil was found and presents a caudal organ similar to that described for K. theloura. Description of the new species and the collection of new and better- preserved specimens of K. theloura, along with SEM observations of the caudal fin structures, allow the reanalysis of the characters defining Kolpotocheirodon and of the autapomorphies diagnosing the type species. The genus is diagnosed mostly by new specialized sexually dimorphic structures found in the lower caudal fin lobe of males, detected through SEM analysis and described herein. Characters previously described to diagnose Kolpotocheirodon are considered autapomorphies for the type species. The basal relative position of Kolpotocheirodon among Compsurini cheirodontines is further supported by the presence of aquasperm in both known species, and lack of the apomorphic elongate sperm cells found in the remaining members of the tribe.

23446: A small clupeomorph fish, Ellimmichthys n. sp. is described from the Aptian-Albian sediments of the Maceió Formation, in the Alagoas Basin, Alagoas State in northeastern Brazil. The new clupeomorph is a small double-armored herring, measuring 45 mm of standard length. It is a mold-countermold specimen preserved in black shales. Although the fish is complete, the preservation, mainly of the skull, is poor. Just a few head bones can be recognized, among them the sculptured frontals and the opercular series. This clupeomorph presents the paraclupeid (presence of laterally expanded and keeled dorsal scutes, some of them with the keel extending posteriorly over the next scute) and paraclupeinae (absence of teeth along the posterior edge of dorsal scutes; and posteriormost dorsal scutes many times the size of the anteriormost ones) characters. Meristic differences mainly concerning to number of vertebrae and pectoral-fin ray distinguish it as a new species. Comparing to the other Ellimmichthys species, this species shows a closer similarity with E. goodi reported for the freshwater sediments of West Africa, corroborating the South American-African biogeographic connection already evidenced by other taxa.

23447: Presence of insemination has been recently described in characid fishes, mainly in two hypothetically monophyletic groups: the subfamily Glandulocaudinae and the tribe Compsurini of the Cheirodontinae. Species of both groups present similar adaptations related or presumably related to insemination, as for example the elongation of the sperm nucleus, development of putative pheromone glands in the caudal fins and accentuated development of secondary sexual features. These characters are considered, however, as independently derived and non- homologous in both groups, through detailed comparisons of its morphology, as well as ultrastructure of the elongated sperm cells. Also, although reproductive biology of externally fertilized characids can be found in the literature, few comparative data are available, due to different methods of measurement and description. This paper presents and discusses characters related to the reproductive cycle of the externally fertilized Aphyocharacinae, Aphyocharax anisitsi, and externally fertilized species of the cheirodontine (genera Cheirodon, Serrapinnus and Odontostilbe), comparatively to the inseminating species of the cheirodontine tribe Compsurini (genus Compsura, Macropsobrycon) and Glandulocaudines (genera Mimagoniates, Diapoma), based in one year analysis for each species. Data discussed include hypothetically derived features related to the reproductive cycle presented by inseminating species and its presence in both inseminating groups. The development of secondary sexual characters is also discussed regarding its correlation with sexual maturation.

23448: This work is the result of a taxonomic survey of Gymnotiformes, a group of freshwater fish, in Colombia. The results showed 55 species, from which the family Apteronotidae possesses 22 species (40%), Gymnotidae 8 (14.54%), Hypopomidae 10 (18.18%), Rhamphichthydae 5 (9.09%) and Sternopygidae 10 (18.18%). 23449: Some fresh water turtles have a pair of cloacal organs, the cloacal bursae. The histological structure of cloacal bursae of eight species of Testudines Podocnemis expansa, Podocnemis unifilis and Podocnemis sextuberculata (Pelomedusidae), Phrynops geoffroanus and Hydromedusa tectifera (Chelidae), Chelydra serpentina (Chelydridae), Trachemys dorbigni and Trachemys scripta (Emydidae) were studied. Besides of light microscopy with different colors, the transmission electron microscopy was utilized to determine the epithelial cells. Podocnemis expansa shows the highest number of blood capillaries in the lamina propria, followed by Phrynops geoffroanus, Hydromedusa tectifera and Podocnemis sextubeculata. Instead of that, the occurrence of gas exchanges in these organs is not consider, until this moment, because of the large width of the blood-water barrier, difficulting the gas diffusion.

23451: Despite the wealth of current literature related to the physiological responses of teleosts (primarily salmonids) to exhaustive activity and the typical stressors associated with commercial- fishing, little study in this realm has addressed the responses and resulting fitness of elasmobranches, namely those harvested directly. The spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) is currently an extremely controversial NW Atlantic ground-fishery, whose actual population calculations are heavily debated among regulators and fisherman. It is highly established that female spiny dogfish possess incredibly long gestation periods and very small liters. Robust females are the larger of the two sexes and most coveted by fishermen when the fishery is directed. Of particular interest is the (discarded) bycatch mortality of the spiny dogfish and the associated stress indicators due to commercial-fishing. These findings will enable the derivation of more accurate population figures while arming regulators with data to help implement appropriate measures in the best interest of maintaining the maximum sustainable yield of the species. Concurrently quantifying the stress indicators allows one to speculate and pinpoint the physiological causes (in addition to physical causes) of post-release discard mortality. Blood samples were taken via caudal peduncle puncture from 230 spiny dogfish across three separate treatments and five separate MW to NW Atlantic sampling expeditions during the course of 2002. In accordance with the conventional haematological stress parameters, deproteinized whole-blood lactate, whole-blood hematocrit, plasma protein, and serum levels of glucose, Cl-, K+, Na+, and osmolality were measured from blood taken immediately following normal otter-trawl, longline and relative short-term captivity. Hematocrit levels of the dogfish captured by otter-trawl were significantly higher than those taken by the less exhaustive longline and the pseudo-controlled captive environments, suggesting that dogfish release a greater amount of red blood cells upon exhaustive aerobic activity associated with otter-trawl fishing.

23452: The change in vegetation from forest habitat and road verge habitat can act as a barrier to animal movements. 23453: The present study provides information on the current conservation status of freshwater fishes and measures for their conservation in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (NBR), South India. 23454: The Chesapeake Bay, Virginia serves as principal developmental habitat and foraging ground for 5,000 to 9,000 loggerhead (Caretta caretta) and Kemp's ridley (Lepidochelys kempi) sea turtles. Each spring, turtles migrate into state waters when sea temperatures reach 18 °C, remaining in Virginia until temperatures drop in the fall. Aerial census data, corrected for surfacing behavior, indicate that highest population densities of turtles observed on the sea surface occur in May and June. During May and June 2002, the respiratory behavior of one adult and four juvenile loggerheads traveling to their summer foraging grounds were determined via radio/sonic signaling. Two turtles tracked were cold-stunned rehabilitated turtles. All turtles were continuously tracked for up to 24 hours post-release. Surfacing and diving intervals were determined based on the average time turtles spent at the sea surface vs. below. Differences between individual surfacing/diving times were tested using analysis of variance (ANOVA). Respiration behavior of the adult turtle differed significantly from the juvenile turtles. There were no significant differences between the respiratory behavior of the cold-stunned rehabilitated juveniles and the other juvenile turtles. Time spent at surface ranged between 7.1% and 12.7%. When migrating, loggerhead turtles spend 10 to 15% of their time at the surface due to metabolic costs of migration. Historic sub-population estimates have been determined based on an average 7.3% surfacing time recorded in the summer and fall months when turtles have established foraging patterns within the Bay. Based on the spring 2002 data, historic sub-population counts may have been overestimated, directly impacting regional fisheries take-limits and management plans. Additionally, all turtles significantly increased their time at surface during half-hour intervals associated with sunrise and sunset, versus half hour intervals occurring during both daylight and nighttime hours. Similar sunrise/sunset surfacing phenomena were observed in the 1980's among twelve juvenile foraging loggerheads.

23455: Since 1979, the Virginia Institute of Marine Science (VIMS) has conducted a sea turtle mark- recapture program in cooperation with local poundnet fishermen within the Chesapeake Bay. With consistent fishing effort, between 14 and 92 live loggerhead (Caretta caretta) sea turtles have been incidentally captured annually since 1980. A total of 457 individual loggerheads were caught in this fisherman's nets between 1980 and 1999. The majority (89.06%) was determined to be juvenile loggerhead sea turtles, with 7.62% adults and 3.32% that were undetermined. Of the 457 turtles caught, 363 turtles were originally captured and tagged from these nets. Fifty-four of these animals were caught subsequently by the same fisherman, representing a 14.8% return to the original site of capture. In addition to the initial tagging event, this fisherman has reported a total of 160 recaptures of these turtles, including multiple recaptures of the same turtles within a season and between seasons. Satellite telemetry was used during three seasons to track the movements of an adult female loggerhead turtle captured repeatedly in the Potomac River poundnets since 1994. This turtle was captured multiple times within a season and between seasons beginning with her original capture and tagging in 1994. Kernel analyses of her tracking data indicate a 75.0% overlap in home ranges between Years One Two and Three, illustrating a concentrated home range for this turtle that is relatively consistent between seasons. 23456: Unlike other regions were crocodilians occur, flooded areas of the Amazon basin are shared by sympatric and huge populations of two caiman species, Caiman crocodilus crocodilus (spectacled caiman) and Melanosuchus niger (black caiman). Individuals of C. crocodilus (n = 12) and M. niger (n = 12) were collected at nighttime and immediately immobilized for sex identification, weight and snout-vent length measurements and blood sampling. Blood parameters included red blood cell count, hematocrit (Hct), hemoglobin concentration (Hb) and the calculated hematological indices. The measured plasma metabolites were glucose, total protein, triglycerides, urea, and ammonia. Water, air and body temperatures were obtained using a digital thermometer. Correlations among air, water and body temperatures were done using simple linear regression analysis. The hematology of two species were similar, with exception of Hct and Hb that were significantly higher in M. niger. Plasma metabolites were also very similar between two species. Glucose and triglycerides levels were low when compared to other reptiles. Total plasma protein was high in both species and meets their carnivorous habits. In M. niger the control of body temperature was totally dependent of water temperature, while in C. crocodilus, it was affected by both air and water temperatures. This pattern could be explained by behavioral/physiological features of C. crocodilus which usually do incursions to the land even at nighttime, probably imposed by size- related hierarchy of the larger species, M. niger, since density of this species is very high at this period in Mamirauá Lake.

23457: Neotropical streams receive inputs from the riparian forest, including tree branches, twigs, leaves and terrestrial invertebrates, which increase habitat complexity and supply food items to the fish fauna. We evaluated the effects of habitat structure on fish species composition in seven first to third order forest streams in the Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project Reserve (INPA/Smithsonian) near Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil. We sampled 20 meter stretches of each stream by underwater observation and collected specimens with hoopnets and seines. Sketches of each sampling site were made, mapping habitats and substrate type. Information on the trophic structure of fish assemblages was assessed by gut content analysis. We collected 333 fish specimens, belonging to seven families, 15 genera and 16 species. Habitat size and substrate type explained most of the fish distribution patterns found. The ichthyofauna occupied predominantly pools with litter banks and submerged roots, preferential habitat of Nannostomus marginatus and predominantly of Hyphessobrycon heteroharbdus and Aequidens pallidus. The most heterogeneous habitats held richer species assemblages and more abundant populations; on the other hand, stream order apparently imposes limits to the habitat's structural complexity, restricting the maximum number of fish species and individuals present at each location. First- and second-order streams trophic structures were based on allochtonous food sources whereas third order streams had a marked contribution of autochtonous items, which indicate different degrees of direct dependence on the riparian forest. Local habitat complexity and the spatial variation along the stream shape the distribution of fish species and individuals, resulting in different patterns of species associations and abundance in first, second and third order streams in Central Amazonia.

23458: I have studied the feeding behaviors of two species of caimans (Melanosuchus niger and Caiman crocodilus crocodilus) during the dry season in an oxbow lake area (Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve), in the Amazonas state in Brazil. 23460: Coral snakes in the genus Micrurus form a Neotropical radiation of the cosmopolitan front- fanged family Elapidae. The genus includes at least two distinct phylogenetic lineages. The species with black rings arranged in triads (BRT) form one monophyletic clade, while another clade includes species with black rings arranged singly (BRS). Data for the latter group indicate that the reproductive cycle is seasonal, with vitellogenesis, oviposition and hatching occurring in the rainy season. Apart from scattered and anedoctal reports on reproduction almost nothing has been published on the reproductive ecology of the species of Micrurus with BRT. This study provides information on reproductive cycles in BRT species and compares reproductive strategies present in these two phylogenetic lineages of genus Micrurus from southeastern Brazil. Information was obtained from the literature and dissection of 248 specimens of M. corallinus (BRS), M. frontalis and M. lemniscatus (BRT). It was possible to detect two reproductive patterns present in the two lineages of Micrurus. In species with BRS females attain larger body size and male-male combat is not expected. On the contrary, males of BRT species reach a larger body size than females and combat already has been reported in at least one species of this group. The two clades also differ in spermatogenic cycles, extension of follicular development, mating period and sperm storage. In species with BRS, females have a short period of vitellogenesis in spring and males have a testicular recrudescence peak in autumn. Thus, mating occurs early in the following spring, utilizing sperm stored over the winter in the male ductus deferens. In species with BRT the vitellogenesis starts before spring and mating occurs in the fall with females storing sperm until the ovulation in the spring. These two reproductive strategies may have arisen during relatively long time ago during divergence of these two phylogenetic lineages. [Funded by FAPESP].

23461: Plethodontid salamanders are generally considered to be poor dispersers and to be restricted to moist, forest habitats. We used two experimental approaches to study the ability of red-backed salamanders, Plethodon cinereus, to disperse through open fields in the Appalachian mountains of the southeastern United States. First, we displaced salamanders from forest edges into fields as well as further into the forest and recorded rates of return to the site of capture. Return rates decreased with displacement distance, but were virtually identical between fields and forests. Second, we created 'islands' of red-backed salamander habitat at different distances from forest edges. Red-backed salamanders colonized these plots within months, though abundance and time to colonization decreased with distance. Our results suggest that red-backed salamanders are actually quite adept at moving through open habitats, at least over the distances considered in our experiment. These dispersal abilities may help explain why red-backed salamanders appear relatively insensitive to some of the effects of forest fragmentation.

23462: Systematic biology rests on an extensive literature of theory and methodology of phylogenetic inference and species concepts but a relatively small literature on the methods of delimiting species. This appears to be changing, and some novel methods have recently been proposed for testing species boundaries. However, few studies have compared the use of several methods in one system. Empirical studies are needed to identify similarities and differences in methodologies (for example do certain methods consistently over/under split taxa, do some methods work well only with certain types of data, etc.), and what these might mean for delimiting species. In this study, we use chromosome and allozyme data from 687 lizards collected from 53 populations to test species boundaries across 8 chromosome races of the Sceloporus grammicus complex in central Mexico. Such a data rich system is uncommon in vertebrates, and the Sceloporus grammicus complex offers an excellent opportunity for comparing methods of species delimitation, and particularly how often different methods converge to the same conclusions about species boundaries. We employ 5 methods of species delimitation, including: population aggregation analysis (PAA), statistical PAA, field for recombination; multidimensional scaling, and genetic distance regression methods. Results of these methods are compared with each other, with preliminary nested-clade analysis based on mtDNA cyt-b sequences, and a consensus used to hypothesize species boundaries in this complex. Discordant results in the number of species recognized by these methods provides insight into both the complexity of the speciation process, and the danger of relying on a single criterion to delimit species.

23465: Stock enhancement is used world wide to boots fisheries and is an option to increase Colossoma abundance in the Amazon. It was never used there, but recently, Amazonian politicians are considering it in order to manage Colossoma populations and develop extensive aquaculture for small farmers. This study tested the effectiveness of stock enhancement in the Amazon floodplain lakes. Because most of the mortality in floodplain lakes is due to predation we also evaluate the main predator of tambaqui juveniles. The experiment was undertaken in 12 similar floodplain lakes (10-60ha) of which we stocked five with 5 cm Colossoma juveniles (1000 ha-1 – 1400 ha-1). The unstocked lakes were used as control. Abundance was measured by CPUE and mortality and emigration with mark and recapture techniques six and eighteen months after the stocking. Stocking increased significantly the abundance of Colossoma in experimental lakes, but mark- recapture experiments indicated that 43 to 80 seeds are needed to produce one six months old fish. We concluded that stock enhancement using 5 cm seeds does not seem to be economically feasible in the first year, but if mortality remains at the same level, cost can me amortized and the break-even price is reached in the second year. Stocking is profitable in the third year and cost ratio may reach 61%, which is higher than those reported ratios for intensively produced tambaqui. 23466: Brazil has a great diversity of ecosystems and about 10% of the world snake fauna are known to occur in them. 23468: The Neotropical genus Oxyrhopus includes 12 species of pseudoboini snakes that occur from southern Mexico to Argentina and Uruguay. 23469: In the past, cartilaginous fishes from the Argentinian shelf (34° to 55° S) were discarded, but currently they are actively exploited (due especially to the opening of new markets). We examined effort (fishing hours), catch (tons), and catch per unit of effort (CPUE, tons/fishing hours) from Argentinian official fishing statistics. From 1992 to 1998 the smallest fleet (up to 20 m length) landed chondrichthyans. Since 1994 a fleet of large boats (> 28 m length) increased its fishing pressure on chondrichthyans. Until 1994 chondrichthyan landings did not exceed 20000 tons per year. Since 1994, chondrichthyan landings exceeded 25000 tons annually in Argentinian ports. The landings peaked in 1998 with 35500 tons. This increase was due mainly to higher landings of skates (Rajidae) from 1994 onwards. From 1992 onwards a decrease in the landings of sharks (many species lumped together) was observed, while the landings of smoothhounds (mainly Mustelus schmitti) and angel sharks (Squatina spp.) were kept at 10000 and 4000 tons, respectively. The trend in CPUE was decreasing for all fleets. The maximum decrease was for the fleet > 28 m, with CPUEs of school sharks (Galeorhinus galeus), angel sharks, smoothhounds, and sharks falling more than 50%, and CPUE of skates falling by 36%, which clearly indicates a negative effect of fishing on abundance. An improvement in the catch statistics for all fisheries is needed for achieving accurate population assessment and effective management. Given that elasmobranchs are poorly known in Argentina, it is also important to carry out studies on ecology, life history and biology. In Argentina there are not management strategies for chondrichthyans, only maximum sustainable quotas are established for smoothhounds, angel sharks, skates and sharks. Taking into account the vulnerability of chondrichthyans, and the growing demand of chondrichthyan products from Argentina, a management strategy should be implemented as soon as possible.

23470: Aquatic adult graybelly salamanders, Eurycea multiplicata griseogaster, coexist in streams with a number of predatory fishes, including sculpin (Cottus sp.). Salamanders have been shown to respond to chemical cues from sculpin with antipredator behavior. We used an associative learning protocol to determine whether salamanders can learn to avoid habitat patches (rocks, grass) based on previous exposure to different levels of predation risk (predator, nonpredator) in each patch-type. Salamanders avoided habitat-types where they had previously been exposed to sculpin stimuli. They did not avoid habitat-types where they had previously experienced only nonpredatory stimuli (tadpole, blank). Graybelly salamanders can use information gained through experience with predators to avoid habitats where risk may be high.

23471: The monophyly of the genus Pituophis has been recognized on the basis of morphology and mtDNA sequences. Recent morphological and mtDNA studies have suggested that the Louisiana pine snake (P. ruthveni) is more closely related to the bullsnake (P. catenifer sayi) than to the pine snakes east of the Mississippi River (P. m. melanoleucus, lodingi, mugitus). Our mtDNA RFLP data generally corroborate the results of previous work using the mitochondrial genome. Nuclear ITS-1 sequences were used to clarify relationships among P. c. sayi, P. ruthveni, and the eastern pine snakes. Our ITS-1 phylogram has striking similarities to the one produced from the mtDNA RFLP data in that there is limited genetic differentiation within the eastern pine snakes, and like our mtDNA data, P. c. sayi and P. ruthveni show much greater diversity than is seen in all of the pine snake taxa east of the Mississippi River. These data indicate that the Mississippi River may have been an effective biogeographical barrier in this group of snakes.

23472: To date, most functional and morphological studies of shark feeding have concentrated on identifying correlations with the feeding mechanisms of coastal and benthic species relative to their ecology. Sandtiger sharks Carcharias taurus are the only species of the primarily pelagic order Lamniformes that have been successfully held in captivity, which provides an excellent opportunity to examine the feeding kinematics of a representative from this largely unstudied order. Carcharias taurus are thought to be opportunistic hunters feeding primarily on fish, squid, and small stingrays. Studying C. taurus allows us to compare and contrast its feeding mechanism and ecology with those of other elasmobranchs inhabiting coastal and benthic environments. Feeding events were filmed for five individuals using high-speed digital videography at SeaWorld Entertainment Park, Orlando over a four-month period in order to determine a general kinematic profile of prey capture. The most notable preliminary differences in the kinematic profile of C. taurus are the presence of cranial elevation an order of magnitude larger than and relatively greater upper jaw protrusion distances compared to other sharks. Cranial elevation added from 7 to 21 cm to maximum vertical gape distance. Protrusion included both an anterior and ventral component, which qualitatively differs from previous studies of jaw protrusion in sharks. Although significant differences were not found between individuals in the majority of timing variables, differences were found in duration of cranial elevation and total bite duration. As with other studies of lower vertebrate feeding, intraspecific differences apparently represent a significant source of variation. Extensive cranial elevation and upper jaw protrusion are thought to enhance the predatory ability of C. taurus by augmenting both vertical and horizontal components of its gape, thereby placing the jaws more in-line with the longitudinal axis of the body and allowing a more perpendicular occlusion of the teeth on prey items.

23473: Amazonian blackwaters are known for their acidity and low ion concentrations. This type of water may disturb ion regulation in fish, but species inhabiting Rio Negro blackwaters survive in this environment. We investigated branchial Na+ and Ca2+ transport in P. axelrodii (cardinal tetra), native to Amazonian blackwaters, and the role of humic substances in this process. Cardinals were acclimated in softwater similar to their natural environment ([Na]=30µM; [Ca]=10µM; pH6.5); some treatments also included addition of humic substances to simulate blackwater. Fish were submitted to four treatments for four weeks: control group (softwater, circumneutral pH), low pH (softwater, pH3.77), humic substances (softwater plus humic acid at 35mgC/L), and humic substances at low pH (softwater plus humic acid at 35mgC/L, pH3.77). Kinetic Na+ and Ca2+ uptake determinations were performed at varying ion concentrations (50- 1600 µM for Na+ and 10-320µM for Ca2+) and varying concentrations of the respective isotope (22Na at 0.5-16µCi/L and 45Ca at 1-32µCi/L). Maximum uptake rates (Jmax) and substrate affinity (Km) were estimated through Michaelis-Menten analysis. Na+ uptake rates in P. axelrodii were high in all treatments, with values ranging between 1,820 and 2,600nmol/g/h, and affinity for the transporter was likewise high, indicated by low Km values (60-70µM Na+). Humic substances stimulated higher Na+ uptake, even under low pH. Maximum transport rates for Ca2+ were similar for all treatments (~20nmol/g/h), except for the low pH treatment in the absence of humic substances (~7nmol/g/h). Ca2+ uptake was not affected by humic substances, although Km values indicated high affinity for the transporters when these organic compounds were present. Concluding, P. axelrodii is specialized regarding ion regulation, displaying high Na+ uptake rates and high affinity for Ca2+ transporters, supporting the view that ion uptake in fish inhabiting blackwaters saturates at very low concentrations. 23474: Urban air pollution reaches wilderness areas. Ozone in air pollution damages leaves of forest trees, but little is known of ozone effects on wildlife. In humans, ozone induces lung injury and inhibits exercise performance. Amphibians may be particularly sensitive to ozone, because the exposed skin surface is a moist respiratory gas exchange organ. We investigated ozone effects on exercise stamina and recovery in the marine toad, Bufo marinus. 1 h and 24 h following single or 7 daily 4 h exposures to 0.4 ppm ozone, toads were exercised to exhaustion on a circular track. The fastest lap and total time and distance traveled were recorded. Post-exercise, buccal pumping and lung breath frequencies were measured every 10 min for 1 h. Single ozone exposure had no effect on exercise performance before exhaustion. However, following exercise lung breath frequency in ozone exposed toads remained elevated longer than in control air exposed animals. 24 h post-exposure, ozone and control exposed toads had similar rates of breathing pattern recovery from exercise. In toads tested with exercise 24 h following 7 days of repeated 4 h exposures, recovery from elevated lung breath frequency was significantly longer than air exposed controls. Thus, single ozone exposure followed shortly by exhaustive exercise prolonged exercise recovery time, and in repeated daily exposure the effect was persistent with exercise the following day.

23475: Anemonefish (Family Pomacentridae) are known for their symbiotic associations with tropical sea anemones. In the northern Gulf of Aqaba, anemonefish (Amphiprion bicinctus) occur in widely dispersed isolated mated pairs, as single adults, or less often as haremic social groups. We compared the ecology of anemonefish in Eilat, Israel and in Aqaba, Jordan. These two study sites are on opposite sides of the upper Gulf of Aqaba approx. 5 miles apart. On average, each anemone in Eilat has less than 1 fish occupying it (mean = 0.7 fish, range 0-4). In Jordan, there are significantly more fish inhabiting each anemone (mean = 1.2 fish, range 0-6: p = 0.01). In fact, most of the anemonefish within the study site in Jordan occupy multiple anemones and live in social groups with two breeding adults along with 2 or more sub-adult/juveniles. In Israel, all fish/pairs within the study site occupy just one anemone. The anemonefish in Jordan are also significantly larger than the anemonefish in Israel (Jordan: mean = 70 mm, range 10-135 mm; Israel mean = 43 mm, range 10-105 mm; p = 0.0001). Additionally, both the numbers of anemones and anemonefish declined drastically from 1996 to 1999 in Eilat, but stayed relatively constant in Aqaba over a two-year period (1998-1999). Furthermore, fish swim significantly farther away from their host anemones in Jordan than they do in Israel (p = 0.001).

23476: Reptiles are an important part of the diet of Indigenous people living in the Brazilian Amazon region but little information is known about the impacts of subsistence hunting on the natural populations. This study quantifies the size structure and sex ratios of harvested populations of Paleosuchus trigonatus, P. palpebrosus, Caiman crocodilus, Geochelone denticulata and G. carbonaria in Amazonia during a 1523 hunting day period between September 1998 and March 2000 among the Waimiri Atroari Indians of central Amazonia. Reptiles represented 23% (1575) of the total Waimiri Atroari catch. G. denticulata was the most common reptile harvested (691) and adults were more frequently taken for both Geochelone species. Juveniles were most frequently hunted among the caiman species and sex ratio were skewed towards males. Tortoises were taken more than expected by their natural densities.

23477: In ectotherms, an increase in body temperature increases metabolic rate and may increase rates of digestive processes. We measured the thermal dependence of the digestive and assimilation efficiencies (DE and AE), gut passage time (GP) and appetite in Cordylus melanotus melanotus, a medium sized crag lizard endemic to South Africa. In an attempt to ascertain the effect that body temperature has on rates of energy gain, measurements were taken at 20, 22, 25, 30 and 32 °C under controlled conditions. Lizards were fed ca. 1 g of mealworms per day for 14 days. Glass beads were used as markers to determine GP and the beginning and end of trials. Faeces and urates were collected daily and oven dried at 50 °C. The energetic content of egested matter was measured by subjecting samples to bomb calorimetry. DE and AE were not affected by temperature (R2 < 0.40, P > 0.25 for males and females). The mean (± SE) DE and AE were 94.38 ± 0.31 % and 87.16 ± 0.60 % respectively. GP was not significantly different between males and females at any temperature (F9,85 = 1.39, P = 0.21), but decreased significantly with increasing temperature (R2 = 0.92, P < 0.01). Appetite was significantly different at the different temperatures (number: F9,90 = 9.53, P < 0.001; mass: F9,90 = 8.95, P < 0.001) and was maximum at 32 °C. Post hoc Tukey tests showed that there were no significant differences in appetite between genders at any temperature (P > 0.1 in all cases). The decrease in gut passage time with increasing temperature was not unexpected since the digestive and assimilation efficiencies are similar over the range of temperatures tested. Lizards are thus assimilating similar amounts of energy per gram of mealworms, but at faster rates at higher temperatures. Our results clearly indicate the thermal dependence of digestive processes in this species, which has important implications for the lizard's energy budget.
